en: Re-30718 – Āgama Text: Śivarātrividhi, Calaliṅgapratiṣṭhā, Mahotsavavidhi, Kriyākramadyotikā, Caryāpāda, etc.
Notes:
Words/letters within brackets are my suggestions (to the best of my understanding).
• Dots ... are used to indicate missing portions, leaf damage, or unidentified characters. • 119 folios. • Dimensions: 390 x 33 mm.
• Typically 05–07 lines per side;
p = control number for the folio (the "image");
f = the folio number as recorded by the scribe.

• l = line number (p.1) Title in the bundle frame: *Āgamagranthaḥ* – *Śivarātrividhiḥ* – *Calaliṅgapratiṣṭhā* – *Mahotsavavidhiḥ* – *Kriyākramadyotikā* – *Caryāpādaḥ*, etc. (p.2 bundle illustration; p.3a same title; p.3b) *Cillarai Āgamagranthavacanapustakaṃ* – *Sthapanavidhiḥ*. (p.4a blank; p.4b, *Haris Om*, *Śivarātrividhi*, l.1)
Now I shall describe in detail the sequence of rites for Śivarātri;
it may be performed in all months, but its performance in the month of Māgha is most highly praised.
In the pairs of the Kṛta and Tretā ages, as well as in the Dvāpara and Kali ages, one should worship the Lord of the Ages (*yugādhipa*) and then distribute [the offerings].
In the Tretā age, the Obstructor (*Vighnakṛt*) is to be worshipped; in the Dvāpara, one should sacrifice to Acyuta.
In the Kali age, Hari is worshipped by the Brahmins, the Indras, and the sages.
Śivarātri has been proclaimed; what is its distinction, O Lord?
This fourfold [system] has indeed been declared as the established tenet (*pakṣasiddhānta*).

Thus, one's own established doctrine (*pūrvasiddhānta*) is indeed the very position (*pakṣa*) that has been proven; likewise, the established doctrine of another (*parasiddhānta*) is also such. O lady of good vows, hear now the distinction between them.
In one month, however, one should observe the vow for two fortnights:
beginning from sunrise on the thirteenth day until sunset,
and beginning from sunset on the fourteenth day until sunrise.
That night shall be Śivarātri; it is considered the most excellent of the excellent.
This established conclusion regarding this position would be pleasing to me:
beginning from sunset, [the time] up to three watches on the fourteenth day.
If the remainder [of the lunar day] extends to the mountain [the next day], it is known as Śivarātri.
That night shall be Śivarātri; one should commence the worship of Śiva.
For this established doctrine indeed removes all defects.
Starting from sunset until twenty nāḍīs have passed.
If it is joined with a lunar node (parvan) afterwards, it shall not be defective;
that night shall be Śivarātri, and one should commence the worship of Śiva.
Thus, these established positions are indeed for the benefit of even the ignorant.
Beginning from the time of the lamp-lighting until fourteen [finger-breadths] less than twenty,
all those nights are declared to be such that no fault whatsoever exists.
That night shall be Śivarātri; one should commence the worship of Śiva.
For this very reason, the established doctrine of others brings welfare to all living beings;
it consists of two watches of the day, the night, and two watches of the transition between them.
The worship of Śiva must not be performed, for it would cause all manner of faults.
It is taught that [Śiva] is to be worshipped during the four watches of the night.
And here, during the first watch, [the ritual proceeds] from the door up to the consecration with mantras.
Having completed the daily worship, one should then commence the evening protection ritual.

At the end of that, having consecrated the Lord of the Gods of gods with the ritual ending in the bathing with products of the cow (*gavya*) and so forth, and having worshipped him together with the fivefold enclosure (*pañcāvaraṇa*).
Offering the food offering known as *nitya* and *naimittaka*,
one should perform all rites such as the fire-oblation (*homa*) and the bali-offering exactly as before.
During the second watch of the night, one should perform a single meditation accompanied by worship;
then the special sacrifice (*viśeṣayajana*) should be performed, followed by the veneration of the seat of enjoyment (*bhogasthāna*).
Having returned at that very moment, one should then place the deity upon a palanquin (*śibikā*).
Having performed the conjunction with the primary liṅga, one should perform the worship during the third watch of the night.
Having performed the ritual according to the rule in the fourth [period],
one should again perform the sacrifice at the time of sunrise.
At every watch, one should worship Caṇḍeśa and Kṣetrapāla.

On the night preceding that day, the best of preceptors should perform the consecration (*adhivāsa*) of the *ba*[-leaf]. Following the very sequence of the consecration, the supreme teacher should carry out [the rite].
One should first worship Vighneśa, and after that, the worship of the Sun.
First, the ritual bathing is prescribed; it should consist of one hundred and eight [offerings].
In the first watch of the day, there should be the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), bilva leaves, and rice cooked with mung beans.
The second ablution is proclaimed... there should be six jars.
In the second [ablution], there should be the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), a lotus, and milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
In the third [rite], there is indeed a ceremonial bathing with twenty-five [substances];
one should offer *kṛsarānna* mixed with honey...
[the bathing, however, should be performed] with sixteen [substances].
Likewise, one should offer sugarcane essence, the *nandyāvarta* design, and sweetmeats.
One should worship [the deity] at each watch with five *bilva* fruits,
followed by milk, curd, ghee, and coconut water in sequence.
One should bathe the Supreme Lord with flavorful substances and other offerings;
one should worship Him with variegated... and all kinds of flowers. One should offer pure food accompanied by side dishes at every watch of the day.
One should especially perform the bali-homa at every watch of the day.
The determination of the lunar day (*tithi*) is now declared:
when the thirteenth solar mansion (*nakṣatra*) is completed within exactly four *nāḍīs*.

But she who is pierced by the [correct] lunar day (*bhūtaviddhā*)— one should observe the Śivarātrivrata on that [night]. Since the vigil is to be performed at night, one should properly nourish that fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*) which extends through the evening (*pradoṣa*).
Where the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha coincides with midnight.
In that Śivarātri vow,
[the merit] would be such where, on the thirteenth day, the great night is pervaded by spirits.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, one should perform the Śivarātri vow and likewise keep a vigil there at the primordial [shrine].
...likewise, one who observes the vow with the *liṅga*:
on that occasion, Śivarātri should be observed during the time when [the moon] possesses the splendor of ten million suns.
Where the fourteenth lunar day is joined with [the fifteenth] at midnight and remains so thereafter,
on that lunar day one should perform the Śivarātri vow. Where the fourteenth lunar day is joined with [the fifteenth] and remains so thereafter...
One should certainly not perform a vow there, as it causes the loss of longevity and sovereignty.

If the fourteenth day is seen to extend from the previous day into the night of the following day, then, because it is encompassed by the neighboring [days], the offering is indeed made. However, at the time of the ritual,
that fourteenth day which is fully encompassed should be accepted.

Beyond that... endowed with prosperity... the ritual should always be performed. Whether it falls on the new moon day, or even on the thirteenth, or the fourteenth—the night is remembered as Śivarātri.

If the [moon] has reached its full extent on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one should observe the vow during both nights if they are equal; otherwise, one should perform the vow during the latter night.
"A merit equal to Śivarātri has never existed before, nor will it ever exist again.
Thus [ends] the chapter on Śiva... in the Svāyambhuva [Tantra].
(Mudrās—)
The trident-makara, the blood-spoon-yoni,
the Kālakaṇṭhī mudrā, and likewise the five-faced mudrā.
One should form the lotus, the cow-seal (*dhenumudrā*), the arrow-seal (*nārācamudrā*), ... [the] necklace, the image-seal (*bimbamudrā*), and the great seal (*mahāmudrā*).
One should place the terrifying one, the jar-seal (*kumbhamudrā*), the goad (*aṅkuśa*), and the *vipsu* (?).

One should contemplate the emergence, the divine mudrā, and silence. One should perform the invocation, the installation, and the presence; that which is called the confinement should be performed, while one should remain detached from the sacrificial pit.
The snap of the fingers, the conch-liṅga, the prostration, and likewise the *manorathapatākā*... [p.7a blank] ...[p.7b, *Dvārapratiṣṭhāvidhiḥ*,
l.1] Now follows the ritual procedure for the consecration of the door (*dvārapratiṣṭhāvidhi*).

Having performed in the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) the ritual beginning with the worship of the doors and ending with the libation of mantras (*mantratarpaṇa*), and having bathed the door-frames (*dvārāṅga*) with astringent decoctions (*kaṣāya*) and other substances, and having clothed them in jeweled garments, one should place upon the bed Brahmā—the *māyātattva* ending with [the principle of] Ātman—at the lower *udumbara* beam; Sadāśiva—the *vidyātattva*—upon the two side-beams; and Viṣṇu—the *śivatattva* ending with Śakti—together with Rudra, upon the upper *udumbara* beam. Having performed the worship and having installed the forms (*mūrti*) and the lords of the forms (*mūrtīśvara*), one should perform the rite of purification (*saṃskāra*) and effect the confinement (*nirudhya*).

Having performed protection by means of three enclosures made of ash, *darbha* grass, and sesame seeds; having gone near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*); having worshipped the principles (*tattva*) and the lords of the principles (*tattveśvara*) as before; having gratified them with three oblations (*āhuti*); having offered the *saṃhitā-mantras*; and having sprinkled [the area] with water from the jar of peace obtained through a hundred recitations of the weapon-mantra (*astra*); having touched the respective parts with the roots, middles, and tips of *kuśa* grass; having recited [the mantras] in sequence according to the number of oblations; and having purified [them]; one should worship *Vāstu* at the entrance.

Having performed the offering of each individual oblation with the *nasta* mantra, having placed the five [substances] beginning with jewels, and having provided a seat with the *praṇava*, one should place a small portion at the door leaning toward the northeast with the *praṇava*. Then, having made a bundle (*poṭala*) of these: barley, white mustard, *krāntā*, *ṛddhi*, *vṛddhi*, sesame seeds, as well as *gomūda*, *dūra*, *goṇḍa*, *mohi*, sesame husks, *muda*, *rocanā*, *āragvadha*, and the preceding [items].

Having tied [the vessel] with a cloth for protection at the top of the *udumbara* wood—and likewise having offered seven oblations with a steady flame—having placed the three principles beginning with the Self (*ātmatattva*) as before in their respective parts within that fire, and having placed Nandin and Mahākāla on the two branches, Gaṅgā and Yamunā at the top of the *udumbara*, and Gaṇeśa, Sarasvatī, and Śrī; having restrained them by the command of Śiva, having offered one hundred or fifty oblations with each of their own names, and having offered one hundred oblations with the *astra-mantra* for the sake of expiation, [one should offer] the *bali*.
Having performed the sacrifice, he should dismiss [the deities] and honor the Guru with gifts of gold, clothing, and food; such is the ritual procedure for the consecration of the gateway.

Having first performed the ritual of satisfying the mantra in the eastern lotus-pavilion, and having bathed both the golden male figure and the pitcher, anointed them with sandalwood paste, covered them with cloths, and placed them upon a bed above the altar, one should meditate on the pitcher—which contains the five [substances] such as gems and consists of honey and milk—as the embodied form [of the deity]. One should contemplate the pitcher and the male figure as the *pralayākala*, joined with palms pressed together in reverence (*añjali*), wearing a crown and adorned with serpents.

Having brought [the breath] from the *dvādaśānta* and meditated upon it as "the awakener of the word of Śiva’s command," one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) with the exhalation (*recaka*), saying: "Oṃ hāṃ hā hām! O Self, by the command of Śiva, you must remain here in this body. Then one should place the deity of the day: "Salutation to Kalā. Salutation to the Lord of Kalā, the Point of Knowledge (*jñānabindu*). Perform, perform the pervasion of agency for the Lord of Kalā. Salutation to the principle of Vidyā (*vidyātattva*)."

Homage to the Sovereign of the Principle of Knowledge (*vidyātattva*), for the sake of discernment. O Knowledge, manifest [your power]! Manifest! Homage to the Principle of Passion (*rāgatattva*). Homage to the Sovereign of the Principle of Passion, the Bestower of Desire. O Passion, cause attachment to the sense objects! Cause attachment! Homage to the Principle of Time (*kālatattva*). Homage to the Sovereign of the Principle of Time, named Kāla. O Sovereign of Time, impel within his [the practitioner’s] constituent parts! Homage to the Principle of Necessity (*niyatitattva*).

Homage to the Lord of Niyati, the Restrainer. O Lord of Niyati, bring about the enjoyment for [me], bring it about! Homage to the Principle of Puruṣa. Homage to the Lord of the Principle of Puruṣa, the Subtle Body. O Lord of Puruṣa, bring about enjoyment within the subtle body, bring it about! [Homage] to Prakṛti. Homage to the Lord of Prakṛti, the Pradhāna Body. O Lord of Prakṛti, fulfill the office of authority, fulfill it! Homage to the Principle of Guṇa. Homage to the Lord of the Principle of Guṇa, the Gross Body.

O Sovereign of the *guṇa*-principles, perform, perform the act of impelling! To the intellect (*buddhi*); to the Lord of the intellect, to the Awakened One (*buddha*), obeisance! To the object of awakening for the Lord of the intellect, obeisance! Perform, perform the form of determination! To the Lord of ego (*ahaṅkāra*), to the Ego-maker (*ahaṅkṛta*), obeisance! Perform, perform the act of self-conceit for the Lord of ego! To the mind (*manas*), obeisance! To the Lord of the mind, to volition (*saṅkalpa*), obeisance! Perform, perform the act of volition for the Lord of the mind! To the two ears, obeisance!

Homage to the Lord of the Ear, who moves through space! O Lord of the Ear, perform, perform the grasping of sound for this [being]! Homage to the Skin! Homage to the Lord of the Skin, Saṅkalpa! Homage to the Lord of the Mind, the Sovereign of Śarva! O Lord of the Skin... perform, perform the grasping of touch! To the two Eyes! Homage to the Lord of the Eye, Prakāśa! O Lord of the Eye, perform, perform the grasping of form for this [being]! To the Tongue!

Homage to the Great-Faced One (*Mahāvaktra*), the sovereign of the tongue-principle. O sovereign of the tongue, perform, perform the act of perceiving taste! Homage to the Nose, homage to Vilambaka, the sovereign of the nose. O sovereign of the nose, perform, perform the act of perceiving fragrance... Homage to Speech, homage to Dundubhi, the lord of speech. O sovereign of speech, perform, perform the act of requesting! Homage to the two hands; homage to Sāmadā, the sovereign of the hands.

(1.6) O you who preside over the hand, perform the grasping of half the foot; *kuru kuru*. Homage to the one who presides over the foot, the Delighter (*ramaṇa*). O you who preside over the mind, perform the instigation of the mind; *kuru kuru*. Homage to the one who presides over the path of the feet, the Lord of the Path, the Swift-Acting (*tūrṇakṛta*). Homage to the one who presides over the subtle sound, the Subtle Resonance (*sūkṣmanāda*). O you who preside over sound, perform the filling of space; *kuru kuru*. Homage to Touch (*sparśa*). Homage to the one who presides over touch, the Most Powerful (*balavattara*).

O Lord of Touch, perform the filling of wind, perform it! Homage to Form! Homage to Bhānumat, the Lord of Form! O Lord of Form, perform the filling of fire, perform it! Homage to Taste! Homage to Jalada, the Lord of Taste! O Lord of Taste, perform the filling of taste, perform it! Homage to Scent! Homage to Gandhāṅga, the Lord of Scent! O Lord of Scent, perform the filling of earth, perform it! Homage to Space!

Homage to the subtle one, the lord of space (*ākāśa*). O lord of space, grant me space, grant it! (l. 4) Homage to Vāyu, the lord of wind, Mātariśvan. O lord of wind, perform the act of moving, perform it! Homage to Agni. Homage to the lord of fire, the repository of splendors. O lord of fire, perform the act of cooking, perform it! Homage to Water. Homage to the lord of water, the master of waters. O lord of water, perform the gathering of flavors, perform it! To Earth.

Salutation to Śrīkaṇṭha, the lord of the earth. (l. 6) Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the mantra, "O Earth and Water, perform the support for this [body], perform it," one should place the ten channels (*nāḍī*) and the ten winds (*vāyu*). Salutation to Iḍā. Salutation to Puṅgalā. Salutation to Suṣumnā. (p. 10a, l. 1) To Gāndhārī. To Śaṅkhinī. Salutation to Kuhū. Salutation to Yaśasvinī. Salutation to Pūṣā. Salutation to Ahnanyā. Salutation to Jihvā. Salutation to Pūṣā. Salutation to Prāṇa.

Salutation to Apāna. Salutation to Vyāna. Salutation to Udāna. Salutation to Samāna. Salutation to Nāga. Salutation to Kūrma. Salutation to Krakara. Salutation to Devadatta. Salutation to Dhanañjaya. Thus, Māyā, by virtue of filling [the body] with her own transformations, is the regulator of time; having performed the placement of the Blessed One as the impeller and the pervader, together with the mantras beginning with Aṅguṣṭhamātra, through her being the means of accomplishing one's own [purpose].

Having enclosed the *ātmatattva*, *vidyātattva*, and *śivatattva*—extending to the limits of the seat of *māyā*—and having performed the protection with *darbha* grass, sesame seeds, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) using the *astra-mantra*; having worshipped the *ādhāraśakti* in the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) and offered libations; having worshipped the sequence of principles (*tattva*) beginning with *kalā* as before and offered three oblations (*āhuti*) to satisfy them; and having performed the *saṃhitā-homa*, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) according to the number of oblations and cause oneself to hear [the mantra].

"By the command of Śiva, you must remain here until the completion of the Prāsāda, serving as the foundation for the principles beginning with *kalā*. By this path, one should arrest the stream [of consciousness]. This has been stated for the purpose of making known its specific location. O Umā, the pedestal (*āsana*) of this temple (*dhāman*) is considered its foot; the *prastara* is its hip. From the foot, the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is desired [as the next part].
The *prastara* is the heart of the other [part]; the altar (*vedi*) is the shoulder, and the neck is the throat.
The head is the head, the crest-lock (*śikhā*), and the top-knot (*cūlī*); thus, this temple possesses a body.

Above the Śukanāsa, on the eastern altar within the interior of the wall, one should place a water-pot (kumbha) at the heart-lotus with the Heart-mantra and seal it. Then, having gone near the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should offer oblations with the Astra-mantra for the sake of expiation and dismiss the sacrifice. Thereafter, the performer should give the teacher a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of three-quarters of the original amount. Now follows the consecration of the pinnacle (cūlikā-pratiṣṭhā).

As before, having performed the ritual up to the propitiation of the mantra for the worship of the Sun-gatekeeper (*sūryadvārapāla*), one should bathe the *cūlikā* joined with the feet of the Fire-god (*śikhin*), bring it to the pavilion for the consecration of the fire (*agnivāsana-maṇḍapa*), and place it upon the bed with its head toward the east. Then, in the circular portion, one should install Rudra of the Śiva-principle ending with Śakti; in the eight-petaled [lotus], Viṣṇu of the Vidyā-principle ending with Sadāśiva; and in the square, Brahmā of the Ātman-principle ending with Māyā.

Having sequentially deposited the forms beginning with Earth (*kṣmādi-mūrti*) and the lords of the forms beginning with Śarva (*śarvādi-mūrtīśa*) in each section, and having performed the confinement (*nirudhya*), one should perform everything as before in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), preceded by the deposition of power (*śakti-nyāsa*), taking up [the materials] for each part, meditating, and reciting mantras. (l. 2) Now follows the procedure for the consecration of the spire (*stūpi-pratiṣṭhā-vidhi*).

In the temple where the ritual bathing has been performed, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) according to the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*), part by part: the *śivatattva* and Rudra from the top of the ears to the end of the crest; Viṣṇu and the *vidyātattva* up to Sadāśiva in the neck; and Brahmā and *māyā* in the shank, as before. Having performed the placement of the forms (*mūrti*) and the lords of the forms (*mūrtīśa*), and having taken [the image], gone [to the bathing place], and recited [mantras]—one should perform everything as before. Then, having placed the five [substances] beginning with gems upon the support of the crest with the root mantra (*mūla*), one should install the crest.

At that time, having filled individual jars with seasonal fruits—one coconut, two oranges, as well as pomegranate, *likuca*, plantain, and ripe jackfruit—one should perform the bathing of the temple (*prāsāda-snāna*) with them. Then, having bathed the staff (*daṇḍa*), having sprinkled the banner (*dhvaja*) with the Weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*), and having enveloped it with the Armor-mantra (*kavaca-mantra*), one should place it upon the northern altar (*uttara-vedikā*) of the temple.

As before, having performed the emanation and placement (*nyāsa*) of the principle of the Self-knowledge (*ātmavidyātattva*) in both [the staff and the banner], the principle of Śiva together with the Lord (*seśvara-śivatattva*), and the embodied forms and their presiding deities (*mūrti-mūrtīśān*), and having restrained [them], performed the fire-oblation (*homa*), proceeded [to the site], touched [them], recited the mantra (*japya*), and purified everything as before; then, having placed Śiva in the staff and the undifferentiated Śiva (*niṣkala-śiva*) along with his limbs (*aṅga*) upon the entire banner, and having provided the sixfold seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*) on the support for the banner-staff and placed the Support-Energy (*ādhāraśakti*).

Having installed the *Daṇḍa* which has become incarnate (*mūrtibhūta*), one should worship the *Aghora-astra*. Thereafter, having joined the banner (*dhvaja*), one should fully worship the *Pāśupata-astra* there. Having offered perfumes and other offerings with the *Vidyāṅga-mantras*, and having prostrated, one should meditate upon the temple as the totality of all principles (*sarvatattva*).
Then, having visualized Ananta and Kālarudra at the lotus-feet, [one should visualize] Kūśmāṇḍa and Hāḍaka on the pedestal (*pīṭha*) together with the subterranean hells (*pātāla-naraka*).
Having meditated upon the world-realms, the guardians of the worlds, the hundred Rudras, and so forth,
as the Egg of Brahmā, one should contemplate it within the shank.
Endowed with the five elements— water, fire, wind, and space— and the eightfold [set],
it is known as the "womb-enclosure" (*garbhāvaraṇa*). It is joined with the intellect (*buddhi*) and the eightfold womb (*yonyaṣṭaka*),
and is associated with the three qualities (*guṇa*) through the method of the nose (*nāsāvidhi*).
One should contemplate the person situated within the jar as being in a lion and in a bull.

On the mañjarī and the vedikā, one should place the four [deities] beginning with Vidyā; on the neck, Māyā together with Rudra; and on the amaladhāraka, Vidyā. In the kalaśa, one should place Īśvara, accompanied by Bindu and Vidyeśvara.
One should know that the matted locks and the crest are the site in the form of a half-moon.
And having contemplated the triple power (*śaktitraya*) within that very staff as sound (*nāda*),
one should contemplate the power of Kuṇḍalinī in the banner as it runs.

Having meditated thus: "Just as [one joins] the *liṅga* and the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) by joining their bases," and having performed the placement (*vinyāsa*) of Śiva as the all-pervading one, he should go near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Having performed the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) with Śiva’s Aghora-weapon mantra, as well as the recitation (*japa*) and the fire-oblation (*homa*), he should dismiss the sacrifice. He should feed the Guru; the performer [should honor him] with gifts of gold, clothing, and food.
Now, the procedure for the restoration of a dilapidated [shrine] (*jīrṇoddhāra*):

Having constructed a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) outside the temple in the northeast or at the exit, and having performed there the rites beginning with the worship of the door-gods (*dvārapūjā*) up to the offering of libations (*tarpaṇa*) on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), one should worship the deities of the site (*vāstudeva*) and offer three oblations. Then, having offered a thousand oblations with the *aghora-astra* mantra for the purpose of causing the movement of the *liṅga*, one should present the directional offerings (*digbali*) outside, perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and effect the ritual integration of the self (*sakalīkaraṇa*). [One should then ensure] the satisfaction of those possessing the *liṅga* through food and other provisions...

The assistant, having entered within, should inform Śiva: "O Lord, this is a sign corrupted by defects. May there be the power for its extraction—such is Your word. Therefore, O Maheśvara, empower me here according to the ritual. Having thus petitioned him, [he should say]: "Come, come, O Vyāpakeśvara! *Hṛdayāya namaḥ*! *Vyāpakeśvara-śirase svāhā*! *Vyāpakeśvara-śikhāyai vauṣaṭ*! *Vyāpakeśvara-kavacāya huṃ*!"

*Vauṣaṭ* to the eyes of Vyāpakeśvara; *phaṭ* to the weapon (*astra*) of Vyāpakeśvara. Having thus worshipped the limbs together, one should cause the being residing within the *liṅga* to hear these words: “Whoever you may be... whoever resides taking refuge in the *liṅga*, leave the *liṅga* and go wherever food is available, known by Śiva. Accompanied by the Vidyās and Vidyēśvaras, Śambhu will not consume the ignorant. Having spoken thus and offered the *arghya* with the *astra-mantra*, one should dismiss [the deity].

Then, having offered a hundred or a thousand oblations for each portion with the *pāśupatāstra* mantra, having sprinkled [them] with water of pacification (*śāntyambu*), touched them with *kuśa* grass, recited [the mantras], and offered the *arghya* in reverse order, one should dismiss the principles (*tattva*) and their lords (*tattveśvara*), as well as the forms (*mūrti*) and their lords (*mūrtīśa*). Having also dismissed the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) residing in the pedestal (*pīṭha*), the mantras of the three parts of the *liṅga*, and the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*), one should perform the dismissal.

Having dismissed that Caṇḍeśa with the *astra-mantra* and having dug [the site] with a spade, one should fix the liṅga, the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*), and the *brahmaśilā*—which are circular like a burning flame and bound with golden cords and so forth—upon the shoulder of a bull. Saying "May there be Śiva," and taking [the bull] along with the people, one should go outside and cast it into deep water. Then, for the sake of the deities, one should offer a hundred oblations of *dūrvā* grass mixed with the three sweets (*trimadhu*). For the satisfaction of the guardians of the directions, one should offer oblations with the mantras of the respective lords of those directions.

Having offered a hundred oblations with the *astra-mantra* for the sake of purifying the site (*vāstu*) of the temple, one should protect the temple with the *pāśupatāstra*. Therein, having prepared the *liṅga* and other objects according to the established measurements as before, one should install them. This very same procedure is to be performed when restoring a dilapidated shrine. Having assigned the groups of mantras to the sword (*khaḍga*), one should have another temple constructed. One should worship from Śambara until the completion of the shrine, and together with the sword, one should perform the protection of the *liṅga*, carrying it out according to the previous measurement.
If it is contracted, it is said that there will be loss of wealth; however, one should have it made according to those proportions using excellent materials.
Now, regarding the consecration of the Self-born [Svāyambhuva] and others—in the consecration of the Self-born and so forth, there is indeed the prescribed recollection of the pedestal alone.
As before, one should perform the oblation and other rites for the multitude of forms of the Lords of the Principles and the Principles themselves.
Because the deity is [manifest] by its own nature, bathing and other rites are prescribed for it.
For the sake of peace, one should perform the Saṃhitā-nyāsa, worship, and the fivefold Haṃsa-vidyā.
Since the Svāyambhuva-Kabāṇa-liṅga was consecrated there by the gods in the past,
one should not carve a mark upon it, nor should there be any such arrangement as [the assignment of] the directions starting with the north.
There is no movement here for the sake of enjoyment and so forth, nor is there a fourth [direction] in the arrangement of Caṇḍa.
The proximity of the arising consciousness should be established as a refinement, like that of a *bāṇaliṅga*.
Or a self-manifested (*svayambhu*) or Bāṇa liṅga grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation to all;
the fruit from its installation and worship is a thousandfold greater than that of others.

This procedure for installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) has been declared; now the consecration (*sthāpana*) is described. [It concerns] the well-proportioned and the ill-proportioned [lingas], which grant all accomplishments to men.
In the case of a mobile linga on a separate pedestal, [the rite is performed] with five or three [types of] devotees.
One should place two parts or one part in the pit for the pedestal (*piṇḍikāvaṭa*).

One should place half of that on the seat (*pīṭha*) and perform [the rite] according to the scriptures. The width of the pedestal should be equal to the circumference of the *liṅga*, and its height should be five times that width.
Then, half the width [of the hall], extending as far as the *gomukha* (cow-mouth) and reaching the neck and throat;
therein, one-third for the *āśābhava* (direction-born) and two-thirds for the *svaśambara* (self-restraint).

As before, when the arrow has been consecrated and the well-consecrated seat is mobile, one should sequentially deposit the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) and the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), and so forth, as previously described. Thus, the installation (*sthāpana*) has been explained; now the stabilization (*sthitisthāpana*) is being discussed.
Regarding the installation of a mobile liṅga—
whether it be a mobile liṅga together with its pedestal, or [the installation] of a commentary and so forth—
the entire procedure is as before; however, in this case, [there is a distinction] regarding the liṅga and the piṇḍikā.
Because there is no distinction [between the two], the consecration (*saṃskṛti*) should be performed either in the pavilion or in the house;
one should mentally conceive the placement of certain elements, such as the precious *brahma-śilā* and the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*).
One should also mentally arrange the joining of the pedestal.
Even when it moves, the consecration is as before, as it is for the Bāṇaliṅga and the Rohaka.
One should bring the width of the top of the liṅga to be equal to the portion for worship;
one should not make it three times the height, nor should one forget the measurement of the base (vakrapīṭha).
One should fashion the height of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) at twice the measure of the [base] width;
it may be circular or square, and provided with a neck (*kaṇṭha*) in the middle.
One should make the circumference of the neck twice the diameter of the *liṅga*.
The wise man should make that [pedestal] high as well, twice the height of the linga.
One should make the water-channel equal in length to the liṅga, located on the exterior of the pedestal;
whether in a pavilion, or in a house, or wherever those pedestals are situated.
The rule for the installation of the *sthirabāṇa* and other [liṅgas] mentioned previously is also remembered here.
Whether it be made of metal or of gemstone, or even otherwise— [that is], of a different origin (*viyoni*)—
he who would install a fixed (*sthira*) liṅga, whether it be made of metal, gemstone, or human [material], [should do so according to this rule].
And because of the abundance of application and yoga, it is indeed called action (kriyā).

In the previously mentioned pavilion, or in a house or other such place, one should perform the installation of the *liṅga* together with its pedestal and *bali* offerings in the initiation pavilion (*dīkṣā-maṇṭapa*). There, having bathed the *liṅga* and its pedestal with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth as before, having smeared them with sandalwood paste and other unguents, and having placed it upon the pedestal and so forth—one should worship a *bāṇaliṅga* preceded by the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the *samhitā* mantras, and offer a thousand or half that number of oblations (*homa*). In the case of a *liṅga* grown from a tree or found at a river confluence, one should perform the ritual placement of the vital breath (*jīvanyāsa*).

One should perform the *saṃhitā-nyāsa* and the fire-oblation (*homa*). Alternatively, because the *jīva-nyāsa* is preceded by the *tattva-tattveśādi-nyāsa*, one should proceed as before: having performed the placement of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) together with their presiding deities—the principles of Śiva, Vidyā, and Ātman—and Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā; and having placed in the directions starting from the west the forms known as Earth, Water, Fire, Air, and Ether, along with their respective goddesses named Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Kriyā, Jñānī, and Icchā. [Then recite: *Oṃ hrīṃ namaḥ to Kriyāśakti*.

Thus, having performed the *jīvanyāsa* upon the body [of the image], having protected it as before, having offered oblations (*huta*), having recited mantras (*japta*), and having completed everything, one should assign the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) to the *liṅga* and the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) to the pedestal (*pīṭha*). Then, at the auspicious moment, having performed the insertion of the gems and other materials into the *brahmaśilā*, and the joining of the *piṇḍikā*, one should effect the union of the vulva and the phallus (*bhagaliṅgasamāyoga*) between the pedestal and the *liṅga* by means of the *śakti* and *śiva* mantras.

Having assigned the seat-mantras beginning with Ādhāraśakti and ending with Śakti upon the pedestal (*pīṭha*), and having assigned the form (*mūrti*), the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*), and the eye (*netra*) upon the *liṅga*, one should invoke [the deity] with the root mantra as before, worship up to the end of the recitation (*japa*) with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), and bestow the name "Amukeśvara. Having requested, "May there be presence here from the moon up to the stars," and having prostrated, one should offer sesame seeds and milk-rice (*pāyasa*) separately a hundred times each with both the root mantra and the *umāmantra*.

For the sake of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), one should offer a hundred oblations together with a full [additional] oblation using the root mantra (*mūla*). Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) that "I shall worship [the deity] for as long as I live," and having performed the worship of the Guru, one should worship daily as previously described. Now, the procedure for the worship of the ephemeral linga (*kṣaṇikaliga*):

having purified the lingas produced from clay, ashes, *kuśa* grass, flour-paste, sugar-candy, and so forth—which are intended for that specific occasion—by means of sprinkling and consecration (*abhimantraṇa*), one obtains worldly results through daily worship according to the rule. At the end of the year, one should dismiss [the deity] and cause [the linga] to flow away.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the consecration of painted liṅgas and the like: one should perform the ceremonial bath of cloth paintings, books, and drawings in a mirror.
For the installation of written and painted images, purification is achieved through meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*).
In the mantra for opening the eyes, one should perform the ritual arrangement of the eight seats and so forth;
because they are located below and are not touched, the worship is performed with *nimbū* flowers.
The incantation with smoke causes no harm; [the installation] of stone, jewels, and so forth is mental.
What was called *sthitasthāpana* is now followed by the description of *āsthāpana*.
Even for manifest images, the previously mentioned procedure applies, with the exception of Caṇḍeśvara.
The first, beginning with the tortoise, and that which begins with the jewel and so forth—these five have been described by me.
One should cast it into the pit of the pedestal, excluding the *brahmaśilā*.
When the interior has been divided by six, having set aside one part from behind,
this five-part installation [is performed] if [the area] is divided by eight.
The installation in the seventh part brings happiness to the images.

(l.4) Having performed the ritual in the pavilion as before, up to the satisfaction of the mantra, having bathed the Goddess with clay and other substances as before, having performed the opening of the eyes, having bathed her again, having placed her upon the bed, having set down the sleep-vessel (nidrākumbha), having worshipped her, and having provided everything from the food offering (naivedya) to the household utensils, one should stand at the feet [of the image] and perform the placement (vinyāsa) of the principles beginning with Earth and ending with Śakti, together with their presiding deities. (ll.5–6)

Having placed a flower-garland and *pratisara* at the knees and the throat for the purpose of visualizing the three sections (*trikhaṇḍa*), one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: above the throat, the *śivatattva*, from the power of will (*icchāśakti*) up to the end of *śakti*; above the knees, the *vidyātattva*, from the knower (*jñānin*) up to *sadāśiva*; and below the knees, the *ātmatattva*, from the earth element up to *māyā*, along with the power of action (*kriyāśakti*). The three sections consist of earth, fire, the sacrificer, water, air, and space.

One should meditate upon Dhātrī as being divine, extremely fierce, lunar, conscious, and preeminent in strength, and install her. Alternatively, having installed Ākāśamūrti reaching to the forehead, Vāyumūrti reaching to the heart, Agnimūrti reaching to the knees, Jalamūrti reaching to the knees, and Pṛthvīmūrti reaching to the feet—namely Jyeṣṭhā and Vāmā—one should install the three principles (*tritattva*) along with Īśvarī, extending from the knees, throat, and head respectively.

*Oṃ hrīṃ sauṃ ma... gau...* (l. 4). By this [phrase] "beloved of Rudra" (*rudradayitā*), or else, the first of the *ka*-group [consonants] with the vowels, the *raudra* [syllable], the fourth [vowel], and that which is designated by the vowels within the pervasive [mantra]; the first word consists of the ninth *māyā* syllable, according to the sequence. [Then there is] the *nāda*, the sibilant (*ūṣman*), the triad beginning with *haṅkā*, and the *prāṇa* together with the pervasive [element]. "That which partakes of *māyā*" is the end. The middle of the word, the beginning, and the one made by *śeka*; and in the middle of the sibilant (*ūṣman*) and in the *sparśa* [consonant], the first from there... (l. 5).

Having performed the *jīvanyāsa* with the formula "The seed-syllable of Māyā is the Great Mantra, pervading the number of the planets," and having visualized the three enclosures with sesame seeds, *darbha* grass, and so forth; having placed upon the pedestal *māyā*, *śuddhavidyā*, and the three principles (*tattva*) situated within the triple-section (*trikhaṇḍa*) up to the region [of Īśvara] together with the *Īśvarīs*; and having performed the placement with "Oṃ Raṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Kriyāśakti," one should meditate. Then, having offered libations as before with the collections of mantras, one should proceed.

Having gone near the Goddess and touched her, and having likewise installed the *ādhāra-śakti* in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should mutter the mantras of the principles (*tattva*) and their lords (*tattveśvara*), as well as the forms (*mūrti*) and their presiding deities (*mūrtīśvarī*). Having performed the union (*sandhāna*) and divided everything into sections as before, one should enter the womb at an auspicious moment (*sulagna*), having first examined the center. Then, having installed the pedestal (*pīṭhikā*) with the mantra "Oṃ Sauṃ, obeisance to Kriyā-śakti," one should install the five [substances] beginning with jewels (*ratna*) therein.

Having worshipped the seat with the *aindrāgna* and other mantras beginning with *dhiti*, one should place the image of Gaurī there according to the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) ending with the *śakti*, and perform the *śrīkaṇṭha-nyāsa*. Then, [reciting] "Oṃ sauṃ, obeisance to Kriyāśakti," one should worship on the pedestal. [Reciting] "Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Jñānaśakti," one should place the image of Gaurī. Having invoked Parāśakti by means of her root-mantra (*mūla-mantra*), and having established her while addressing her as "Amukeśvarī," one should worship her. The mantras are as follows: "Oṃ hāṃ āṃ, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti."

Īṃ, salutation to the bulb (*kanda*). Ūṃ, salutation to the stalk (*nāla*). Ṛṃ, salutation to Dharma. Ṝṃ, salutation to Jñāna. Ḷṃ, salutation to Vairāgya. Ḹṃ, salutation to Aiśvarya. Eṃ, salutation to Adharma. Aiṃ, salutation to Ajñāna. Oṃ Aum, salutation to Raudra. Aum, salutation to Anaiśvarya. Am, salutation to the lower covering (*adhacchadana*). Aḥ, salutation to the upper covering (*ūrdhvachadana*). Paṃ, salutation to the lotus (*padma*). Raṃ Haṃ, salutation to the filaments (*kesara*).

Saṃ, obeisance to the pericarp (*karṇikā*). Kṣaṃ, obeisance to the filaments (*puṣkara*). Hrām, obeisance to Icchā. Hrīṃ, obeisance to Dūtī. Hrūṃ, obeisance to Kriyā. Hreṃ, obeisance to Vāc. Hraiṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvarī. Hroṃ, obeisance to Jvālinī. Hrauṃ, obeisance to Vāmā. These are the nine powers (*navaśakti*). Gāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Gaurī. Gauṃ, obeisance to the form of Gaurī. Hrīṃ Sauḥ, obeisance to Mahāgaurī, the beloved of Rudra.

Alternatively, having invoked him with the fifteen-syllable root *mahāvidyā* mantra: *gāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*; *gaḥ astrāya phaṭ*. Or else: *hrūṃ hūṃ* [and] *hrāṃ lakṣitāyai namaḥ*; *hrīṃ kāminyai namaḥ*; *sauḥ kāmamālinyai namaḥ*. Thus, having worshipped the attendants of Gaurī at the conclusion of the recitation (*japa*)—either with five, seven, or nine enclosures (*āvaraṇa*)—using the fivefold offerings (*pañcopacāra*), and having performed the expiatory fire-oblation (*prāyaścittahoma*), one should perform the rite for Caṇḍa and Vināyaka starting from the first day until the end of the fourth day.

Now, the procedure for the installation of the Sun (*sūryapratiṣṭhāvidhi*): Having performed the bath and other preliminary rites upon the seat and bed of Vidyā, one should install the Sun there. One should install the *tattvas* as previously described, including the three [principles] ending with Īśvara; then Māyā, along with Sadāśiva and Śakti, and [the principles] ending with Vidyeśvara, as well as Līlā, Agni, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā. "Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ, obeisance to Śiva-Sūrya. This is the installation of the individual soul (*jīvanyāsa*). One should conceive of the triple-sectioned seat (*pīṭha*) on the pedestal, extending from Māyā, Vidyā, and Sadāśiva, and having established everything through Śakti, who is primarily Oṃ.
Then, according to the rule, the Guru should duly install Sūrya, ending with the Śakti, along with Sthāṇu. Now follows the procedure for the installation of Vighneśa:
having performed his ablutions, one should place Gaṇādhipa upon a bed on the seat of Vidyānta.
Having deposited the three principles along with Īśvara—namely Māyā, Vidyā, and Sadeśika (Sadāśiva)—...
One should place the void (*kha*), wind (*vāta*), fire (*agni*), water (*ap*), and earth (*sisi*) at the end of the knees, throat, and head, respectively;
likewise Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā.
Furthermore, [one places] earth, fire, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), sun, water, wind, moon, and the void.
Āmoda, Pramoda, Sumukha, and likewise Durmukha.
Avighna, Vighnarāja, and Bhakṣyādhipa with five hands—
these are known as my eight forms, born from the syllables of my mantra.
Then, having invoked that which is called the twenty-eight syllables and the group of eight six-syllable mantras with their root-mantra, one should worship them according to the prescribed rite.
Up to Māyā and Vidyeśvara, that is the conceptualization of the three sections (*traikhaṇḍaka*) within that sacred seat (*pīṭha*). Now follows the ritual procedure for the installation of Skanda:
Guha, having performed his ablutions and other rites, [is placed] upon a bed on a seat ending with Māyā.
And the paths of the knees, the throat, and the head are known as Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva.
Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the five [deities] beginning with Mūrti up to Aṇḍayī and Śuddhavidyā,
then, in the eight directions, the Lords of the Vidyeśvaras are said to reside upon the earth and the other elements:
Ṣaṇmukha, Śaktipāṇi, Kārtikeya, and Guha.
Skanda, whose vehicle is a peacock, and Senānī Viśākhaka;
the Egg-holder at the edge of Mohinī, with the arrangement of the three regions (*traikhaṇḍa*) upon the seat,
accompanied by Senā and Vallī on the left and right sides.
And [he performed] the supreme of the supreme worship of the A-mantras known as Kalātiśiras,
according to the rite of the five offerings preceded by the five enclosures.
Having invoked [the deity] and worshipped him well, one should likewise worship in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
The pit is proclaimed to be hexagonal, located either in the northeast or in the southeast. (Now follows the installation of the Liṅgodbhava and others—)
Now, he indicates the installation of the *liṅga* and other [images] with a single verse:
"One should perform the installation of the *liṅga* of the Enemy of Tripura (*Purāri*), the Lord of the Dance (*Nṛtteśa*), and others as well, in the same manner as before;
one should carry out what has been declared regarding the general installation of unmentioned mantras."
One should cause the consecration to be performed, extending as far as the state of Sadāśiva.
As before, one should place [the goddess] who has bathed upon the bed on the altar in due order:
[the powers] called Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva, reaching from the knees to the head.
One should deposit Māyā up to the limit of Sadeśa-śakti, just as [one deposits] the elements beginning with earth:
fire, the sacrificer, the sun, water, [the moon], and ether;
then darkness, delusion, decay, sleep, death, Māyā, the serpent, and old age.

The five [deities]—Vāta, Aghora, Rātri, Ravajvara, and Ātisroghavākrakriyājña—are the presiding goddesses (*adhināyikās*). One should install them within the three principles (*tattvas*) beginning with *Ātman*, which possess intense forms. Up to the levels of *Māyā*, *Vidyā*, and *Śuddhavidyā* (the end of *Sadeśānta*), there is the conceptualization of the three sections (*trikhaṇḍa*) upon the sacred seat (*pīṭha*). One should worship according to the prescribed ritual using the syllables known by the number of lunar days (*tithi*).
(Now follows the procedure for the installation of Dakṣiṇāmūrti—the brief indication of the procedure for the installation of Dakṣiṇāmūrti.)
Kauśika, Kāśyapa, Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭhika,
and Jaya are established to the south of the Lord of the South.
Likewise, Bhāradvāja, Agastya, Gautama, and Atri.
The sages conceive of a triad of principles within the earth-principle (*pṛthivītattva*) among the [twenty-five] principles:
the Self (*ātman*), the Inner-Self (*antarātman*), and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). One should install these as the presiding deities therein.
With that very root-mantra, one should worship Dakṣiṇeśa.

Now, regarding the installation of Brahmā as indicated by the *pratiṣṭhā*: having placed Brahmā upon the bed after he has performed his ablutions, one should install him in sequence from the knees to the neck and head, enveloping him with the three principles (*tattvas*). One should place the world-protectors (*lokapālas*) all around, or else install the eight creators (*dhātṛ-aṣṭaka*). Indeed, the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*) extends to the very limit; thus, the arrangement of the three sections (*traikhaṇḍa*) is made upon the pedestal. With the six-syllabled mantra, one should perform everything as previously described. Now follows the procedure for the installation of Viṣṇu:
in the installation of the deity Vāyu, the three principles (*tattvatraya*) are to be known once again.
On that seat, one should likewise worship up to Prakṛti and up to Prajñā as before.
These subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are established in Pradhāna; this triad belongs to Hari.
[The forms] Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, and Pradyumna are Trivikrama;
Vāmana, Śrīdhara, and Hṛṣīkeśa are likewise considered [the remaining forms].
Likewise, Dāmodara, as well as the eight guardians of the forms (mūrtipās), beginning with Earth (Kṣmā).
In the system of five, Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa,
Pradyumna, Aniruddha, and Śrīdhara are recorded as the guardians of the images.
One should establish the *vyālika* ending with *prakṛti* by means of the seed-syllable *Śrī*, as well as the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*).
The Brahman-pada consists of the three principles (*tritattva*) ending with *aṇḍa*, *buddhi*, and *pradhāna*.
"The egg [is] up to the intellect (*buddhi*) of Kṛti; the fruit is the conceptualization of the three sections.
'One should worship with the eight-syllable mantra'—thus it was previously stated.
The intellect of the Egg of Ardhanārīśvara is situated within the limit of Māyā."
One should conceive of the venerable reality on the seat according to the ritual of the portion of the fierce intellect.
In this same way, Harihareśa should also be installed by those of noble mind.
In the half [image] of Hari, the ritual actions and mantras are to be understood as before, according to the prescribed rule.
In the Kṣetrapāla [mandala], one should conceive of the principles (tattvas) from the Egg (aṇḍa) up to Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā).
In the Pīṭha [mandala], one should conceive of them from the Egg up to Māyā, according to the procedure previously described.
[The mantras are: Hetughna, Śastripuraghna, Vahni, and Yamajihvaka.
Kāla, Karālīka, Ekāṅghri, and Bhrama—thus [they are] also known.
Or alternatively:
Anala, Agnikesa, Karālacaṇḍi,
Ghaṇṭārava, Mahākrodha, and indeed Piśitāśana in the sixth [position].
Saptama, Piṅgalākṣa, and likewise Ūrdhvakeśa are considered [the attendants].
These are indeed the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās), and the forms are traditionally held to be Earth, Fire, and the others.
In the consecration of Nandin and the rest, one should thus arrange this pervasion.
The conceptualization of the three sections for the seven Mothers is exactly as follows:
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī,
Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Māhendrī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Vīrabhadraka.
The wise one should fashion an image of Vīravighna as the Lord of Obstacles (Vighneśa);
and the seed-syllable of Gaṇapa is *gaṃ*, accompanied by the letters *ya-ra-la-va-śa-ṣa-sa-ha*.
Endowed with the *bindu* and *nāda*, and joined with the fire of *māyā*,
the best of teachers should install the images there, their faces painted with various forms; the Goddess, facing north, he should install.
Then, one should install Vighneśa facing east;
in the western region, one should likewise perform the installation of Śarabha with its respective mantra.
Now follows the procedure for the installation of Bhakta.

That which is joined with the first vowel ending in *sa*, and likewise endowed with the nasal drop (*bindu*), is declared to be my own mantra; it is the syllable *śa*, and then the syllable *va* from the left.
One should not conceive of the Brahmā-nyāsa with this very mantra ending in *sa*.
And the limbs of Brahmā are for the water for the feet; at that time, the mantra consists of its initial syllable.

The syllable *hrīṃ* is established as the feminine; by means of it, the conceptualization of the limbs of Brahmā is performed. Furthermore, the triad of principles known as Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva has been proclaimed.
One should sequentially establish the Self, the Inner Self, and the Supreme Self by means of the mastery over the meaning of the three principles.
Even for a woman, it should be exactly thus; for the elements beginning with earth are considered to be her form.
In the fivefold system, there would be eight [deities], while in the other, there are indeed only five, beginning with Earth (*kṣmā*).
In one view, Indra and the others are the guardians of the forms (*mūrtipāḥ*), whereas in the other, Nivṛtti and the others are the guardians of the forms.
Having assigned the respective seats (*pīṭhas*), one should assign the form and the body of the form.

One should perform the placement of the letters starting from 'a' and ending with 'kṣ', including the 'sa' and beginning with the 'mūrdhan'. However, in the case of the Niṣkala [form], one should perform the placement of the Kalās; in the Sakala [form], one should place Śrīkaṇṭha.

Now, the Śrīkaṇṭha-nyāsa—namely: *oṃ hāṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ aṃ* to Śrīkaṇṭha and Pūrṇodarī, *namaḥ*. Thus [up to] the end of the hair. *Anantāya namaḥ*; *virajarāyai namaḥ*. On the forehead: *iṃ* to Sūkṣma, *namaḥ*; *śālmalyai namaḥ*. On the right eye: *īṃ* to Trimūrti, *namaḥ*; *lolākṣyai namaḥ*. On the left eye: *uṃ* to Amareśa, *namaḥ*; *vartulākṣyai namaḥ*. On the right ear: *ūṃ* to Arpiśa, *namaḥ*; *dīrghakoṇārthaye namaḥ*.

In the left ear: *ṛṃ* obeisance to Bhārabhūta; obeisance to Dīrghamukhī. In the right nostril: *ṝṃ* obeisance to Nidhaneśa; obeisance to Gomukhī. In the left nostril: *ḷṃ* obeisance to Sthāṇu; obeisance to Dīrghajihvā. On the right cheek: *ḹṃ* obeisance to Hara; obeisance to Kuṇḍodarī. On the left cheek: *eṃ* obeisance to Caṇḍīśa; obeisance to Ūrdhvakeśinī.

On the upper lip: *Aiṃ*, obeisance to Bhautika; obeisance to Vikṛtamukhī. On the lower lip: *Oṃ*, obeisance to Sadyojāta; obeisance to Jvālāmukhī. (L. 2) On the row of upper teeth: *Aum*, obeisance to Anugraheśa; obeisance to Ullāsinī. On the row of lower teeth: *Am*, obeisance to Akrūra; obeisance to Śrīmukhī. In the nose: *Aṃ*, obeisance to Mahāsena; obeisance to Vidyā. In the mouth: obeisance. *Kaṃ*, obeisance to Krodheśa.

Salutation to Mahākālī. On the right arm: *khaṃ* salutation to Caṇḍa; salutation to Sarasvatī. On the right elbow: *gaṃ* salutation to Pañcāntaka; salutation to Siddhi. On the right wrist: *ghaṃ* salutation to Śivottama; salutation to Trailokyavijaya; salutation to Vidyā. On the palm of the right hand: *ṅaṃ* salutation to Ekarudra; salutation to Mantraśakti. On the tip of the right fingers: *caṃ* salutation to Cakṣuḥmeṣa; salutation to Ātmaśakti.

On the left upper arm: *phaṇaikanetrāya namaḥ*; *bhūtamātre namaḥ*. On the left elbow: *jaṃ caturmukhāya namaḥ*; *lambodaryai namaḥ*. On the left wrist: *jham ajeśāya namaḥ*; *bhrāmiṇyai namaḥ*. On the palm of the left hand: *ñaṃ candrāya namaḥ*; *gatakāyyai namaḥ*. On the tips of the fingers of the left hand: *ṭaṃ somāya namaḥ*; *khecaryai namaḥ*. At the base of the right thigh: *ṭhaṃ lāṅgaline namaḥ*.

*Mañjarī*, obeisance! On the right knee: *Ḍaṃ Dāhaka*, obeisance; *Rūpiṇī*, obeisance! On the right calf: *Ḍhaṃ Ardhanārīśa*, obeisance; *Vikariṇī*, obeisance! (l. 3) On the sole of the right foot: *Ṇaṃ Umākānta*, obeisance; *Pākhādī*, obeisance! On the tip of the sole of the right foot: *Taṃ Sthāṇu*, obeisance; *Pūtanā*, obeisance! At the base of the left thigh: *Thaṃ Ḍiṇḍimuṇḍa*, obeisance; *Bhadrakālī*, obeisance! (l. 4)

On the left knee: *daṃ* salutation to Atri; salutation to Gomātṛ. On the left calf: *dhaṃ* salutation to Īśāna; salutation to Śaṅkhinī. (l. 5) On the sole of the left foot: *naṃ* salutation to Meṣa; salutation to Gajinī. At the tip of the left foot: *paṃ* salutation to Lohita; salutation to Kālarātri. On the right side: *phaṃ* salutation to Śikhin; salutation to Kapardinī. On the left side: *baṃ* salutation to Chagalaṇḍa; salutation to Kāminī.

On the spine: *bhaṃ* to Dviraṇḍa, salutation; to Vajriṇī, salutation. At the navel: *maṃ* to Mahākāla, salutation; to Māyā, salutation. At the heart: *yaṃ* to the Self of the Skin, salutation; to Mupālī, salutation; to Sumukhī, salutation. On the skin: to the Self of Blood, *huṃ* to Jaṅga, salutation; to Revatī, salutation. In the domain of blood: to the Self of the Left Thigh, salutation; to Vināśin, salutation; to Mādhavī, salutation. In the domain of flesh: *vaṃ* to the Self of Delight (*moda*), salutation; to Khaḍgīśa, salutation.

To Vāruṇī, salutation! In the fat—*adhyātmane* (line 4), to Baka, salutation; to Vāmā, salutation! In the bones—*ṣaṃ*, to the marrow-self (*majjātmane*) whose form is Manu, salutation; to Śvetādharakṣopasāriṇī, salutation! In the marrow—*saṃ*, to the semen-self (*śuklātmane*) who is Vṛṣa, to Sahajā, salutation! In the semen—*haṃ*, to the vital-breath-self (*prāṇātmane*) who is Lakulīśa, to Lakṣmī, salutation! In the ear—*laṃ*, to the generative-organ-self (*liṅgātmane*) whose form is Manu, to Vyāpinī, salutation!

On the *liṅga*: having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) at the tip of the *liṅga* with "kṣaṃ, salutation to Mahāmāyā, whose nature is wrath"; [then] the *mātṛkā* syllables: *ma ma ṣa a ka ca kaca*; *gaṃ* together with its class-consonants; *ma* as the armor (*kavaca*); *i ī kṣaṃ* for Vāmā; the limbs [of the weapon]: *kra*; *ma* is the heart; ... [is] the head; *vaṃ* is the crest-lock (*śikhā*); the armor is *i ī*; the eye is *kṣam*; the weapon is *astra*.
Having performed the placement of the vital breath (*jīvanyāsa*) with its own mantra, one should also place the limbs.
Then, having held them in sequence, one should offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) to each of the principles (*tattva*) and the lords of the principles (*tattveśvara*).

Having purified each [deity] together with their forms and the lords of the forms by offering three oblations for each, one should establish them upon the pedestal provided with the installation of gems and other elements.
Having performed a hundred fire-oblations with the Aghora-mantra to ensure the absence of defects,
one should likewise take up [the mantra] beginning with one's own name joined with the "haṃsa" syllable, or else it may be taken in the second [form].
The second [syllable] of the seventh [group], joined with the fourteenth of the first [group] and united with the *bindu* and *nāda*, is called the human seed-syllable (*mānuṣa-bīja*).
It is known as the short *Brahman*; one should conceive the long vowels as its limbs.
And [he saw] the Rākṣasas, the Piśācas, the gods, and likewise the Siddhas.
The best of guides should thus arrange the mounts of the gods:
[the deities] Kāyeka, Suvinaya, Sattakra, and the twenty-five Tattvas.
One should place the sleep-pitcher upon the head of the image;
likewise, [one should place] Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā.
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, and the illustrious Pūṣā;
Pūṣā is sufficient... and Śaṅkhinī is recorded as the tenth.
One should then place these channels (*nāḍī*) within that very form.
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, as well as udāna and vyāna.
The elephant, the tortoise, the discus-bearer, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya;
the knees, the ears, and the feet—these are the three principles within the domain of the elements and the physical body.

The Guru should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the Self (*ātman*), the Inner Self (*antarātman*), and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) as the perpetual presiding deities. Having performed the previously mentioned placement of the individual soul (*jīvanyāsa*),
he should purify [the image] and establish it upon a pedestal provided with the placement of jewels and other elements.

Now, the procedure for sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*): A *liṅga* that has been completed [but] not worshipped for a year, or one that has been defiled by a dog, a crow, or similar creatures, or one that has been resorted to by low people— [for such a case, this rite is prescribed].
Being worshipped in this world, it produces thousands of great faults;
therefore, the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of that very [image] as it stands is now being described.
One should have everything, such as the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), constructed according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Having bathed [the image] as before with the Weapon-mantra, the image-maker and others [should proceed].
Alternatively, having first performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the three principles (*tritattva*) or the three principles beginning with Mūrtipā,
as before, one should begin by worshipping that *liṅga*.

Having offered oblations as before for each section and having sprinkled [the area] with water from the peace-pitcher, one should then recite the mantra as many times as the number of oblations and install [the deity].
At the end of the *pūrṇāhuti*, as before, one should mentally place the pentad beginning with stone and jewels.
Having installed the previously mentioned seat (*āsana*) upon that, as before,
one should install the *liṅga* endowed with the *mūrti-mantra* and the pedestal (*pīṭhikā*) with the *pīṭha-mantra*.
Having mentally superimposed Śiva, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of His respective limbs.

Having offered the *arghya* as before, and having performed the worship and the fire-oblation (*homa*), the preceptor should perform the dismissal (*visarjana*) of the mantra according to the sequence of the fourth day.
Thus has the ritual sprinkling been described for a liṅga that has not been worshipped for six months or more;
it effects purification and bestows the fruit of the primary image.
Thus has been composed this instruction for the awakening of disciples, which is independent of all others and transcends the rites of installation, liṅgas, and so forth.
The characteristic of the limbs of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) is not supreme...
lest there be a theft of the awakening to the sequence of ritual action (*kriyākrama*).
Therefore, one should proceed to that stainless [text] by means of the venerable *Netra*, the noble *Śiva*, and the *Tāraka*.

The best among those who know the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*), possessing an excellent body, an ocean of the sciences such as Nyāya, and a bestower of the knowledge of the Veda; foremost in the exposition of the Śiva doctrine, he has likewise performed the acquisition of knowledge (*jñāna*) from his most excellent spiritual preceptors, as well as the rites of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).
Now, the procedure for the lineage succession of the Gurus:
The *gotra* is to be known as fourfold, and the *gocaras* are recorded as sixteen.
There are four *gotra-munis*, and likewise, the *sthānas* are four.
Thirty-six brothers are proclaimed as sages (*muni*s);
fifteen monasteries (*maṭha*) are mentioned, and four trees are declared.
"She is known as Gāyatrī, Vikṛtibhārati, and Manonmanī"—
thus some have declared the lineages (*gotra*) of Śiva’s powers (*śakti*).
Others say that those beginning with Śivā are the presiding deities (*adhiṣṭhātrī*) over Gāyatrī and the others, being their respective spheres of activity (*gocara*).
The supreme masters who know the established doctrine consider this to be "as it truly is."
"The sphere of activity is called the family (*kula*)," according to the venerable *Kāraṇaśruti*.
Therefore, for the sake of fulfilling the lineage, time, and so forth, I shall praise you as you are renowned.
The lineage (gotra) resides within the [mantras] named Śivaśikhā, Jyotis, and Sāvitrī; it is the conceptualization of the Bindu, Nāda, the gross Bindu, and the presiding deity of the Nāda.
From Śiva, from Śakti, from the *bindu*, and also from the *nāda*, there is a fourfold [manifestation];
the station consisting of the light of the *kula* is sometimes fivefold for the gurus.
[It resides] in Śālmala, in the one named Śāka, in Puṣkara, and in the one named Kuśa.
Furthermore, the four [groups] situated in sequence are entirely black on the other continents.
Each one has sixteen varieties consisting of four strands;
O Śivā, these are the Prājāpatya, Mahīpāla, Kāpotā, and Granthika.
The Kuṭikās, Vetālās, Padmas, Haṃsas, and Śikhākulas; the Dhṛtarāṣṭras, Bakas, Kaṅkas, those called Gopālas, and the Jyotiṣāskatas.
The Kaṭikas and the Māṭharas, as well as the Nāḍikas and the Daṇḍins, are in other [lineages].
Bhāradvāja is in the Śiva-kula, and Kuśika is in the one called Śikhā.
Kāśyapa is to be known in Jyotiṣa, and the sage Gautama is in Sāvitra.
Bhāradvāja's is the Śacchakra, and Kuśika's is the Pauṇḍara.
The Nāgara [tradition] was taught by Kāśyapa, while that originating from the city belongs to Gautama. Those who are masters of the lineage are likewise called brothers.
Śaṅkha, Mukaṇḍusūna, Pauṇḍara, the one known as Śubhra,
the one called Śuka, Śaunaka, and Manu Kṛṣṇapiṅgala—
these nine are declared to be the younger brothers of Bharadvāja.
Namuci, Dakṣasaṃjña, Śuṣma, Valmika, and Nandana.
Parāśara, Vyāsa, Bodhāyana, and Sanātana—these were the brothers of Kuśaka; hence, they are known as the nine in the Śikhā lineage.
Aṅgiras, he known as Sthūlava, Śāṇḍilya, and he named Agastya; Āpastamba, Uśanas, Bhūti, Śaṅkukarṇa, and Virājaka.
These are the brothers of Kāśyapa, or rather, they are not [his] in the third [generation]:
Bāḍabogalla, Vasiṣṭha known as Saṃjña, Māṭhara, Uttarika, Maugalya, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, Kātyāyana, and Uṣaspati.
Born within the domain of Sāvitrī, they were the brothers of Gautama.
The monastery named Kailāsa is proclaimed as the first; Pauṇḍra is the second;
Valāhama is the third; and Kalpagrāma is the fourth.
The fifth is to be known as Badarī; after that is Devadāruvana.
Kandarpa is the seventh; then Śākhā, beginning from the north. From that follows Dakṣiṇāraṇyaka, and beyond that is Govinda-aṇumata.
The *āmada* is like a peacock in its intoxication; the *golakī* is like a *raṇabhadra*.
Adorned with *kadamba*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *vaṭa*, and *āmaṭha* trees—
this is common to all; yet our lineage is said to be [distinguished] by Śiva,
the supreme presiding deity whose power possesses unshakable earrings.
The family of Śiva has become manifest, presided over by the power of Gāyatrī.
Therefore, [the teaching] beginning with the Mantramaheshas, the Ganas, and the Devas in due order,
consists of the knowledge of the self as the wheel of channels (*nāḍicakra*), characterized by the yoga of Vijaya and so forth.
The lineage of Śiva descended upon the great sage Drāviḍa;
by him alone was grace bestowed through [the transmission of] the Nā...ṣya and other [teachings].

From that lineage of the three Gurus known as Paiṅgala, the awakening knowledge of Śiva (Śivajñāna) was transmitted in due order to the man named Paitāmaha. From him, the four *gocaras* arose, established in the Prājāpatya and other [stages]. Through non-violence, the desire to serve the Guru, purity, self-study, and the restraints (*saṃyama*), and by the qualities of truth and non-stealing, they were characterized. Thus, from the *gocara* of the Prājāpatya [stage], [the lineage flourished].
The lineage of gurus has arisen, centered upon the distinguished mantra of Śiva.
Within that lineage is the supreme guru Laṭapa, the venerable Vyāpakaśiva;
he is the lord of the monastery named Āmada, who exists as the primordial abode.
His disciple was the illustrious Gauḍaja Āsatsarveśapaṇḍita.
In the city of Nīlalāṭa, the Guru made his residence.
Thence, Śiva, the Lord of the Earth, pierced the lofty Hṛllāṭa.
The preceptor residing in the auspicious city of Kalyāṇa was the wise Vardhatikṛt;
his younger brother was the teacher Sarvavidyādhipa,
who was the preceptor of the illustrious King Bhoja, the discernor of the meaning of all the Āgamas.
Then Somaśiva was born from him; he was the lord of the vow (vratīśvara) in that region.
Then there was the preceptor Pūrṇaśiva, honored by the king in Vārāṇasī;
after him came Āryottuṅgaśiva, a householder from the region of Ubhuda.
From him [arose] Vidyeśānaśiva; from him these two noble Īśvaras [proceeded];
and from that one known as Vidyāntaśiva arose the one born in the land of Cola.
The teacher Vārāṇasīnātha mastered the science but did not reach its further shore.
Then there was Brahmaśivācārya, a preeminent ascetic among the Ṭalāṭas.
After him came Mūrtiśiva, who likewise resided in the city named Vijaya.
Born as a householder in Māyāpurī, he was thereafter the teacher of all souls.
His disciple was the preceptor Śrī Kamaṭhaśiva, a bull among the Gauḍas,
who had not yet arrived for the initiation of the illustrious Abhrasabheśāna and others.
The illustrious Vikramādicolesha appointed him as his own preceptor;
thereafter, the eminent Gauḍa became the venerable Dhyānaśiva.
Our Guru composed commentaries on twenty-eight tantras.
He who, having worshipped Coleśvara, should then worship Sabheśa;

From him was born one named Hṛdayaśaṅkara, whose disposition was pure and who had reached the further shore of all the Āgamas. From him [came] this one, the foremost among the sons of my grandfather’s paternal uncle, widely renowned on earth as the sovereign of the Śaivas; he was the younger brother of that [Hṛdayaśaṅkara], our father’s maternal uncle, Parameśvara. Then, having been favored by the illustrious Mādhya Śiva, he was made my preceptor.

To him, who is the very eye of Śiva... who is preeminent in the knowledge of the Vedas and other sciences, who is the direct manifestation of the unique Śiva, and who is exalted by his power, I speak—as one who is directly favored by him.
[He praised] this one named Parameśvara— the stainless jewel of Atri’s lineage, the glory residing in Kāñcī, who touches the highest goal, and who severs the bonds of our own kin.
The wise lord on earth, knowing that I was endowed with the name Aghoraśiva, favored me by bestowing upon me that very name.

The Lord Śrīkaṇṭhanātha, an ocean of compassion, having condensed the Āgneya-tantra in many ways for the sake of Śarajanman (Kārttikeya), spoke [it]. Among those [works], within the six compendiums known as the Kālottara, there are three hundred and fifty [verses] in the Brahmin recension,
and thirteen hundred and fifty in the Tairyasya recension.
Whatever has not been explicitly stated here, though it was indicated but not fully revealed,
is all contained within this extensive compendium, having been considered for the benefit of those who seek it.
This has been practiced by our most excellent ancient gurus in the *Uttuṅgaśivapaddhati*, both daily and on special occasions.
This daily ritual and other rites, together with their ancillaries, have been performed with devotion according to the *Siddhāntasārapaddhati*, following the instructions received from our own guru,
the venerable Sarvātmaśiva.
Having heard it, I have composed this very elucidation of the sequence of ritual actions.
In the year of Nāda... [Yeśaka], while the Kali age was prevailing, it was written with three thousand five hundred verses.

Thus ends the ritual procedure for the consecration of the doors and other elements, as composed by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya, whose other name is Parameśvara, in this work entitled the Kriyākramadyotikā.

Now, the procedure for the Great Festival (mahotsava): Hari Om. First is the sacrifice to the bull (vṛṣayāga), second is the hoisting of the banner (dhvajāroha), third is the large lotus (bṛhanāla), and fourth is the offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa).
The worship of the sacrificial hall (*yāgaśālārcana*) and the [rite] beginning with the weapon (*astra*) thereafter;
the seventh is the offering of the oblation (*balidāna*), and the eighth is the sequence of the procession (*yānakrama*).
The ninth is the *pariveṣa*, and the tenth is the sequence of *nīrājana*;
the eleventh is the *kautuka*, and the twelfth is the *tīrthasaṃgraha*.
On the thirteenth day is the *svarṇotsava*, and the fourteenth is the *tīrthaka*.
The fifteenth is the descent; the sixteenth shall be the ceremonial bath.
"Following this, there is the marriage [festival] consisting of seventeen feasts (*maktotsava*).

Having understood the festival through such distinctions as these, the procedure for the nine festivals—ranging from the highest of the high to the lowest, categorized as Śaiva and so forth up to Daivika—is now prescribed. It is as follows: *(Note: The asterisked portion appears to be a scribal or editorial mark; the text following it is continuous with the preceding sentence.)*

One should begin the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) during the first part of the night. In this regard, the preceptor and the others—having refrained from ascending [the ritual seat] until the descent [is complete], having observed a single meal, sleeping on the ground, abstaining from oil massage, sexual union, and eating the food of others, and having bathed three times a day—should have their hair shaved, put on new garments, perform the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), and after first saluting their chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), proceed as follows. Starting from the first day until the end of the ninth day, the ritual offering (*bali*) must be performed twice daily.

On the tenth day, having offered the *bali* in the morning, one should commence the powder festival (*cūrṇotsava*) and the pilgrimage (*tīrtha*) on that same day. However, if it is the ninth day, [the ceremony] must be performed prior to the mounting (*ārohaṇa*). In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, it ends with Ārdrā; in Puṣya, with Puṣya; in Māgha, with Māgha; in Phālguna, with Uttaraphalgunī; in Caitra, with Citrā; in Vaiśākha, with Viśākhā; in Jyeṣṭha, with Jyeṣṭhā or Mūla; and in Āṣāḍha, with Uttarāṣāḍhā.

One should cause a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) to be constructed on the seashore during the full moon; or at the beginning of a river and so forth when joined with a festival; or in the month of Māgha until the sixth day, or until the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Jyeṣṭha; or under the asterisms (*nakṣatra*) of the preceptor, the king, the patron, the deity, the village, and so forth, or under the asterism desired by the performer.

One should perform the *tīrtha* rite at sea during the forenoon; on lotus ponds (*puṣkara*) and the like during the afternoon; and in a river at midday. If there is an abundance of lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), one should perform the *tīrtha* in the evening. When two lunar mansions or two lunar days (*tithi*) coincide within a single month, that [time] should be preferred, provided it is joined with the conjunction of the solstice (*viṣuvāyana*) or other such [auspicious] transitions (*saṃkrānti*). From the commencement of the ascent (*ārohaṇa*) until the end of the *tīrtha*, this period within a single month is most excellent.

One should perform the Śivatīrtha rite until the end of the day, the end of the year, or the end of the eclipse. During the festival of Śiva’s preeminence, the ritual bath (avabhṛtha) should be performed in the morning. Regarding the raising of the banner at night—[as stated in the Vināyakotsava]: "At night, in the evening; by day, in the morning"—one should cause the banner to be raised at night [if it is the evening] and in the morning [if it is the day].
One should not place a banner upon a banner; rather, a bull-banner (vṛṣabhadhvaja) should be made.
If the raising of a banner is undertaken for others [besides Śiva], a great fault arises.

One should not perform a festival for a deity or the consecration of a cow on a single plot of land, such as within a village; if done so, it results in misfortune for the king and his kingdom. Prior to the commencement of the festival, one should refurbish everything from the mounts and vehicles up to the chariots, and from the temple of the deity up to the streets. One should then decorate [the area] with plantain trunks, betel-nut trees, coconut palms, breadfruit trees, and the like, using seasonal fruits, sprouts, flower garlands, mirrors, door-arches, canopies, banners, and so forth, extending to the water-stalls and rest pavilions.

Having caused the ground to be swept, sprinkled with water, and so forth, one should perform the purification of the site (*bhūśuddhi*). At the conclusion of the festival of Bhadrakālī, one should perform a festival for Vighneśvara—either for nine days, seven days, three days, or a single day. For instance: having specifically worshipped Vināyaka, Skanda, Vīraśāsta, the twenty-five images, the Śiva-weapon, the *bhasta*, Caṇḍa, Avigraha, and others, preceded by the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).

Having adorned [the image] with all ornaments and being honored by the preceptor, the officiating priests, and the king, [he], together with the Brāhmaṇas and the astrologers, at an auspicious moment, for the sake of the festival, after first performing the worship of Vighneśa, caused the declaration of the *puṇyāha* (day of merit) characterized by the title "Mahādeva" to be recited; then, having worshipped Vighneśa preceded by the ritual bathing, having offered sacrificial food consisting of various kinds of eatables and drinks, and having fed the Brāhmaṇas, he prayed, "May there be no obstacle."

Having gratified all those engaged in the temple work, as well as the poor, the blind, the wretched, and the helpless, with food and clothing, one should place the king of weapons, Caṇḍeśvara, preceded by Vināyaka, upon a chariot or a palanquin. Accompanied by an umbrella, chowries, various processional items, perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, diverse musical instruments, and the chanting of the Vedas, one should circumambulate the city and install [the deity] in the bathing pavilion (*snānamaṇḍapa*). Then, one should proceed with the collection of wood, just as in the case of a *śilpa-brahman*.

Having examined the top and the root of one tree from among the *bilva*, *khadira*, *devadāru*, *campaka*, *arjuna*, *aśoka*, *śirīṣa*, *veṇu*, and others; having worshipped Śiva; having offered a sacrificial oblation (*bali*); and having performed the ritual confinement (*niruddhya*), he should cut it with an axe.
