If it falls toward the east, the north, or the northeast, it is auspicious; otherwise, he should abandon it. Then, having made it auspicious, having placed it upon the shoulder of a carpenter, and having brought it back, he should bathe it with products of the cow (*gavya*) and tie a protective thread (*kautuka*) at its front.

Having again caused the *puṇyāha* (day of merit) to be proclaimed and having placed [the object] in the pavilion, one should wipe it with oil and other substances, and cause betel-nut offerings (*tāmbūla*) and ritual fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to be given to everyone. There, having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), having placed the staff in the center, having adorned it with garments and the like, having embellished it with garlands and so forth, and having fumigated it with incense, one should worship the three principles (*tatvatraya*) together with the Lord (*seśvara*) starting from the portion of Śiva in the directions of the four Vedas, the *apasvaśrava*, and the *vṛtta*. Then, one should raise [the object] with the *praṇava* (OM).

Having placed it in its proper position, one should consecrate it according to the procedure for general consecration (*sāmānyapratiṣṭhā*), up to the pinnacle (*stūpyanta*), the crest (*cūlikānta*), or the gable-ends (*śukanāsānta*). One should have it constructed with three staffs (*yaṣṭi*) and three planks (*phalaka*), together with two secondary staffs (*upadaṇḍa*) and a bell, along with one hundred and eight tufts of *darbha* grass, [and] *darbha*... staffs, and rings; this is the ritual procedure for the collection of wood and the consecration of the staff.
(The Ritual Procedure for the Collection of Clay—)

Having gone to a place such as a riverbank accompanied by the images of Vighneśvara and others, and accompanied by the sounds of various musical instruments and the chanting of the Vedas, one should collect earth as previously described. Having had that earth conveyed by attendants of Maheśvara, by female dancers (*udragaṇikā*), or by elephants and so forth, and having circumambulated the city, one should enter the temple and deposit it upon the altar for the offering of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*).

Having offered to Vighneśa [Gaṇeśa] modakas, cakes, sugarcane, coconut, wood-apple (*kapittha*), citron (*mātuluṅga*), plantain, and other desired fruits, as well as chickpeas, mung beans, betel, and so forth, one should worship him with all ritual services (*sarvopacāra*). This is the procedure for the collection of earth. On the eve of the hoisting of the banner, at night—or during the third [watch]—one should perform the rite of germinating seeds (*aṅkura*) as previously described. Thus ends the procedure for the offering of germinating seeds.
Now, the procedure for the bull-sacrifice (*vṛṣabha-yāga*):

On the night before the hoisting of the banner (*dhvajārohaṇa*), one should have the site prepared and purchased. Then, having worshipped Śiva and made a formal request, the preceptor (*guru*), having adorned the bull’s station with canopies and other ornaments, shall sit facing north on a firm seat. Having performed the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅga-nyāsa*) and so forth as previously described, and having offered the *arghya*, he shall worship the Lord of the Bull (*vṛṣeśa*) who is to be accomplished, and offer an oblation of mung-bean rice.

Having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) before him with rice and other grains, having drawn a lotus in its center, and having strewn it around with *kuśa* grass and flowers, he should establish [the deities] and worship the bull in the central jar, preceded by the sixfold arising seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*). Then, in the directions from the east to the northeast—[he should worship] with the root mantras beginning with the seats: "Homage to Ukṣāya Gopati"; "Homage to Śṛṅgin Nandin"; "Homage to Vṛṣapati"; "Homage to Vṛṣāṇin Śaṅkukarṇa Mahodara. Thus, having worshipped with these and the other root mantras.

Alternatively—having fully worshipped the world-protectors (lokapālas)—the banner-cloth (*dhvajapaṭa*) should have its hand, leaf, and so forth [arranged such that] the width is one-fifth [of the total], the tail is equal to the width, the top-knot (*śiraḥ*) is half of that, or half of that again.

Having taken white, fine, smooth cloth produced from saffron-dyed material and divided it into three parts, one should paint a bull in the middle section—or in one-third of that third part—with white; its neck and hooves with red; its tail with yellow; and its eyes with black and white. Having painted a full water-jar in front of it, and behind it a lamp, a *śrīvatsa*, and other auspicious forms, one should begin the ritual of the banner (*dhvajayāga*).

Alternatively, having laid out the length of the staff and the width of the cloth as before, and having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should sprinkle [the area] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and other substances, worship the bull and the mobile seat (*calāsana*), and on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in front of it, perform the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) according to the prescribed method up to the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) as previously described. Following the purification of the image (*beraśuddhi*), one should prepare two further sacrificial mounds elsewhere, place the banner-cloth in the center, and perform the "opening of the eyes" (*akṣimocana*) using the *Sūrya* and *Soma* mantras from a golden needle, or by means of the *Vṛṣagāyatrī*.

Having recited: "We know him whose horns are sharp; we meditate upon him whose feet are the Vedas; may that Bull inspire us," and having performed everything beginning with the inspection of the cow, one should sprinkle [the image] with earth, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and auspicious water. Having bathed it in a mirror with the products of the cow and other substances, one should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) in water. Having lifted it from the water and brought the banner-cloth (*dhvajapaṭa*) into the sacrificial hall, one should place it upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*). After worshipping the sixfold seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*) and forming the ritual intention (*saṃkalpa*) preceded by the meditation on the form (*mūrtidhyāna*).

Having covered [the deity] with a garment, having placed [him] within the *brahman*, having established the *nidrākumbha* (sleep-pitcher), and having arranged the ox and other [emblems] around [it], one should worship. Standing at the base of the bull, one should install the thirty-four [principles] from the head down to the feet, as follows: "Obeisance to the principle of Sadāśiva (*sadāśivatattva*); obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the principle of Sadāśiva. Beginning thus and ending with "Obeisance to Śrīkaṇṭha, the lord of the earth-principle (*pṛthivītattva*)," one should complete the worship.

Having conceptualized [the area] as three sections and having offered a flower garland and a protective cord (*pratisara*), one should, as before, resolve it into three parts. In each part, proceeding in order from the east, [the deities are assigned] according to the measurements of earth, fire, water, moon, and ether; these are the *mūrtis*. Having installed the guardians of the *mūrtis*—Ukṣan, Gopati, Śṛṅgin, Nandin, Vṛṣa, Pariviṣāṇin, Śaṅkukarṇa, and Mahodara—and having performed the ritual placement of the life-force (*jīvanyāsa*) with the root mantra, one should worship them with the rites of installation and other offerings.

One should construct three outer enclosures with ashes, *darbha* grass, and sesame seeds. Having petitioned the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), one should worship in the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the mantra: "Obeisance to Ādhāraśakti. Having thus worshipped the fire, one should offer three oblations (*āhuti*) and worship with: "Obeisance to the principles of Self (*ātmatattva*), Knowledge (*vidyātattva*), and Śiva (*śivatattva*), and to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. Having thus worshipped, one should offer three oblations for each. Then, having worshipped with: "Obeisance to the deities of the elements beginning with Earth (*kṣmādi*) and to their presiding lords," one should offer three oblations for each.

Having offered one hundred or fifty oblations for each of the limbs of Brahmā (*brahmāṅga*), and having performed the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), the Guru, holding the *śāntikumbha* vessel in his hand, approaches the bull. Having sprinkled [it] with the water from the *śāntikumbha*, he divides it into three parts using the roots, middles, and tips of *kuśa* grass while reciting the root mantra. Having touched [them], recited [the mantra], veiled them with the *varman* mantra, and restrained [them], he issues the command to the presiding deities of the principles (*tattvādhipa*) and, having bestowed the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), restrains [them].

Or, with devotion, one should perform [the rite] for a single night through fire-offerings (homa), the chanting of the Vedas and other scriptures, or great festivals of dance and song. Having offered the sacrifice of the bull (vṛṣayāga) and the seat of Śiva (śivāsana), as well as the oblation to the directions (digbali), the Guru should sleep as before. Thus ends the procedure for the consecration of the bull (vṛṣādhivāsanavidhi).

Having performed the ritual of bathing and so forth on this [auspicious] day, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), having performed the ritual of self-protection (*sakalīkaraṇa*), and having prepared the general offering water (*sāmānyārghya*), one should carry out the entire procedure for the daily self-worship (*ātmapūjā*). Then, having worshipped the cloth painting (*paṭa*), the ritual jar (*kumbha*), and the other items in their proper order, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of fuel sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge (*caru*) into the fire. Having offered the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and sealed [the fire], one should construct three mandalas within the pavilion and other areas.

Having summoned the attendants, having sprinkled them with the *astra* mantra, and having had them don turbans and upper garments; then, having raised the cloth-painting (*paṭa*) together with the water-jars and other items, accompanied by all musical instruments, amidst the sounds of conchs and drums as well as the chanting of the Vedas and other hymns, one should perform a circumambulation of the village, enter the temple, place the painting on one [altar] and the jars on another, and upon three sacrificial mounds (*sthaṇḍila*), recite the *puṇyāha* formula and sprinkle everything with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) along with the *arghya* water.

Having sprinkled the bull with water from the jar, and having adorned it with perfumes and other offerings as well as jars [containing] oxen and so forth, and having offered the sacrificial oblation such as chickpeas and the like, one should likewise sprinkle the King of Weapons (*astrarāja*) with water from that jar, adorn it, offer it, and perform the recitation (*japa*). Then, having offered the powder of *rajanī* to the King of Weapons and having applied it oneself, one should cause the King, the devotees, the attendants, and all others to receive the *rajanī* powder. Thus, may there be auspiciousness.
(The Ritual for Hoisting the Banner:

Then, having adorned the banner-pole, the preceptor should worship its length with the Gāyatrī mantra. Having mounted the deity upon a chariot or similar vehicle, with the trident at the front and the preceptor leading the way, followed by the patron (*yajamāna*) and all the devotees, accompanied by every kind of musical instrument, together with auspicious sprouts, joined by various types of umbrellas, chowries, and lamps, and provided with offerings for the procession, they should circumambulate the city in all directions—accompanied by song, dance, and the offering of oblations—and then enter the temple.

Having brought [the flagstaff] to the site of the banner and caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should sprinkle the altar together with its pedestal (*vedikā*). Having worshipped [the deities] on the altar, beginning with Śakti and ending with Īśa-Śakti, one should meditate upon the staff as follows: it measures one *pāda*, possesses three eyes, has its interior adorned with a line of hair, is white in form, and is shaped like a lotus-seat (*padmāsana*) mounted upon the tip of a parrot’s beak. Then, having invoked Sadāśiva into the staff—

On the staff and the board, the wise ones should worship the three *śaktis*; on the secondary staff, Soma and Soma; on the two ropes, the deities Takṣan and others; and on the cloth or the banner, the bull—worshipping them in this sequence. Having offered green-gram rice or milk-rice to the bull, having presented incense and lamps, and having given gold, grain, fruit, betel, and so forth to the Brahmins, one should wrap [the image] with the cloth and the rope. Then, having requested Śiva, "Let the festival that is to be performed be carried out."

Having performed the recitation of the *Bṛhattāla* hymn and having offered countless coconut offerings (*nālikera-bali*) for the purpose of dispelling obstacles, the preceptor (*deśika*), at an auspicious moment (*sumuhūrta*), standing at the base of the staff (*daṇḍa*) together with various musical instruments, sprinkles it with water of honor (*arghya*). Having first touched the self-manifested [Liṅga] along with the guardians of the forms (*mūrtipāḥ*), he should raise the *maghra*. Having wrapped it around in sequence, he should tie it at the base of the staff.

From this point until the conclusion of the *tīrtha* rite, one should worship the bull three times or twice a day. Afterwards, having gone to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and performed the expiatory oblation (*prāyaścitta*), one should dismiss the fire of the bull-sacrifice. Pure dance (*śuddhanṛtta*) should be performed in the cardinal and intermediate directions; such is the procedure for the hoisting of the banner (*dhvajārohaṇavidhi*).

A woman should eat that ball of food; even one without sons shall obtain a son. It destroys disease and removes all defects. This remnant of the bull is offered for the one who raises the banner; thus is the establishment of the banner-wielder made within the kingdom.
There is no untimely death there, nor is there misfortune even among evildoers.
There is no fear of calamity there, nor of enemies, nor of cattle, nor of confusion.
And even for yogins, their perceptions are mostly perverted;
the rain-god pours rain according to its own season, there is abundance of food, and the kings are victorious.
All beings become peaceful, as do those who carry water and those who offer milk;
even a person ungrateful to others, a slayer of Brahmins, or a killer of cows attains liberation from sin upon seeing a settlement of Dhvajins—
how much more so for one who performs the threefold service?
When the raising of the great banner is performed, the fruit is multiplied ten millionfold.
Now follows the procedure for the *bṛhattāla* (the great rhythmic cycle):
It has been stated in the *Utsavapaddhati* that, for the purpose of pleasing all the gods,
the *bherī* drum is struck when the evening protection rite (*sāyarakṣā*) is concluded.
One should begin the rite of invoking the deity either before an image of the god or at the top of his banner.

Having prepared three sacrificial altars (*sthaṇḍila*) there, one should place a trident on one, a cloth-painting (*paṭa*) in front of it, and a drum (*bherī*) at its tip. One should then set down the staff of the southern *vyāna* breath. Then, at the base of the trident, one should arrange the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), mantras, and digits (*kalā*). For example: on the central petal, "Salutation to the Śiva-principle (*śivatattva*); salutation to Rudra, the lord of the Śiva-principle. On the left petal: "Salutation to the Vidyā-principle; salutation to Viṣṇu, the lord of the Vidyā-principle."

On the southern petal: *namaḥ* to the Reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*). *Namaḥ* to Brahmā, the Lord of the Reality of the Self. On the leaf-tip: *namaḥ* to Pārvatī. In the region of the bulb: *namaḥ* to the Commander of the Army (*senānī*). On his attendant: *namaḥ* to Vighnarāja. At the tip of the staff: *namaḥ* to Madana. In the middle of the staff: *namaḥ* to Bhāskara. At the base of the staff: *namaḥ* to Caṇḍeśvara. On the seven petals beginning with the southeast: *namaḥ* to Brāhmī; *namaḥ* to Māheśvarī.

Homage to Kaumārī! Homage to Vaiṣṇavī! Homage to Vārāhī! Homage to Māhendrī! Homage to Cāmuṇḍā! In the center of the western petal—homage to Jyeṣṭhā! In the center of the [petal of] Kubera—homage to Kātyāyanī! At the base of the trident—the eleven Rudras, the twelve Ādityas, the Vasus, the deities of the Aśvins, and the eighteen Gaṇas should be invoked and worshipped. Having summoned them and uttered blessings, one should strike the drum and cause [the music] to be played.

Then, having wrapped the drum with variegated cloth, one should worship Rudra in the center, the Mothers on the seven pegs, the nine planets on the leather, and Vāsukī [on the frame]. Having worshipped them in sequence and adorned them with perfumes and other offerings, one should strike the drum. The preceptor, meditating upon the Śāstra in the form of a drop (*bindu*), should strike it three times with *darbha* grass. If that sound reaches the ears of living beings, they become free from sin.

Having performed the five preliminary sacrifices (*pañcādyaka*), having donned the sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*) and upper garment (*uttarīya*), and having applied perfumes, garlands, and so forth, he should place a flower in the hand of that [disciple]. He too, with the permission of the teacher (*ācārya*), should cast the flower onto the drum (*bherī*). Having placed it upon his shoulder while the drum is being beaten, he should strike it to the *nanditāla* rhythm. Then, having summoned Śiva and all the other deities, the eighteen classes of attendants (*gaṇas*), the lords of the quarters beginning with Indra, as well as the oceans, mountains, continents, and the entire subterranean realm (*pātāla*), he should strike [the drum].

Having arrived at the station of Vṛṣabha, having performed worship and offered the *bali*, and having gratified [the deity] with dance, handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), the *rāga* Śuddhavarāṭi, songs, and so forth; thereafter, for the sake of bathing the central and other deities—accompanied by the King of Weapons (*astrarāja*), Soma, Skanda, the Goddess, Vināyaka, Skanda, Nandin, Caṇḍabhakta, Vigraha, and others, together with all auspicious things—he should resort to the station of Brahmā. Having performed everything there in the place of that mandala, such as the sprinkling on an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-prokṣaṇa*) and so forth, and having worshipped the seated form (*āsana-mūrti*), he should take parched grain and flowers in his hand.

Having meditated upon Brahmā with the *musalamudrā*, having invoked and worshipped him, and having offered the *naivedya* together with perfumes, flowers, and incense, as well as the *bali* offering, one should thereafter please him with dance, song, instrumental music, and so forth, using the *brahmatāla*, the *megharāga*, and the *daṇḍapāda*. Immediately after, resorting to the direction of Indra (the east), one should offer the seat and other offerings in that maṇḍala as before, and please [Indra] with the *samatāla*, the *gāndhāri*, and the *ūrdhvapāda* and so forth. In the same manner, in the south-eastern direction, one should perform the *kollitāla* and the enclosure (*āvaraṇa*).

Having gratified [the deities] with the [verses] beginning with *lilitam* (l. 6), one should perform the *bhṛṅgitāla* in the southern direction, the *kauśika*, and the *bhujaṅgatrāsa*, etc. In the southwest (*nairṛta*), having gratified [them] with the *mallatāla*, the *nāṭṭabhāṣā*, and the *bhujaṅga*, etc.; and in the western (*vāruṇa*) direction, the *navatāla*, the *śrīkāmara*, and the *kuñcita*, etc. Relying on the northwest (*vāyavya*), [one performs] the *balitāla* for *tarkeśi* and the *bhrāmara*.

In the north, likewise, having made the offering of *ālāḍa* according to the ritual of *tarkarāga*, one should go to the northeast (*īśāna*) with *śālāpāṇi*. Having gratified [the deity] with the *pratyalibhūmi* and other offerings, and having circumambulated the temple clockwise starting from Indra and the others, one should enter the abode and cast the remainder at the base of the banner or upon the pedestal of the *liṅga*. This is the procedure for the great *tāla* rite.
(The Worship of the Sacrificial Hall):

Then, following the previously described method for performing the auspicious rite of the sprouts (*maṅgalāṅkura*), the worship of the sacrificial hall (*yāgaśālārcanā*) follows. In front of the deity, or in the northeast, southeast, north, or west—having provided a western entrance to a pavilion measuring five cubits or more—one should construct in its center an altar as prescribed, together with a mirror-like surface and a secondary altar. Outside of that, from the east to the northeast in sequence, the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*) are to be made: the triangle, the semi-circle, the crescent moon, the triangle, the circle, the hexagon, the lotus, and the octagon.

Between Indra and Īśāna, there should be either a circle, a square, or, according to the five-fold system, a circle as the primary [fire-pit] in the northeast and squares in the four directions. Alternatively, having made one [central pit] circular and square, and having smeared it with cow dung, one should arrange the canopy, banners, garlands of *darbha* grass, and so forth; the eight auspicious objects at the gates, namely: the mirror, the full water-jar, the lamp, and the other six auspicious emblems of the gods.

Having prepared this weapon—consisting of the vajra, the śakti, the staff, and the discus—together with the collection of implements such as the sacrificial knife and ladle, the ritual procedure for worshipping the sacrificial hall follows immediately after the ascent.
(The Ritual Procedure for the Weapon [Astra] Sacrifice:

The preceptor, together with the officiating priests, having performed the evening twilight (*sāyaṃ-sandhyā*) and the special twilight (*viśeṣa-sandhyā*) rites, enters the temple. Having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) before the deity and sprinkled it with water empowered by the *astra-mantra*, he washes the jars—which are well-polished, provided with handles, and made of gold, silver, or clay up to earthenware; which are equipped with *kūrca*-grass bundles, lids, fine cloths, sprouts, and threads; and which are endowed with gold, gems, and other such items according to the prescribed characteristics—using water empowered by the *astra-mantra*. He then fumigates them with incense.

Having filled [the vessels] with scented water using the *hṛdaya* mantra, one should place the *śivakumbha* in the center upon the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) and the *vardhanī* to the north, and then arrange eight jars around them. (l. 6) One should worship the *kumbha* with the *mūrti-mantra* and the *vardhanī* with the *śakti* mantra, and then worship the jars beginning with Ananta and ending with Śikhaṇḍin. Having summoned the attendants, starting with Nandin and ending with the weapons, and having placed the *śivakumbha* and *vardhanī* in their respective positions, one should hold them in sequence. (p. 35b, f. 32a, l. 1)

Having circumambulated the celestial chariot (*vimāna*)—which extends from the *vajra* to the *cakra*—with the sounds of conchs and drums and the chanting of the Vedas and other scriptures, and having entered the sacrificial hall (*yāgaśālā*), one should scatter in the center of the altar (*vedikā*) eight *droṇas* of rice, half as much of husked grain (*taṇḍula*), half as much of sesame seeds and parched grain (*lāja*), and the seven types of grains. Having established the *śivakumbha* and the *vardhanī*, as well as the jars of the *vidyeśvaras*, in the midst of that [scattering], one should install [the deities] beginning with Dharma and ending with Sūrya in their respective places.

The preceptor, together with the officiating priests and the patron, having first performed the worship of Vināyaka and caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited; having performed the worship of the Sun as usual; having dismissed [the deities]; having sipped water for ritual purification (*ācamana*); having performed the ritual of self-protection (*sakalīkaraṇa*); having prepared the general offering of water (*sāmānyārghya*); and having worshipped the doors starting from the east—having worshipped two [deities] at each door, beginning with Nandin and ending with Caṇḍa, as before; having propitiated the permanent door-keepers in the west; and having worshipped Vāstunātha in the southwest (Nairṛta).

Having seated [the disciple] facing west to the south of the Brahmā-throne, and having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and so forth, as well as the special *arghya* offering, one should adorn oneself and the image-keepers (*mūrtipāḥ*) with perfumes and other offerings up to the *uṣṇīṣa*. Having prepared the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) according to the prescribed rite, and having purified the pavilion with water mixed with the *pañcagavya*, one should worship the *śivakumbha* and the *vardhanī* vessel as before, up to the recitation of mantras. Then, having meditated upon the world-protectors (*lokapālāḥ*) together with their vehicles and weapons, one should worship them.

Having worshipped Mahālakṣmī, Gaṇapati, and the lineage of gurus, he should cause all [the participants] to hear the command of Śiva. Then, having sat down to the south of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), he should worship the seat in the *śivakumbha* from Śakti up to the final Śakti. Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) by means of the postures of the staff (*daṇḍabhaṅgi*), the shaven head (*muṇḍabhaṅgi*), the face (*vaktrabhaṅgi*), and the digit (*kalābhaṅgi*), and having meditated upon and invoked Śiva—endowed with all the paths—as previously described, he should perform the placement of Śrīkaṇṭha in the *vardhanī* vessel [visualizing her as]:
two-armed, with a beautiful face, full breasts, and in the prime of youth.
Clad in fine linen, peaceful, with a slightly smiling face.
One should meditate upon the Goddess in due order, seated upon a throne, adorned with all ornaments, and wearing a crown and a casket.

Having meditated thus, having invoked [the deities] by means of their root-mantras, and having worshipped them with the fivefold enclosure (*pañcāvaraṇa*) and the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), one should present the food offering (*naivedya*) and the recitation (*japa*). Having offered these and praised them, and having made the request, one should worship Dharma and the others in the corners starting from the southeast (*āgneya*). Then, having proclaimed the command of Śiva, they should proceed to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Having performed the rites beginning with the consecration of the pit up to the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should divide the fire into nine or five parts and cast it into the pits starting from the east.

Having worshipped each respective Śiva along with his limbs, they should perform oblations in the various fire-pits (kuṇḍas), including the offerings of cooked rice (caru), the fire-entry (havana), and the expiatory rites (prāyaścitta), accompanied by the recitation of the [specific] mantras. Having especially worshipped the stone in each of those pits: an Aśvattha tree in the east, an Udumbara in the south, a Plakṣa in the west, and a Vaṭa in the north; a Śamī in the southeast, a Khadira in the southwest, a Māyūra in the northwest, and a Śrīvṛkṣa in the northeast. However, the Palāśa tree should be used for the principal [fire-pit], and it is approved for all locations.

Having offered beautiful parched grains, mustard seeds, barley, sesame, mung beans, black gram, peas, chickpeas, and *kulattha* and mustard seeds, they should perform oblations at the end of each substance with the root mantra one hundred and eight times, or a thousand times, or half that number, together with the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). Having performed the salutation to the ears, having restrained the fire, and having caused the protection of the *homa* as well as the protection of the root-mantra, the *liṅga*, and so forth to be bestowed, he himself, together with the officiating priests, having taken up the trident and brought it there to either the northeast or the northwest, should install it.
One should perform it in this very manner every day, both evening and morning; thus ends the ritual procedure for the weapon-sacrifice (*astrayāga*).
Now follows the ritual procedure for binding the protective thread (*rakṣābandhana*):

Then, from among golden, silvered, or cotton threads, one should take a protective thread (*rakṣāsūtra*) consisting of [threads spun on] an auspicious day, fierce, and ninefold; sixteen finger-breadths in length, equal in girth to the *liṅga*, and equal to the stalk of the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*). Having filled the base with rice, parched grain, and flowers, and having drawn a lotus in its center and placed the thread upon it, one should place ashes, turmeric, *dūrvā* grass, perfumes, flowers, fruits, gold, betel, and so forth all around. Then, that thread should be purified with the *tryambaka* mantra and with ashes.

Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and having worshipped [the deity] preceded by the sixfold rising from the seat (*ṣaḍutthāsanapūrva*), having offered incense and lamps and circumambulated the temple, he enters within, worships Śiva, offers incense and lamps, meditates upon [the goddess] Sukī, and—having held [the image] in the center of the *liṅga* with the root mantra—binds it to the pedestal at the level of the palm with that same root mantra. Having applied ashes with the *tryambaka* mantra and having placed turmeric (*rajani*) upon that...

Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, one should bind the *kautuka* on the middle petal of the King of Weapons (*astrarāja*). For the primary images (*bera*) of the deities beginning with Astra and ending with Bhakta, one should bind it on the right hand using the *triyaṃbaka* mantra together with the *hṛdaya* [mantra]. For the three female images beginning with Gaurī, one should bind the *kautuka* on the left hand using the root-mantra of Gaurī. Having bound the *kautuka* for oneself, for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), for the bearer of the sacrificial offering (*balivāhaka*), for the drummer (*bherītāḍa*), and for the ten weapons, one should then apply ashes and powder over them.

Having placed the *kautuka* (protective thread) upon the middle of the flagpole, one should bind it very firmly with a flower at the knots together with *rajanī*. To all [the participants], one should give powdered *rajanī*, gold, fruit, betel, and so forth. This is the ritual for binding the protective thread (*rakṣābandhana-vidhi*).
Then Bali [should perform the rite]:

at the great festival, in the evening or in the morning, he should offer the *bali* sacrifice, either from the station of Brahmā (*brahmasthāna*) up to the flagpole (*dhvaja*), or from the bull (*vṛṣa*) and so forth up to the *balipīṭha*. It is as follows: in the stations beginning with the station of Brahmā, one should construct a pedestal (*pīṭha*) made of stone, brick, or solid wood, possessing the correct characteristics. It should be seven units in length, half that in width, and twelve or eight *aṅgulas* in thickness, provided with three layers of clouds (*meghalātra*). Alternatively, it may be fashioned from clay or plaster, equipped with a single pedestal, a pericarp (*karṇikā*), and eight petals. One should fashion these pedestals according to the rules.

Having adorned each respective direction with five powders, one should cook either one *droṇa* or half a *droṇa* of rice. Taking [the cooked food] in a vessel for offerings (*balipātra*), one should sprinkle it thoroughly with the weapon-mantra (*astra*). Having brought half of that into another pot, one should fashion the rice into the form of a *liṅga* possessing the proper characteristics and meditate upon it:
on the right, joined with a trident, endowed with a fierce gaze, adorned with serpent ornaments, with hair standing erect, and likewise with bulging eyes.
One should worship this divine Pāśupata [mantra] in the center of the *liṅga*.

Alternatively—having worshipped Śiva as before—the Preceptor (ācārya), together with the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), equipped with the ten weapons and royal insignia, adorned from the sacred ash up to the turban (*uṣṇīṣa*), accompanied by attendants, provided with various banners, parasols, chowries, and so forth, along with the sounds of various musical instruments, bells, and the chanting of the Vedas (*brahmaghoṣa*), and accompanied by dancers, singers, and musicians, should present the sacrificial offering (*bali*).

Regarding the special *bali* offerings for the nine-day festival (*navāhotsava*), they are stated in order: on the first day, [offer] to Vighnarāja, svāhā; on the second day, to the Bhūtas, svāhā; on the third, to the Ṛṣis; on the fourth, to Indra; on the fifth day, to Brahmā; on the sixth, to Viṣṇu; on the seventh, to Rudra; on the eighth, to Īśvara; on the ninth day, to Sadāśiva, svāhā. On these days, at the conclusion of the worship of the *haviḥ-liṅga*, one should perform the rite by casting pure food mixed with clarified butter and soaked in curd, in the measure of a hen’s egg.

The special offering (*viśeṣabali*): at the cow-pen—to Rudra Kumbhodara; on the *kuśa* grass—to Laṅkā; among the *nandī* plants—to Gaṅgā; at the pond—to Kṣetramūrti; at the assembly hall—to Sarasvatī; in the treasury—to Darbhā; at the main gate—to Mahālakṣmī; and [at the door]—to Bhīma, with the formula "Svāhā! Thus one should offer the oblation in the evening and in the morning. Having entered into dissolution (*laya*) from the station of Brahmā (*brahmasthāna*) up to the pedestal (*pīṭha*) or up to the staff (*daṇḍa*), one should cast the remainder upon the offering pedestal (*balipīṭha*). Then, having discarded the food-linga into the water.

Having washed one's feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and having smeared oneself with pure ashes, one should enter; such is the procedure for the circumambulation of the offering (balibhramaṇa).
Now, the procedure for the procession (*yānakrama*):

Having adorned [the deity] according to the previously mentioned rite, one should bring the Lord—accompanied by Śakti and endowed with various ornaments, flowers, and radiance—from His primary abode to a chariot, a stage, a palanquin, a litter, or similar vehicle; having invoked Him there, offered incense and lamps, and worshipped Him with a handful of flowers, one should begin the circumambulation together with the *beras* (images) beginning with Śakti and ending with Bhakta.

In front [of the image], accompanied by various ornaments and musical instruments such as kettledrums (*bherī*), [the priest should place] Śaila and the others; in the space between them, Nandin and Vināyaka; and Subrahmaṇya in the middle together with the Goddess. To the left or right of the front, Soma and Skanda, and in front or behind, the devotees and the *bherās*. Behind those, the preceptor (*deśika*) should place Caṇḍeśvara. Standing in his respective position, he should recite the *mūla-mantra* or the *aghora-mantra* a specific number of times. In front stands the king.

Behind [the deity], accompanied by the sounds of the Vedas and other scriptures, and following after them, those born of the four castes and the devotees of Maheśvara obtain the fruit of the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*). Having thus gratified the God: on the first day, at dawn, [one should offer] a *rāga*; at night, a *haṃsa*. On the second day, the *sūryasomayantra*; on the third, the *bhūtayantra*; at night, a *siṃha*. On the fourth day, a *nāga*; at night, one should perform the serving of food within the interval of the circumambulation of the bull.

For example: in gardens and similar places, at a designated spot, accompanied by those who recite the Vedas, offer praise, play flutes and lutes, sing, dance, and by groups of *rudra* performers and courtesans, one should gratify the Lord at every step with offerings of fruits and the like, as well as betel and other items, and then lead him into the temple. On the fifth day, [the image] should be placed upon a mechanical carriage (*rāvaṇayantra*) equipped with a palanquin on its top. On the sixth day, having mounted it upon a litter (*śibikā*) or a sedan chair (*ghaṭaka*), one should perform the powder festival (*cūrṇotsava*) as will be described below.

Having bathed the deities with water consisting of saffron, flowers, turmeric, and other substances, and having anointed them all with saffron paste, one should sprinkle them. On the sixth day, [the bathing of] the elephant; on the seventh, the chariot; and on the eighth, having performed the mounting of the horses, at the time of the procession, the Rudra-prostitutes—mounted on horses, bearing weapons such as spears and the like, equipped with bows and shields, and adorned with all ornaments—should circumambulate [the deity]. In the meantime, one should carry out the suppression of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous.

Having caused all the *dharma* and *adharma* [of the deceased] to be proclaimed, one should cause them to enter into dissolution (*laya*). On the ninth day, [the image] should be placed on a swing (*āndolikā*) equipped with a human mechanism and a bell. At night, black incense should be offered. On the tenth day, having seated the deity upon a lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*) of jewels and having circumambulated the city and other sites, one should carry him around in a distorted manner on the roof of a palace or atop a banner, and then cast him into a crossroads (*catuṣpatha*). [Then follows the ritual for the waving of lights (*nīrājanavidhi*): On the roof of a palace or atop a banner, having carried him around in a distorted manner, one should cast him into that crossroads.

Immediately thereafter, the preceptor should have the *nīrāñjana* rite performed by married women (*suvāsinī*) or by the attendants of Rudra (*rudragaṇikā*). Then, having offered a lamp in a water-vessel (*ghaṭadīpa*) to the deity, the attendants of Rudra—carrying the *ārātrika* lamp together with the vessel-lamp and holding the *nīrāñjana*—should perform circumambulations in due order accompanied by dance, song, and all kinds of musical instruments. Having thus circumambulated the temple in the morning along with Śailādi, Nandin, Vināyaka, Skanda, Devī, Bhakta, and Caṇḍeśvara, they should proceed [to their respective places].

Then, having caused [the deity] to enter the temple of Somāskanda accompanied by auspicious songs (*maṅgalagāthā*) and all musical instruments, and having established him in the pavilion or other location, one should draw a curtain. Having offered the great oblation (*mahāhavis*), and having worshipped with all ritual services (*upacāra*), one should offer coconut juice, sugarcane juice, *mudga* beans, and fruits appropriate for that time, up until the removal of fatigue. Having adorned the Brahmins with perfumes and flowers, one should feed them. One should also feed the devotees of Śiva and others, including the blind and the like, without discrimination.
Alternatively, one may construct the vehicle in another manner; thus ends the procedure for the sequence of the vehicle.
Now, the procedure for the *nīrājana* rite:

For the purpose of the *nīrājana*, one should take five vessels made of gold, silver, copper, or bell-metal, each with a width of one *vitasti* and a rim (*oṣṭha*) of one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*). Having placed them upon the mandala, one should worship them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using the fire-seed syllable (*agnibīja*) and the Brahma-mantras. Having consecrated them with the four purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), and having displayed the trident-mudrā (*śūlamudrā*) and the cow-mudrā (*dhenumudrā*), one should take lamps filled with clarified butter along with hymns of benediction (*svastisūkta*) and auspicious recitations. Placing [the vessels] upon one's head and circumambulating [the deity], [one performs the rite].

Having placed [the image] before the deity in the mandala, one should rotate it three times each from the head down to the feet while reciting the Brahma-mantras. Having offered the mirror, umbrella, chowries, fan, ashes, and so forth, and having presented a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to Śiva with the root mantra (*mūla*), one should prostrate. Then, having had it carried by courtesans as before, accompanied by musical instruments and the like, one should cast it either before the pedestal (*pīṭha*) or before the bull (*vṛṣa*). After performing the washing of the feet and other rites, one should enter the temple; such is the procedure for the *nīrājana* rite.

Now, the procedure for the collection of the *tīrtha* [sacred water]: Hariḥ Om. (l. 6) Now, on the day prior to that of the *tīrtha*, one should collect the *tīrtha*. Having performed the protection (*rakṣā*) as before and having had the benedictions (*āśis*) recited, one should prepare a single sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in the middle of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) as before. (p. 40b, f. 37a, cūrṇotsavam, l. 1) Having placed the vessel for the *manonmanī* in the center and eight vessels around it, [one should place] in the center—
[One should meditate on her] possessing the radiance of a perfected gem, three-eyed, adorned with a digit of the nectar-moon, wearing a red iron crest-ornament,
bent by the weight of full and lofty breasts, at the onset of youth,
endowed with various ornaments, residing in a lotus, and whose form is transferred through the seed-syllable.
"I bow to the Goddess, the source of the universe, who is adorned with the noose and the goad, and who grants the gestures of fearlessness and boons.

Having meditated thus and having performed worship, he [should worship] in the eight jars starting from the east: "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Gaṅgā; salutation to Yamunā; salutation to Narmadā; salutation to Sarasvatī; salutation to Sindhu; salutation to Godāvarī; salutation to Kāverī; salutation to Tāmraparṇī. Having worshipped them with all the ritual offerings beginning with the invocation, and having invoked [the deity] upon his head along with the weapon-mantra, he should circumambulate the city accompanied by all musical instruments.
"Having caused [him] to enter for the purpose of bathing at the Nandī and other sacred fords (tīrtha), this is the procedure for the collection of the sacred fords."

Now, the procedure for the powder festival (*cūrṇotsava*): On the days of the gathering at the sacred sites (*tīrtha*), one should begin the powder [rite] after the offering of the *bali*. (p. 41a, l. 1) Having drawn two lotuses on two altars (*sthaṇḍila*) in front of the temple, having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), and having strewn them with *darbha* grass, one should install a trident (*śūla*) on one of them. Having fashioned a mortar and pestle from trees such as the *plakṣa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, or *vaṭa*, and making them marked with the proper characteristics from *khadira* wood, one should place them on the other altar, sprinkle them with water while reciting the *astra-mantra*, and consecrate them with the four purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*).

Having wrapped the mortar (*lūkhala*) and pestle (*musala*) with a cloth, and having worshipped the three mortars in the center as dedicated to Brahmā, one should worship the eight jars of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) surrounding the *rudrakumbha*. Alternatively, having worshipped Śiva, one should place *dūrvā* grass together with the *devīkoṣṭha*, turmeric, oil, ghee, betel, fruit, fragrance, flowers, and ashes upon the petals starting from the east around the mortar; then, having consecrated them with the four purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), one should worship the Earth in the mortar and Meru in the pestle.

Having cast that into a mortar, with either the *Padamantra* or a hymn of praise (*bhaktastotra*), [the officiant] should have it ground by courtesans using strokes of a pestle. Then, mixing the powder with oil and taking the powder along with gold in the hand of the preceptor (*ācārya*), he should cause it to be applied together with ashes to the primary image (*mūlaliṅga*). Having placed a turban of saffron (*kuṅkumoṣṇīṣa*) upon it, smeared it with that paste, offered it, and presented incense and lamps, he should likewise smear all the other images (*bera*) with that same preparation.

Having displayed the lotus mudrā and holding it oneself, and having given the *uṣṇīṣa*, betel, and other offerings to everyone, one should circumambulate the city and so forth together with the trident and enter the temple. Alternatively, one should worship the *astrakumbha* and the *vajra* and other vessels. This is the ritual procedure for the powder festival (*cūrṇotsava*).
(The Ritual for Bathing at a Sacred Site [Tīrthasnānavidhi]:

Thereafter, having placed the hand upon the previous spot, one should perform the bath at the sacred site (*tīrthasnāna*). For the purpose of removing the fault of touching those who should not be touched by anyone, for the sake of attaining the grace of the sacred site, for the sake of attaining the fruit of all the gods until the end of the aeon (*yugasamāpta*), and for the sake of attaining the state of *sāloka* and other realms, [one should worship] the gods—having performed the preliminary rites (*praghādika*)—along with the *antardhānika* jar on the bank of the sacred site, accompanied by conchs, drums, cymbals, the moon, Skanda, and others, as well as sprouts, umbrellas, chowries, various musical instruments, the chanting of the Vedas, and hymns of praise.

Having established [the altar], and having placed upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) before it the eight jars of the Gaṅgā and others, as well as the *aghora*-vessels and *pālikās*, and having specially worshipped them; having invoked Durgā in the northeast and performed the invocation of the thirty-three deities, the eighteen classes, and the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) in the vicinity of the trident; and having released the *kautuka* of the deities beginning with the Weapon (*astra*), one should cast [it] into the center of the sacred ford (*tīrtha*).

Having consecrated [the deity] with the respective vessels, beginning from Śiva and ending with the weapons (*astra*), together with the *pālikās*, one should perform the ritual bath along with all the people. (l. 3) Then the Preceptor, having dismissed the deities of the sacred waters (*tīrtha*) and entered the temple, should consecrate the individual vessel for each of the deities. Having offered food offerings (*naivedya*), incense, lamps, and so forth, and having entered the temple, while all remain in their places accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas (*brahmaghoṣa*), the Preceptor should place the consecrated rice grains (*āślakṣata*) into the hands [of the participants]. The Teacher (*deśika*), preceded by a benediction (*āśīrvāda*), should cause them to enter their respective places. This is the procedure for the ritual bath at the sacred waters (*tīrthasnānavidhi*).
Now, the procedure for the ritual bath of the jar (*ghaṭasnānavidhi*):

For the sake of fulfilling the festival of Hara, for the purpose of ensuring the stability of the people, for the attainment of grace (*prasāda*), and for the accomplishment of proximity to the deities such as Indra and others, one should perform the ritual of the jar-bath. Having specifically performed the fire-oblation (*homa*) in the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*), they should offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) into the pits. (L. 2) Having joined [the offerings] to their respective directions within the principal [pit], and having worshipped Śiva, and having again offered the full oblation, and having specially worshipped the Śiva-jar and the other vessels, and having joined them together, one should offer incense and lamps.

Having given the prescribed sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor and others, and having given garments, gold, and so forth to the attendants and others; having lifted the jars as before and circumambulated the temple; and having placed them within the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*), one should perform the consecration (*abhiṣecana*) upon the primary liṅga preceded by the ritual deposition (*nyāsa*) of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*). Having consecrated the *vardhanī* jar on the pedestal and the jars of the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśa*) in their respective directions; and having consecrated the Goddess with a jar preceded by the ritual deposition of Śrīkaṇṭha, one should present the great oblation (*mahāhavis*).

Having offered incense and lamps, he should go to the fire-sanctuary. Having offered more than a hundred oblations into the Śiva-fire with his own head [as the vessel] while reciting the root mantra and the Aghora-weapon mantra, and having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), he should unite the fire with the Lord of Sacrifice (*yāgeśa*). According to the method instructed by the Guru, having united the deities of the five enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇa*)—the Kumbha, Vardhanī, and the rest—with their respective locations, he should dismiss them. Having offered abundant sacrificial food (*havis*), he should perform the ritual bathing (*snāna*) for the image; such is the procedure for the pot-bath (*ghaṭasnānavidhi*).

For the purpose of suppressing the wicked and protecting the virtuous, one should perform the afternoon rites preceded by the recitation of the *Bṛhattāla* hymn during the long day—beginning with the forenoon—or at night. Having yoked the God, in the most excellent manner, to a bull while he stands upon a banner, and having mounted the bull upon the form situated before Śiva, and having joined the deities of the enclosure to that enclosure, one should worship according to the prescribed ritual. On that day, there is the silent offering (*maunabali*).
(The silent offering:)

Since it has been stated that [the offering] belongs to the deities who share in the oblation at the conclusion of the *homa*, one should begin the silent *bali* offering for that purpose. The *ācārya*, having gone near Soma and Skanda, and having worshipped [the deities] beginning with Śakti and ending with Śakti, should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the thirty-one digits (*kalā*)—namely the *daṇḍabhaṅgi* and *muṇḍabhaṅgi*—as well as the *śrīkaṇṭha-nyāsa*, and then meditate:
"[He is] black, with his left foot resting on the right knee, bestowing boons and fearlessness;
and with his left [hand], he holds a *ṭaṅka* and a bracelet."
I worship Guheśa, who is joined in the middle by the Goddess, whose two feet rest upon his left side as he sleeps,
and who is accompanied by Skanda with his two hands holding a lotus.

Having thus performed worship along with the limbs and the fivefold enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇa*), having meditated upon and worshipped the Goddess as will be described below, and having prayed for the welfare of the world; then, having received permission from her, observing a vow of silence and joining his palms in *añjali*, he places the goddesses beginning with the Weapon (*astra*)—accompanied by the *annaliṅga*—upon the vehicle.

Equipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as well as swords, shields, weapons, and the like, assuming many forms while moving within the heart, observing a vow of silence, and without the sound of musical instruments, [the practitioners] should offer the *bali* at the junctions such as the *brahmasthāna*, at the sacred seats (*pīṭhas*), or at those respective locations—preceded by the lowering of the banner accompanied by the sound of musical instruments. Having dismissed the deities of the junctions in due order as before, and having circumambulated the temple, they should enter and descend.
Having placed [the offerings] in the previous location, one should dismiss all of them into food, a liṅga, or water; such is the procedure for the descent (*avarohaṇa*).
Now, the procedure for the Caṇḍotsava:

thereafter, having brought the image of Caṇḍa into the sacrificial hall, having consecrated it with its [own] water-pot (*kumbha*), having worshipped it according to the rules, and having adorned it with the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*) and so forth; having offered a hundred, a thousand, or half that number of oblations into the fire as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*); and having dismissed even him, one should circumambulate the temple together with devotees in the form of a triangle, and install him in his place—this is the procedure for the Caṇḍotsava.

(The Procedure for the Feast of the Preceptor)—Thereafter, one should worship the preceptor and cause him to receive a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). One should bestow gifts ranging from cattle, land, gems, gold, and jewels down to garments. The satisfaction of the preceptor’s mind is [the goal]; therefore, his satisfaction is Supreme Śiva. (l. 5) Having thus worshipped him along with the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) as if he were Śiva himself, one should place him upon a chariot, a palanquin, or similar conveyance.

Accompanied by various musical instruments, dances, songs, and the like; by the chanting of the Vedas and other scriptures; by hymns of praise from the devotees; and with various kinds of lamps such as those for the royal parasol and fly-whisks—having circumambulated the city together with the king, the patron, and all the people, he should cause [the image] to enter his own home by means of a vehicle. This is the procedure for the festival of the Preceptor (*ācāryotsava*).

(The Ritual for Ascending the Chariot—) Or, on the seventh [day], the mounting of the great chariot (*mahāratha*) should be performed. Having performed the binding of the protective cord (*rakṣābandhana*) during the first part of the night, and having performed the ritual bathing and consecration (*abhiṣeka*) at dawn following the morning ablutions, and having completed the daily worship; then, according to the procedure for the sacrificial bed (*śayyādhāvidhi*), one should perform the oblation of the *caru* offering according to the path prescribed for the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), ending with the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) as before. [One should offer]: ghee with the Root Mantra (*mūla*); fuel-sticks (*samidh*) with the Īśa-mantra; the *caru* with the Aghora-mantra; parched grain (*lāja*) with the Heart-mantra; sesame with the Vāma-mantra; *gulā* with the Armor-mantra; and wood-apple (*bilva*) with the Eye-mantra.

Having offered oblations according to one's capacity with the *Īśāna* mantra, having offered grains and other materials with the *Hṛdaya* mantra, and having offered oblations with the *Vyāhṛtis*, one should give the *pūrṇāhuti*. Having restrained the Lord of the Sacrifice (*Yāgeśa*) and entrusted him to protection, one should present a full water-pot, a vessel of sesame seeds, and a cow with its calf, and then give [these] to the Brahmins. Having fully worshipped Vighneśa and offered sweetmeats (*modaka*), one should offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*) to the deities.

Afterwards, having prepared [the clay] in a silver basin with saffron, agallochum, camphor, sandalwood, turmeric, and so forth; or, having placed *pāṭala*, blue lotus, jasmine, *puṇnāga*, *campaka*, and other flowers into the mud within the basin; having wrapped the basin with saffron-colored cloth and the like; having set it down upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) before Śiva; having worshipped the mud while wet with the seed-syllable of Kāma (*kāma-bīja*) and with the root-mantra (*mūla*) in the basin; and having consecrated it by offering incense and lamps.

The preceptor, having likewise applied [the paste] to the primary liṅga and other images, together with the officiating priests, shall himself don a turban moistened with mud and saffron. He should then give turbans moistened with mud to the patron, the devotees, and all other people. Afterwards, having sprinkled the chariot with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the water of the *puṇyāha* rite, and having consecrated the chariot with the four purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), he should mount the deity upon it and establish it there.

One should worship all the gods upon the chariot. On the wheels: *oṃ hāṃ sūryāya namaḥ* (Salutation to Sūrya); *candramase namaḥ* (Salutation to Candra). Around [the wheels]: *haraye namaḥ* (Salutation to Hari); *vajriṇe namaḥ* (Salutation to Vajrin). On the single pole: *dvidaṇḍakāya namaḥ* (Salutation to Dvidaṇḍaka). Having thus worshipped, [one should worship] on the banners the *Śatarudras*; on the limbs, *Dharma* and the others; on the pedestal (*sthalikā*), *sadāśivāya namaḥ* (Salutation to Sadāśiva). At the joints: *dakṣiṇāmūrtaye namaḥ* (Salutation to Dakṣiṇāmūrti); *viṣṇave namaḥ* (Salutation to Viṣṇu); *brahmaṇe namaḥ* (Salutation to Brahmā); *skandāya namaḥ* (Salutation to Skanda).

Having thus worshipped; at the edge of the chariot—the world-protectors (*lokapālas*); in the ropes—"Salutation to the serpents" (*uragebhyaḥ*); having worshipped in this sequence, and having adorned [the chariot] with various cloths, garments, and so forth; having made it beautiful in the cardinal and intermediate directions and at the sides of the doors with lions, plantain trees, betel-nut palms, pillars, coconuts, and various cloths; having appointed Brahmā as the charioteer; having invoked the *Pāśupata* weapon along with the parasol; and having worshipped the bull upon the banner—one should meditate [upon him] as five-colored, greatly radiant, granting fearlessness and bestowing boons.
He has six feet, a single belly, and four arms holding a trident and a noose.

Having one face and three eyes, possessing six parts and endowed with auspiciousness; its foot is joined with a wheel, it is the support of the elements, and it is moistened by skin. Its *pauḍha* part is called the beautiful knee, and the upper part is the thigh.
The belly is said to be the seat of the gods, and the heart is the group of pillars.
The two shoulders are declared to be the peak (*kūṭa*), and the throat is said to be the earring (*karṇa*).
The head is the crest (*śikhā*) and the tuft (*cūli*), while the charioteer and the path are established [therein].
This meditation on the chariot is proclaimed as the cause of all auspiciousness.

Having meditated thus, one should perform worship. In this manner, having mounted the Goddess, Skanda, Vināyaka, and Caṇḍeśvara upon their respective chariots, and having smeared them with vermilion while reciting the *hṛdaya* mantra; having donned the *kaṅkama*-helmet while reciting the *uṣṇīṣa* and the *kavaca* mantras; having offered fruits, cakes, and so forth; having worshipped them with red flowers; and having given gifts—having bestowed various foods, garments, gold, fruits, betel, and so on upon the preceptor and the other devotees—and having satisfied everyone.

At an auspicious moment within a favorable portion of the day, having first performed a rite of well-being (*svasti*), and having circumambulated the city accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments, [the image] should be lowered from the chariot and brought into the temple. After performing the preliminary bathing and bathing [the deity], and having bestowed garments and other gifts upon the artisans and the chariot drivers, one should present a great sacrificial offering (*mahāhavis*) and cause it to be distributed to everyone. Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the mounting of the chariot.
Hereafter follows the procedure for black aloe-wood (*kṛṣṇagandha*): it is the cause for the attainment of desired objects and the birth of excellent sons;
it destroys faults such as the killing of a Brahmin and annihilates all enemies.

Whoever, be they anyone at all, enjoys the fruit resulting from the sight of the dancing form: following that—having brought the dancing form into the assembly pavilion (*maṇṭapa*), having performed the protection ritual as before on the evening of the eighth day; having placed fruits, betel, and so forth in their hands; having adorned both of them with variegated garments and the like; having offered food offerings (*naivedya*) and the rest; having circumambulated the temple; and having established [the image] in the pavilion—one should pass the remainder of the night by viewing the entertainment. On the following day, after having conducted the conclusion of the festival, one should prepare two sacrificial mounds (*sthaṇḍila*) in front of the deity in the evening.

Having drawn a lotus, having strewn it around with *darbha* grass and flowers, and having placed gālāgaru in its center, one should perform the recitation of the *puṇyāha* preceded by the worship of Vināyaka. Having duly worshipped the *śāntikumbha* in two ways, and having performed the rites from the consecration of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍasaṃskāra*) up to the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) according to the procedure prescribed for the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), one should worship Maheśa therein. Then, having offered *śamī*, parched rice, mustard seeds, barley, sesame seeds, and so forth—one hundred and eight times each—with their respective root-mantras, [the rite is completed].

Having offered *bilva*, blue lotus, plantain, breadfruit, and so forth, as well as the three sweets (*madhutraya*); having offered the *vyāhṛtis* at the conclusion of the substances; having presented the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*); having bathed the deity and adorned him; having placed black fragrant paste (*kṛṣṇagandha*) in a small vessel filled with rice; having wrapped it with a cloth; having sprinkled it with water from the peace-vessel (*śāntikumbha*); having mixed it with camphor and other perfumes; having purified it with the *astra-mantra* and concealed it with the *varma-mantra*.

Having consecrated [the materials] with the limbs of Brahmā and worshipped them with the root mantra; having displayed the *dhenumudrā*; having offered water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the guest-offering (*arghya*), incense, lamps, and so forth; having performed the oblation of the residual drops (*sampātābhihuta*); having completed the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and dismissed the fire; and having circumambulated the temple accompanied by the sounding of conchs, drums, and musical instruments, one should enter the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*), offer [the deity] to the primary *liṅga*, and subsequently install it before Maheśa.

Having performed the placement (nyāsa) upon the seat beginning with Śakti and ending with Śakti, having worshipped with the forms of the staff and the skull, and having placed the Lord Śrīkaṇṭha— who consists of a hundred kalās—
[the practitioner] should meditate [upon him] as having matted hair, the moon, gold, a crow, an enemy’s head, bones, and the celestial river (Gaṅgā).
From the white [deity], one should visualize [the deity] bearing a *ḍamaru*, a staff, and a yellow garment, clad in a tiger-skin loincloth;
with his right hand extended holding a snake and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), and his left hand holding fire; he is reclining upon a green serpent and stands upon a bed of ashes.
Having bent his right foot and raised his left,
he stands with his feet adorned by sandals shimmering with millions of jewels, small bells, and banners, positioned between the two [legs].

I worship the Lord of Dancers, Śiva, who is smeared with ashes, joined by Umā, and possesses three eyes; he has Dakṣa at his ear-ornament, Vaktra on his left ear-lobe, and is united with Gaurī, Kalā, Naya, and Savi. (Gaurīkalānayāsavidhi, p. 46b, f. 43a, l. 1)

Having thus invoked [the deity], and having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the Goddess and of Śrīkaṇṭha—who consists of twenty-five kalās—one should meditate as follows: *Oṃ himāyai namaḥ* | on the head. *Vidyāyai namaḥ* | on the face. *Mṛtyave namaḥ* | on the heart. *Śuddhāyai namaḥ* | on the ear. *Jarāyai namaḥ* | on the right arm. *Medhāyai namaḥ* | on the left arm. *Svadhāyai namaḥ* | on the belly. *Swastyai namaḥ* | on the navel. *Pālinyai namaḥ* | on the vulva.

Salutation to Jvālinī; at the secret place (*guhya*). Salutation to Kṛṣṇā; on the right thigh. Salutation to Smṛti; on the left thigh. Salutation to Kṣamā; on the right knee. Salutation to Mati; on the left knee. Salutation to Prajā; on the right shank. Salutation to Cintā; on the left shank. Salutation to Dhṛti; on the back. Salutation to Kriyā; on the right side. Salutation to Kṣānti; on the left side. Salutation to Śānti; on the left foot. Salutation to Bhrānti.

On the right foot: *namaḥ* to Compassion (*dayā*). On the right hand: *namaḥ* to Mindfulness (*smṛti*). On the left hand: *namaḥ* to Fortitude (*dhṛti*). On the right breast: *namaḥ* to Twilight (*saṃdhyā*). On the left breast: *namaḥ* to the Body of Knowledge (*vidyādeha*). At the heart: *namaḥ* to the Three Eyes (*netratraya*). In the eyes: *oṃ hrīṃ*, *namaḥ* to the Heart (*hṛdaya*). At the heart: *namaḥ* to the Head (*śiras*). On the head: *namaḥ* to the Crest (*śikhā*). On the crest: *namaḥ* to the Armor (*kavaca*). To the armor: *namaḥ*.

With the mantra "Astrāyai namaḥ," one performs the snapping of the fingers. Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of Śrīkaṇṭha according to the previously mentioned method, one should meditate [on her] as follows:
dark-complexioned, two-eyed, two-armed, possessing the triple bend (*tribhaṅgī*), with her right and left feet placed in a bent position.
Or the Supreme Goddess may have her hand resting [on his shoulder], adorned with a bracelet and a blue lotus.

Having thus worshipped both [deities], offered incense and lamps, presented an offering (*naivedya*) consisting of flour-cakes, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), fruits, sweetmeats (*apūpa*), and so forth, and given betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*), one should apply the black fragrant unguent (*kṛṣṇagandha*). One should cause it to be applied on the forehead with the *ghora* mantra, on the crest-lock with the *śikhā* mantra, and on the arms with the *sadyojāta* mantra; or one may cause it to be applied everywhere with the *sadyojāta* mantra alone. Thereafter, one should cause it to be applied to the forms (*mūrti*) beginning with Sadāśiva. For the thread-images (*sūtrabera*), one should apply it on the forehead, the neck, or the heart with the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*) or the *hṛdaya* mantra. Subsequently, one should cause the black fragrant unguent to be applied to all those from the preceptor (*deśika*) down to the devotees.

Having placed the Lord upon the jewel lion-throne, and having seated Gaurī on his left with her right hand [supporting him], the King should stand to the left or in front. Having performed song and dance on both sides by the dancers, female dancers, and musicians, and having danced together with instrumental music as far as the seven planets, he should enter the temple; there, he should perform the rites of the eye-salve and so forth as before. Afterwards, having established [the image] in the assembly hall (*āsthānamaṇṭapa*), [he should proceed].

Having offered the eight-limbed *arghya* together with fruits and having presented [the offerings], one should worship with *nīrājana*, collyrium, and other rites. Afterwards, having bathed [the deity] with the *gavya* bath and other rituals, and having consecrated pure camphor as before, one should apply it to all limbs. Having adorned [the deity] with excellent jasmine flowers and garments, one should present milk-rice (*pāyasa*). After offering incense, lamps, and so forth, at the time of procession, the carriage should be moved very slowly in a line.

There, having performed the *paṅkti* [purification] as before with recitation, dance, song, and so forth; having performed everything such as the removal of collyrium (*nīrāñjana*) as before, one should enter the temple. Having worshipped with all the ritual offerings (*upacāra*), one should pass the remainder of the night by means of viewing entertainments. At dawn, having worshipped the Lord of Dance (*Nṛtteśa*) and adorned him, one should perform the *tīrtha* rite as before at a river or similar site. Then, having removed the protective thread (*kautuka*), one should circumambulate the city and other sacred sites.

In a pure location, having caused the proclamation of the suppression of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous, as well as the announcement of all legal proceedings; having dispelled any quarrel regarding the favor of the Goddess; and having caused her to enter the pavilion without a formal circumambulation, one should establish her in her own place, consecrate her with ablutions and other rites, and have pure dances performed. Thus ends the ritual procedure for the black incense.

Immediately thereafter, on the tenth or seventh day, one should perform the marriage according to the rules through the formal ritual (*aupacārika*), as well as the festival for the Goddess, the festival for the devotees, and the festival for the auspicious vow (*kalyāṇavrata*).
Now follows the procedure for the festival for the Goddess:

One should hold a festival for nine days, seven days, three days, or one day. On the eleventh day and night, having decorated everything including Indra’s celestial chariot (*vimāna*), and having consecrated the Lord with a ritual sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*) preceded by bathing and adorned [with ornaments], one should place all the deities upon their respective chariots. At the time of the final circumambulation, having consecrated a water-shed (*prapā*) in the northeast direction with [offerings] beginning with flowers and ending with banners, one should bring Śiva, who is situated in the chariot, into its center; and there, O Goddess, [one should worship] as before, up to Caṇḍeśa.

Having caused the king, the sacrificer, and the musicians to perform three circumambulations, at the time of entering the temple—whether at the front of the gatehouse or atop the palace—one should cause them to dispel any playful quarrels and provide entertainment. Then one should cause them to enter according to the prescribed rite. Thus ends the ritual for the festival of the Goddess.
Now follows the ritual for the festival of the devotees.

Then, having installed those respective fixed and movable icons (*bera*) and others before Śiva and in the pavilion, and having consecrated the fixed and movable icons and others through the preliminary ablution (*snāna*), he should perform the powder festival (*cūrṇotsava*) as previously described. Having taken up the powder for the devotee-icons (*bhaktaberāṇām*), the preceptor should cause it to be distributed among the initiated practitioners (*sādhaka*), the initiates, and the devotees; then, having given saffron turbans, sacred threads (*pavitra*), garlands, and so forth, and having praised [Śiva] with the hymns of the devotees, he should give betel leaves and other offerings to the devotees of Śiva.

Having circumambulated the city and entered the temple, having seated everyone in their respective places, having offered the oblation, and having presented incense and lamps, one should cause those skilled in singing the praises of Śiva to be given garments and other gifts; such is the procedure for the festival of devotion.

(Pañcakṛtyakam— ) On the following day, having performed in sequence the great ablution (*mahāsnāna*), preceded by the fire-oblation for peace (*śāntihoma*), the image-oblation (*mūrtihoma*), the directional oblation (*diśāhoma*), and so forth, and having consecrated [the deity], one should cause the removal of fatigue (*śramaharaṇa*).
The festival (*utsava*) is said to be fivefold, consisting of persistence, emanation, and dissolution.
Concealment, grace, and the fivefold activity beginning with emanation; these are the [five] primary functions.
The auspicious rite of planting the sprout, the hoisting of the banner,
and the binding of the protective thread are declared to be the ritual of emanation (*sṛṣṭikarma*).
This is joined with the festival of the vehicle, the performance of fire-offerings (*homakarma*), and the distribution of oblations (*balibhrama*).
The activity of maintenance has been declared; now the activity of withdrawal is being described.
Combined with the powder of rātri, as well as the mounting of a chariot,
and likewise the festival of kālāguru, which is well-known in the Āgamas.

The festival of silence (*maunotsava*), concealment (*tirobhāva*), the journey of power (*śaktiyātrā*), and grace (*anugraha*)—these [occur] at the beginning and end of the days of the sacred site (*tīrtha*). Love (*praṇaya*) is said to be quarrel (*kalaha*). The fivefold activity (*pañcakṛtya*), beginning with emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), is joined with the seed (*bīja*) and the field (*kṣetra*).

Thus ends the procedure for the festivals beginning with that of Vināyaka and ending with those of the devotees, composed by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya, whose other name is Parameśvara, in the *Kriyākramadyotikā*. Accompanied by the illustrious Tripurasundarī. Now follows the procedure for the monthly festival (*māsotsava*):
the moment of the solar transit (*saṅkrānti*) is subtle and difficult to discern even for one with keen vision.
And by union with that, furthermore, the thirty channels above are purified.
In the northern course there will be thirty auspicious [nāḍīs], and likewise thirty in the southern;
in the past and future, the nāḍīs are said to be those born of Hara and Aḍaja.
The transits, the equinoxes, and especially the two solstices—
when the sun is in Taurus, Scorpio, Aquarius, and Leo—
this is called Viṣṇupada; it yields fruit exceeding that of the equinoxes and other such times.
The sun's transit occurs in Virgo, Gemini, Pisces, and Sagittarius as well.
O twice-born ones, the sixty-four [nāḍīs] known as the "mouths of the eighty-six" are said to be the most meritorious;
sixteen nāḍīs belong to the period before the transit and sixteen after it. However, the nāḍīs of the current Libra and Aries transits consist of ten on either side.
It will be so when Viṣṇu is in the path of departure, and likewise when he is in the state of poison.
At the commencement of the six-aśīti period, at the end of the northern course [of the sun],
upon the sighting of Rāhu, at the transits [of the sun], and on occasions of marriage, calamity, or prosperity.
In the case of vows for the attainment of specific treasures (*nidhi-kāmya-vrata*), one should perform acts such as bathing and giving gifts;
and at that very time, one should conduct the festival of the deity and the worship of Śiva.
Those *nāḍī*s (periods of time) which are joined with the *yāryā*s are remembered as most meritorious.

Then, at the time of the *saṅkrānti*, having bathed the deity as before preceded by the ritual ablution (*snāna*) and other rites, and having adorned the primary *liṅga* and all other [images] with ornaments; accompanied by the sound of all musical instruments and together with the images of the devotees of Vināyaka, Soma, Skanda, and others, one should lead them in circumambulation around the village, the city, or the temple. Having performed the preliminary rites for oneself and others at the site of Brahmā or in front of the bull, one should install [the deities] in their own places.
When this is done in the kingdom, no monthly defects (*māsadoṣa*) shall occur.
Therefore, with every effort, one should properly perform the festival. Thus ends the procedure for the monthly festival.
Now, the procedure for the fortnightly festival (pakṣotsava): On the eighth part of the fourteenth day, the moon becomes waning;
or again, on the eighth part of the new moon (amāvāsyā), the moon indeed becomes full once more.
O Nivālinī, you who have seen the sword-moon, you are considered to be the one in whom the moon and sun have vanished;
indeed, the new moon day begins from midday and continues thereafter.
When the fourteenth lunar day (*bhūta*) is joined with the fifteenth (*siddhā*), it becomes the full moon (*sāndreyā*).
When even a single *ghaṭikā* remains of the new moon (*amāvāsya*), that is then the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipat*).
The fourteenth day (*bhūta*) joined with the fifteenth (*vi-siddhā*) should be used for rites pertaining to the gods (*daiva*) and the ancestors (*pitrya*).
Among the lunar days (pratipad), the new moon day (amāvāsyā) is that which extends through the forenoon (pūrvāhṇa).
In divine rites, one should always act as if possessed by a spirit;
likewise, [this applies] when the sun is in Libra, Capricorn, Pisces, Virgo, or Gemini.
The new moon day of the Bhūta-vardhamāna should be diligently honored;
on the fourteenth day, when it reaches its fullness in the Nandā and other [tithis],
one should perform the festival of the deity on the Bhūta day and practice at the sacred ford.

The new moon (*amāvāsyā*) on a Monday, the seventh lunar day (*saptamī*) on a Tuesday, and the fourth lunar day (*caturthī*) on a Tuesday yield fruit equal to the *viṣuvat* [equinox]. If the new moon falls on a Monday during the asterism Ārdrā, it becomes equal to Śivarātri. One should perform a night vigil (*jāgaraṇa*) and carry out a festival for the deity. If the new moon is joined with the asterism Ārdrā on a Monday, one obtains from that vow the fruit of ten million sacrifices, ascetic penances, and gifts.

Then, on the new moon day, having performed the great consecration (*mahābhiṣeka*) for the stationary and portable images of the primary *mūla-liṅga* and others, preceded by the offering of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and having adorned them with all ornaments and presented the great sacrificial food (*mahāhavis*), one should lead the Deity in circumambulation—without the procession of offerings (*balibhramaṇa*) to villages, hamlets, and so forth—but accompanied by umbrellas, chowries, and the like, together with many diverse lamps and various musical instruments. Having brought [the Deity] to the station of Brahmā (*brahmasthāna*), and having performed the lustration (*nīrājana*) and other rites as before, one should install [the Deity] in its own place.
Thus, the mortal who causes [this] to be made shall attain a meritorious state.
One desiring a son obtains sons; one desiring a daughter obtains an auspicious maiden;
one desiring wealth obtains abundant riches; and one desiring liberation attains liberation.
The rain-clouds will not fail to rain in their season, there will be freedom from disease and no calamities;
by means of the Amāvāsya festival alone, one shall attain all desires. Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the Amāvāsya festival.
Now follows the procedure for the Full Moon sacrifice:
The Full Moon is considered to be twofold—namely, Rājā and Anumatī;
that which is the earlier Full Moon is Anumatī, while the latter is Saha.
