The end of the fortnight, known as the fifteenth day, is traditionally called the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*);
it is desired on the sixteenth day, while the intermediate [full moon] occurs on the fifteenth day.
On the fourteenth day it is "inferior," and on the seventeenth day it is "sinful. All the first lunar days (*pratipad*) are [inauspicious] for brothers until the sun has risen;
they are renowned as "complete" (*saṃpūrṇā*) for divine rites, O Purifier.
Pairs [of breaths] belong to the Yamabhūtas, and [pairs] to the Ṣaṇmunis, Vasus, and Randhras.

The twelfth lunar day conjoined with the eleventh is [dedicated] to Rudra, and the full moon is conjoined with the fourteenth; likewise, the new moon is conjoined with the thirteenth. This pair of lunar days yields great fruit.

There too, as before, having performed the ritual up to the offering of food (naivedya), preceded by the worship of Vighneśa and others, one should lead the deities beginning with Vighneśa—adorned with all ornaments—on a circumambulation starting from the front [of the temple] and install them in their respective places as before; thus, by the command of Śiva, every flaw of omission in the ritual procedure shall perish. This is the procedure for the Full Moon Festival (Paurṇamāsotsava).
Now, the procedure for the festival of the lunar mansions (*ṛkṣotsava-vidhi*):
Now, worship performed under all the lunar mansions is dear to Śiva.
O twice-born followers of Hara, I shall briefly declare its fruit.
The lunar day (vāra) is said to possess one-fold merit; the lunar date (tithi) shall be ten-fold.
Yoga is ten times more meritorious than that, and the astrological period (karaṇa) is said to be ten times more so than that.

Therefore, the *lagna* is ten times [more significant] than that; from that, the great *rakṣa* (or *lakṣa*) is said to arise for the sake of liberation. One should fast there at the *rakṣa*, and perform bathing and the rites for progeny. Or rather, when the constellation (*nakṣatra*) of the half-watch (*ardhayāma*) has arrived, it does not wait for the day. Therein indeed are worship, bathing, and giving. If two constellations occur in one month, the former is to be taken and not the latter.
If the latter is conjoined with a yoga, so too are the equinoxes (*viṣuva*) and solstices (*ayana*).
O best of sages, for a festival or a rite dedicated to the gods, one should preferentially accept either a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*) or an eclipse that coincides with the day of Hari.
In the evening when the wind is predominant and the Vyāpinī muhūrta prevails, one should perform the pilgrimage;
having worshipped Śiva under the Kṛttikā asterism, one becomes endowed with wealth, grain, and other riches.
Having offered supreme happiness in this world and even final union [with the Divine] at the end,
one should worship Śaṅkara under Rohiṇī for the sake of destroying untimely death.
…… having worshipped Īśvara with those of great strength and prowess, [one attains success].
He shall become vigorous and endowed with the luster of sacred knowledge, O best of practitioners.
Those who worship Hara under the asterism Ārdrā obtain all prosperity;
those worthy of worship, performing worship under Punarvasu, slay their enemies along with their followers.
Under Puṣya one gains nourishment for the body, and under Śleṣā one obtains excellent sons;
O Lord of Gods, the worshipper there likewise obtains many sons.
Having eaten well at Suśiva, one shall become possessed of the best of kinsmen.

In Pūrvaphalgunī, there is good fortune joined with groups of five starting from five; in Uttaraphalgunī, one becomes a giver of abundant gifts such as wealth, grain, and excellent jewels. In Hasta, however, one attains the excellence of being a remover of [misfortune] and a lord of wealth.
The worshiper of Hara [gave] Paduminī, who was endowed with beauty, virtues, and noble lineage.
In Cittā, the worshipper immediately obtains what exceeds his own expectations;
he is endowed with great gain, as is trade and commerce.
Having acquired it, he dwells in happiness for a very long time.
By worshipping Śiva during the Viśākhā constellation, one obtains many desired objects.
For those performing [the rite] under Anurādhā, they should give two cows and an upper garment;
under Jyeṣṭhā, it is indeed desired that one certainly obtain half of Dhaniṣṭhā.
Under Mūla, by worshipping Śiva, the wise man shall attain bodily health.
In Pūrvāṣāḍhā, glory is attained through the worship of Mahādeva;
in Uttarāṣāḍhā, the act of worshipping Śambhu shall bear fruit immediately.

If there is worship of Hara during Śravaṇā, one will obtain an auspicious daughter; by worshipping Śiva during Dhaniṣṭhā, one obtains great and abundant wealth. Having offered oblations during Sukharā, one becomes inclined toward giving gifts; and during Abhijit, the protector of the gods, one becomes a knower of the arts of eloquence.
One obtains the Veda endowed with its six limbs and the correct accent;
and during the worship of Śiva under the Vāruṇa asterism, one attains success as a physician and medicinal herbs.
If one should fully worship Śiva under the Proṣṭhapadā asterism, [the same results follow].
He obtains many goats and cows; there is no doubt in this matter.
O twice-born ones, when the moon is in the constellation Uttaraproṣṭhapadā, the wise man who worships Śiva shall,
by the command of Īśvara, be liberated from all diseases.
For all men and women, and even for kings,
great anger arising at any time shall perish through the worship of Śaṅkara.
Furthermore, a man who worships under the asterism Aśvinī shall obtain elephants and horses.
By propitiating Śiva under the asterism Bharaṇī, one obtains long life;
therefore, with every effort, one should perform worship during these asterisms.
If one is unable to perform it oneself, one should have the worship of Śaṅkara performed by others.
Having caused [an image] to be fashioned from lead, one obtains that fruit;
one should perform the worship of Śambhu and hold a festival under those respective fixed asterisms. Under Ārdrā, fasting, that merit is multiplied by ten million times ten million.
Or even by performing worship, one obtains sons and grandsons through this vow.
Whether he be a son of the *samaya*, a practitioner (*sādhaka*), or even one who has not been initiated—
if anyone does not observe [the vow] on the day of Śarva, he too shall go to hell.
O best of the twice-born, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, kinsmen, maidens, widows, virtuous women, or those observing the vow of ascetics—
everyone should perform [this rite] on every lunar day, in every month, and in every season.
Having performed his bath at the time of evening and having observed the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā), he should proceed.

Then, having performed the worship of Śiva, and having likewise performed the worship beginning with that of Svāyambhuva and others, up until the festival, he should bathe [the deity] according to the prescribed rule.
Having circumambulated the Lord Śiva and praised him with those intent on hymns, and having bowed many times with devotion, he should return to his own home and feed [the devotees].
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, while holding a rudrākṣa in the presence of Śiva,
he should then make a formal vow (*saṅkalpa*) and practice this for one year as a householder.
Whatever desire the practitioner desires, that very thing he obtains.
At the end of the year, one should perform the concluding rite (*udyāpana*) for the *mahimā*;
having invited the Brahmins, one should give them sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's means.

He who recites this obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices, of a hundred million sacrifices, and of the gift of ten million maidens. His portents perish, as do the terrible afflictions caused by enemies.
Freed from all diseases, endowed with sons, grandsons, and wealth,
one who offers oblations here enjoys great pleasures, long life, and happiness.
This nasal medication is the supreme among vows, the most excellent of the excellent.
On the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, at twilight, and on Mondays.
What fruit does a man obtain by worshipping Hara on the occasion of Vyatīpāta?
By what means does one obtain that fruit—the supreme fruit of those [meritorious acts]?
Whether one is a slayer of a Brahmin, a liquor-drinker, a killer of a cow, or one who violates the teacher’s bed—
one is liberated from the multitude of great sins by that supreme vow.
[It should be given] to a devotee of Śiva, one who is peaceful, a learned Vedic scholar, or a householder.
For one who is impoverished and afflicted by a great disease, [one should perform] the Pramardavrata.

Thus ends the procedure beginning with the Great Tāla [dance] and ending with the Ṛkṣa festival, in the *Kriyākramadyotikā* composed by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya, whose name is synonymous with the Supreme Lord’s method for expiation (*parameśvarapara-prāyaścittavidhi*). Homage to the venerable Gurus!
Now, the procedure for expiation (*prāyaścitta*):
The mending of a mind that has been excessively agitated by fasting unto death (*prāyopaveśana*) is called *sandhāna*;
the mending of one who has fallen [from his state] is traditionally known as *prāyaścitta*.
Through the neglect of one's own conduct, a human being goes to hell;
for the purification of one whose conduct has been neglected, the Guru should prescribe an expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
[This applies] when a limb is afflicted by a severe disease, or during fears of kings and thieves.
They perform these duties for the sake of the gods; they incur no sin in case of constant neglect.
The student and the householder have two types of atonement;
these two are further proclaimed to be of two kinds according to whether they are committed intentionally or otherwise.
But for one who acts with desire toward another who is without desire, the expiation is declared to be double;
it is double again for a student of the ritual (bhautika), and it is the same for a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin) engaged in a sacrifice (naiṣṭhika).
For one dwelling in the forest, it is threefold, but for ascetics (*yati*s), it is fourfold;
[the age limit] is from above eighty years until sixteen years.

One should prescribe an expiation for that aged person or child; and for women and those seeking protection, an expiation has been declared. For one who is unable to perform it himself, however, the penance from another shall be double.
For one who is incapable, his son or brother, or his wife and others, or paternal relatives [shall act].
When the [rite] has been thus analyzed, the penance must then be performed accordingly.
I shall now declare the procedure for the ritual bathing (*snāna*), as enjoined in the Śiva-siddhānta.
That is declared to be threefold: obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmyaka*).
Each one is said to be further divided into three types—lower, middling, and superior.
[This is accomplished] by twenty-five breath-retentions (*kumbhaka*) minus nine, which is five.
In the middle [section], there are forty-nine, eighty-one, and likewise sixty-four jars.
One hundred and eight is the best; two hundred and sixteen [is the next];
five hundred and eight, and one thousand, are said to be the ninefold [counts].
The triad of rites—daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya)—is considered to follow this sequence.
Austerities such as the *kṛcchra* and others have been proclaimed; among them, that which is performed for three days is designated as *taptakṛcchra*.
The Atikṛcchra consists of two Parāka penances followed by the Cāndrāyaṇa rite;
then there should be eating once every three nights for three days, and fasting for three days.
Thus is the Kṛcchra penance fully described; it is known as the Prājāpatya.
One should drink warm water for three days, eat only milk for three days, and consume only warm clarified butter for three days;
when these are performed for three days each, it is complete.
This is known as the Taptakṛcchra, and it is also called simply Kṛcchra.
Therein, for twenty-one days, one subsists on the three fruits and milk;
this is known as the *atikṛcchra*, and the *parāka* is described here.

Abstaining from food for twelve days is known as the *parāka* penance. Increasing [the intake] by one mouthful per day during the bright fortnight and decreasing it during the dark fortnight is declared in the rule for the *cāndrāyaṇa*; this water-based rite is composed of water alone.

As before, having prepared an auspicious maṇḍapa, or having constructed a circular *kuṇḍa* of the size of an elephant (*hāstika*) in its center—or for the rite of pacification (*śānti*), in the west—one should place four jars (*ghaṭa*) or four *vardhanī* vessels upon a heap of grain. Having performed the worship of Vighneśa and recited the *puṇyāha* formula, one should worship Śivāstra in one eastern jar, preceded by the visualization (*dhyāna*) to be described hereafter; and one should worship [Aghora] in the southern jar, preceded by the visualization of Aghora as previously stated.

Alternatively—having worshipped the Aghora-weapon as will be described (p. 54a, l. 1), one should worship the Pāśupata weapon in the western jar; having worshipped it as will be described, one should likewise worship Pratyaṅgirā in the northern jar. Those initiated in the five directions should recite the Śiva-knowledge of the Kāmika and other scriptures, which arises facing those respective directions, innumerable times. Should they not recite the Tatpuruṣa and other mantras innumerable times in the eastern and other directions?

They should recite the *Ṛgveda* and the other Vedas, as well as the *Śāntika*, *Pauṣṭika*, and *Pratiṣṭhā* mantras in the number of syllables prescribed for the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*). Having worshipped these [mantras] in sequence until the end of the recitation, thereafter, in the central fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*), they should perform the ritual—from the consecration of the pit (*kuṇḍasaṃskāra*) up to the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) involving the *caru* oblation—as previously described. Then, having worshipped each individual image (*mūrti*) in due order, they should offer oblations (*juhuyāt*). Alternatively, together with the guardians of the images (*mūrtipāḥ*), they should invoke the respective deities into the four fire-pits and offer oblations.

They should offer into the fire every day, morning and evening, one hundred, one thousand, or five hundred oblations consisting of the three roots, the three sweets, sesame, dūrvā grass, sacrificial grain (*akṣata*), and milk-rice (*pāyasa*), or a mixture of rice and peas (*kṛsara*), along with three blades of *kuśa* grass, the three fruits, and mustard seeds, accompanied by the *pūrṇā* offering. At the end of the word "svāhā," they should recite: "O Blessed One, [grant] the state that [removes] all disturbances... again, *kurukuru*. This should be joined with each mantra at ten-day intervals; in the case of a multi-day rite, having restrained Śiva right there.

Having gone into the presence of the gods and reported the *soma*-rite, and having performed the protection (*rakṣā*), one should pray for the destruction and eradication of misfortune. [The rites should be performed] on the first, third, fifth, seventh, ninth, eleventh, thirteenth, fifteenth, and twenty-first days; and with the lunar mansions beginning from the first day of the fortnight (*pakṣati*) and all the other constellations—thus, the peace (*śānti*) is attained through this uninterrupted and extensive performance.
Now follows the *śāntihoma*:

in the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), as before, having placed a single water-pot (*kumbha*) upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) covered with all kinds of grain and adorned with all ornaments; having established eight pots around it; and having worshipped the firm seat (*sthirāsana*) in the central pot—one should meditate upon the *Pāśupatāstra*, mounted upon the seat of the *praṇava*, invincible, and the great abode (*mahālaya*).
Five-faced and ten-eared, with three eyes in each countenance,
fierce and formidable with bared fangs, emitting a loud roar and exceedingly difficult to conquer,
adorned with a garland of skulls and crowned with the crescent moon.
With squinting eyes, adorned with great serpents, and licking his fangs with laughter;
possessing the brilliance of ten million times ten thousand suns, he is the crusher of the hosts of obstructing spirits.
Endowed with ten extremely fierce arms and terrifying weapons,
he holds in his right hands a sword, a bow, a great trident, and a noose that grants fearlessness;
and in his left hands, a shield, an arrow, a skull-cup, a boon-granting gesture, and a spear.
Possessing a luster like that of emerald, with a beard, mustache, and eyebrows [of that same hue], and likewise hair on his head of such a kind.
"One should meditate upon the Great Pāśupata Lord, who grants the accomplishment of all aims.

Having thus meditated, and having performed the rites from the invocation (*āvāhana*) up to the worship of the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga-pūjā*) with the mantra: *oṃ ślīṃ paṃ śuṃ huṃ phaṭ namaḥ svāhā*, and having worshipped the *vajra* and other implements in the vases of the east and other directions as before, and having offered various food offerings (*naivedya*) and so forth, and having offered the recitation (*japa*), one should go to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and sit down. Then, having performed the rites from the consecration of the pit (*kuṇḍasaṃskāra*) up to the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) at the end of the offering of the sacrificial porridge (*caruhavana*).

In the midst of that—(p. 55a, l. 1) having worshipped the King of Weapons (*astrarāja*) as before; and for the removal of respective defects, having offered a hundred, a thousand, half [of those], or one hundred and eight oblations of sacrificial wood (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), sesame seeds, *sattu*, the three sweets (*madhutraya*), the three sweet substances (*madhuratraya*), the three fruits, and *caru* with their respective mantras, ending with the *pūrṇāhuti*; (l. 2) having performed the oblations up to the end of the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) and concluding with the *pūrṇāhuti*; having offered incense and lamps; and having transferred [the fire] into the water-pot (*kumbha*), one should dismiss the fire.

Regarding those vessels for placing the water-pots with which one should sprinkle [the site] with water: in the case of a multi-day rite, having caused the recitation of the *Kāmika* and other scriptures, as well as the recitation of the *Śānti*, according to the number of days prescribed for the *śānti*—just as before—one should feed the Brāhmaṇas. Thus ends the procedure for the *śānti-homa*.
The procedure for the *diśāhoma* (the directional oblation):

another [rite] is a subsidiary of the expiation (*prāyaścitta*), while this is a subsidiary of the ablution (*snāna*). Having installed the *liṅga*, the image (*bera*), the water-pot (*ghaṭa*), and so forth upon the altar in the center of the eastern and western pavilions; having placed the *śivāstra* (the weapon of Śiva) in one pot before that [altar] and eight pots around it; one should worship the *śivāstra* in the central pot, adorned with all splendors. Having prepared the seat as before:
[one should meditate on it as] four-faced, with blazing hair, possessing a radiance like a mass of lightning.
His head is adorned with the moon’s orb, and his four sprout-like hands are joined in the *ardhaparyaṅka* posture; he possesses terrifying prowess,
is endowed with twelve eyes, and holds a spear, a trident, and displays the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons.
I bow to the divine Śivāstra, the crusher of bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and wicked rākṣasas,
whose eyes are red and who is exceedingly fierce.

Having meditated thus, and having worshipped with all the ritual offerings (*upacāra*), and having prepared [the oblation] either in the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) or on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), one should satisfy [the deity] therein up to the point of the *caru* offering and the expiation (*prāyaścitta*), and then request the fulfillment of one's desires and ask for forgiveness (*kṣamāpayet*). Alternatively, they say: in the center [place] the *śivakumbha* and the *vardhanī*; in the eastern direction, the *vāstra*; in the west, the *pāśupata*; in the south, the *aghora-astra*; and in the north, the *pratyaṅgirā*. Then [recite]: "Oṃ Hrīṃ! To the one clad in black! as a single phrase. And then: "O lion-faced one, O great-faced one!"
And those of a most terrifying complexion hear every sound other than that.

Then, one should extract the supreme mantra-word "Karmavidhvaṃsanī" (Destroyer of Karma); thereafter, one should extract "Chedinī" (Cutter), and also "Sarvabhūtadamanī" (Tamer of All Beings). Then, from "Sarvabhūta," one should extract the word "Bandhabandha" (Bind, bind!).
The phrase "sarvavighna" and the word "cindhicindhī" [are used].
The word "nikṛnta" occurs as "sarvavyādhinikṛnta," and the word "nikṛnta" [is found] at the end of all [the preceding words]. In the subsequent [section], there is the word "bhakṣabhakṣa.
Furthermore, the word "tadaṃṣṭre" follows [the sequence] "jvālājihve karāle."
In the *pratyaṅgira* [mantra], the word "paścāt" comes after the word "namaḥ."
The mantra for the removal of defects is "svāhā," consisting of the Pratyāṅgirā.
Having worshipped the Supreme Goddess Pratyāṅgirā upon a firm seat in the center of the Vardhanī, which is endowed with all splendor,
one should meditate as follows:
[He visualizes] the face of the Lord as having a lion’s mouth with fierce fangs and fire, endowed with upward-pointing crests;
resembling black collyrium, it is possessed of three round, red eyes.
She carries a trident and a *ḍamaru* drum in her two left hands;
she carries a severed head and a sprout in her two right hands.
Wearing black garments and tearful, she should be depicted as one who delights in the night.
Adorned with ornaments suitable for pearl jewelry, he was the embellisher of all his limbs.
I shall meditate upon Pratyaṅgirā, who is endowed with a loud laugh and passion, clad in a black antelope skin, and the destroyer of diseases, obstacles, and enemies.

Having meditated thus, and having worshipped [the deity] with all the ritual services (*upacāra*) beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) using the root mantra—concluding with the worship of the *vajra* and the other deities of the enclosure (*āvaraṇa*) and the ritual vase (*kalaśa*)—one should worship Pratyaṅgirā in the center of a lotus-pit (*padmakuṇḍa*) or a womb-pit (*yonikuṇḍa*). One should then offer oblations (*juhuyāt*) one hundred, fifty, or twenty-eight times for each of the following: fuel-sticks (*samidh*) from the *pakṣa* tree and others, products of the cow (*gavya*), sesame, *dūrvā* grass, milk, sacrificial porridge (*caru*), the three sweets (*madhutraya*), the three roots (*mūlatraya*), the three *kāśa* grasses, white mustard seeds, cloves (*lavaṅga*), nutmeg leaves (*jātipatra*), sacred sandalwood (*śrīgandha*), saffron (*kuṅkuma*), and yellow orpiment (*gorocanā*), and so forth.

Having given [the gift] together with the complete expiation (*prāyaścitta*), and having prayed to the Goddess for the pacification of that misfortune, one should cause the bathing with the water contained in that jar to be performed upon the deity or the patron (*yajamāna*), and then cause the protection by means of sacred ash (*bhasma-rakṣā*) to be made. Alternatively, they say that one should worship the four weapons as before and Pratyaṅgirā in the center; this is the method for the *diśā-homa*.
Regarding the *saṃhitā-homa*:

having worshipped Śiva, together with the Brahmā-aṅgas and the [divine] seat, in either the perpetual fire (*nityāgni*) or the special fire (*viśeṣāgni*), one should perform the oblation (*homa*) by offering fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and other materials one hundred, one thousand, or half that number of times, using the mantras of the Brahmā-aṅgas, for the removal of those defects. One should then perform the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) and so forth. This is the *saṃhitā-homa*, excluding the jar (*ghaṭa*).
Now follows the procedure for the *mūrti-homa*.

On the roof of a palace, or elsewhere on a prepared altar (*sthaṇḍila*) in the center of a pavilion (*maṇṭapa*), one should install the *śivakumbha* and the *vardhanī*, as well as the eight *vajra*-designated jars in the eight directions—each equipped with cords, lids, and filled with water mixed with cloth, gold, jewels, medicinal herbs, and perfumes. Having performed the purification of the pavilion and other rites as before, one should worship Śiva in the central [jar] and worship the Aghora-weapon (*aghorāstra*) in the *vardhanī*.

Alternatively, having established the Śiva-vessel and the Vardhanī in the center, one should worship the Aghora-weapon (*astra*) therein. One should worship the thunderbolt (*vajra*) and the other [weapons] around it. Having worshipped with "Huṃ phaṭ namaḥ to the seat of the weapon" and "Huṃ phaṭ namaḥ to the form of the weapon," one should meditate:
[upon him who is] as radiant as a thousand suns and has the roar of the clouds at the time of universal dissolution.
His face is radiant with the brilliance of blazing fangs;
he has three eyes, his tongue is a woman, and his eyebrows, beard, and hair are aflame.
He wears a serpent as a sacred thread and holds a trident, a sword, a spear, and a mallet.
Four-armed and four-faced, with the crescent of the autumn moon as his crest-jewel,
dancing, of massive body, and adorned with serpent ornaments.

Having meditated thus: "The crushing of the arrogant gods, dānavas, and daityas," one should recite the mantra beginning with *oṃ purasphura*, followed by the word *prasphura* twice; then the word *tanurūpa*, followed by the words *caṭa caṭa*; then two instances of *praca*, followed by the words *kahakaha*; then the words *vama vama*, and a second time *bandha*; then *paraṃ ghātaya* a second time, followed by what is called *aghora-astra*, ending with *huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Having recited this mantra, one should perform worship, completing the rites from the invocation (*āvāhana*) up to the recitation (*japa*), and then worship [the deity].

Having invoked the King of Astras (*āstrarāja*) into either a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), one should offer oblations—consisting of fuel sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), sesame seeds (*tila*), milk, *dūrvā* grass, the three sweets (*madhuratrika*), and sacrificial food (*haviṣyānna*)—one hundred, one thousand, fifty, or one hundred and eight times for each, using the Aghora-Astra mantra, together with a final full-oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), for the sake of removing those defects. Alternatively, having established the Śiva-pitcher (*śivakumbha*) in the center and the Vardhanī pitcher, and having installed the eight deities beginning with Śarva in the eight directions according to the two systems—the system of the eight [deities] and the system of the [eight] quarters—one should worship the forms (*mūrti*) beginning with Earth.

Then, having performed the oblations up to the end of the expiation (*prāyaścitta*), one should offer one hundred and eight or fifty oblations separately with the respective mantras using wood from the *pālāśa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *vaṭa*, *śamī*, *khadira*, *māyūra*, *plakṣa*, and other trees. Having offered the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and having sprinkled either the *liṅga* or the patron (*yajamāna*) with that water, and having applied its ashes, one should perform everything according to the number of days prescribed for the pacification rite (*śānti*).

In this case as well, the patron (*yajamāna*), having adorned the reciters of the *Kāmika* and other [tantras]—as well as those who have recited the *adhyayana-śānti* and the hymns (*stotra*)—with perfumes, flowers, garments, and so forth, led by the preceptor (*ācārya*), and having bestowed the prescribed sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and paid homage, should pray for the pacification of misfortunes (*duritopaśānti*). The preceptor, together with the mother and father [of the patron], should bestow a blessing of well-being (*āślakṣatā*). One should satisfy the poor, the blind, the wretched, and the helpless with food and clothing. This is the *mūrtihoma*.

Regarding touch (*sparśa*): having touched one initiated into his own *jāti* and so forth, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on (*sacelasnāna*). Upon touching a *śūdra*, one should immediately perform a bath with one's clothes on. Upon touching any of the intermediate castes (*antarāla*), one should perform two baths. At the time of seeing a *caṇḍāla*, one should always recollect Sadāśiva. Having heard of his sin, however, one should mutter the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) one hundred times. If [the contact] occurs in the vicinity of a staff’s length (*daṇḍamātra*), two baths must be performed.

If one touches [the person] out of negligence, one should know that there must first be a bath in water; then, having performed a bath with ashes, one should mutter the Śiva-mantra one hundred times. But if the touch was intentional, one should perform twice as much as previously prescribed. Upon seeing him at the time of eating, the wise man should discard the remainder of that food. Then, having performed the two baths and having muttered the root mantra eight hundred times, if [the breath] moves through the nostril at the tip of the nose, he should go to a difficult river and, having smelled cow dung...

One should immediately recite the five-syllable mantra (*pañcākṣara*). Having eaten the food of those who have not been initiated into one’s own caste, or having stayed in a new house in a village, one should recite the *vyomavyāpin* mantra once; if there is a specific desire, one should recite it a hundred times. Upon eating the food of a king, a Brahmin should recite the *ghora-mantra* a hundred times. Having eaten the food of a Vaiśya, one should recite [the *ghora-mantra*] up to a thousand times according to the sequence. Having eaten the food of a Śūdra out of desire, one should quickly perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance.

One who intentionally commits the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances, or the *cāndrāyaṇa*, should perform the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* after eating for one day [of forbidden food]. By eating continuously for a month, one attains the status of a *śūdra*. Constantly associating with a *śūdra*, one should behave exactly like a *śūdra*. Having engaged in sexual intercourse with a *śūdra* woman, one should then perform the *taptakṛcchra*. For those who exceed a month, the *taptakṛcchra* and other *kṛcchra* penances increase month by month.

For six months or even for a year, one should perform the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances. Beyond a year, in the case of such association, no expiation is prescribed; for that conduct, death is specifically the end. If one should eat from the leaves of the castor, arka, banyan, or holy fig tree—whether intentionally or out of desire—one should recite the Śiva-mantra a hundred times. When [eating] remnants mixed with ghee, or milk devoid of salt, having recited his *hṛdaya* mantra, all faults are brought to rest.

If one sees hair or bones during the meal—or if one sees a newly dead insect and so forth—one should discard a small portion of the food, wash the hand with ash, touch [the body], and after recollecting [the deity], one becomes purified by drinking water from the *veśa* [temple]. One should avoid garlic, fish, meat, and the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*). If, however, one has eaten these through negligence, one should recite the *Śiva-mantra* while pure; if one eats them out of desire, one should recite the *Śiva-mantra* one hundred times.

Killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, stealing gold, sexual intercourse with the wife of one’s teacher (*gurvaṅganā*), and association with those [who have committed these acts] constitute the fifth. Adultery with the teacher’s wife, drinking liquor, and killing a Brahmin—these three are declared to be expiated at the end of life; now hear of their [expiations]: He who, out of greed, steals silver should perform the *Aindava* vow. Thereafter, he should perform the *Taptakṛcchra*.
For those who exceed a month [of theft], he should perform the *Taptakṛcchra-Atikṛcchra*.
For six months or even a year, he should perform the *Kṛcchra* and the *Cāndrāyaṇa*.
If there is a union after a year has passed, no expiation is prescribed;
for that conduct, [the penance lasts] until death, especially.
If one should conquer the end while reciting on leaves of castor, arka, vaṭa, or aśvattha,
one should recite the Śiva-mantra a hundred times, whether out of desire or even from mere whim.
Having recited the Heart-mantra of that [deity], which cuts through all faults, over food-leavings mixed with ghee and milk from which salt has been removed;
If [impurity] occurs upon seeing hair or bones, it is the same as when seeing nails, insects, and so forth;
having discarded a small amount of food and washed one's hand with ash.
O Lord of Gods, by touching [these], by remembering them, or by drinking water, one becomes purified;
one should discard garlic, fish, meat, and the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*).
But having consumed [forbidden food] through negligence, one should recite the Śiva-mantra while pure;
if one should eat out of desire, one should recite the Śiva-mantra one hundred times.
[Even for] the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, and likewise the theft of gold—
...and likewise the arrival of the Vr̥ṅga-nāgas; through their conjunction, there would be a fifth [type].
These three—violating the teacher’s bed, drinking liquor, and killing a Brahmin—are declared to result in death at the end of life;
now hear about their deaths.
He who steals silver out of greed should perform a divine vow; for stealing gold, he should perform twice the penance for every ten *gadyāṇas* up to one hundred,
but for amounts exceeding that, the rule for gold is remembered as being double.
In the case of stealing gold from the finest jewel-ornaments, one should perform the prescribed rite for theft of gold;
for all other metals and alloys, one should perform the Parāka penance.
For the theft of grains, the Kṛcchra penance is required, while for sesame seeds, the Mandapa is traditionally prescribed.
For stealing base gems, one undergoes the Ghorakṛcchra penance for twenty thousand days.

For stealing clothing, bedding, seats, and the like, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for fifty thousand repetitions accompanied by the Gāyatrī; this is equal to the sin of violating the Guru’s bed.
Killing a cow, being a *vrātya*, theft, performing the *cayana* rite for women, not maintaining the sacred fires, selling [the Veda], marrying before an elder brother,
taking wages for work not performed, and likewise failing to perform work for which wages were paid.
Having lived abroad, they have become alienated from their noble kin and have turned to the practice of trade in salt.
The killing of a woman, a deer, or a kṣatriya; living by reprehensible means;
atheism; the abandonment of religious vows; and the sale of one's own children.
The purchase of grain, the theft of livestock, officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy of the *ājya* offering, the abandonment of father, mother, or friend, the sale of a pond or a grove,
the defilement of a maiden, and officiating at the sacrifice of one who marries before his elder brother;
The giving away of a daughter to him alone, crookedness, and the violation of a vow.
The undertaking of lending and buying, the indulgence in liquor and women, the abandonment of Vedic study, the sacred fire, and one's sons, as well as the abandonment of kinsmen;
Cutting ice for the sake of fuel, living by harming women or by medicinal herbs, performing rituals involving violence, the employment of spells, addiction, and the selling of oneself.
Studying false scriptures, practicing sorcery against the sources [of livelihood],
and the selling of one's wife— each of these is a minor offense (upapātaka).
Purification for a minor offense (upapātaka) may be achieved by a Brāhmaṇa through the Aindava rite,
or by consuming milk for a month, or even by [eating] the varāka grain.
Alternatively, the specific distinction regarding one who has not been marked by Aghora is now proclaimed:
for the killing of a Brahmin, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya, one should perform a fourth part of the penance for the murder of a Brahmin.
One should perform an eighth part [of the penance] for killing a Vaishya, and a sixteenth part for killing a Shudra;
likewise, for killing living beings unintentionally, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred times.

One becomes pure by reciting the Śatāghora mantra one hundred times after committing a sin consisting of the injury of living beings, provided that the collection of living beings lacks bones or is born from sweat (*svedaja*). For [the injury of] those not yet born, one should recite it one hundred times; however, for unintentional [injury], half of that.
Having purified oneself with wild flowers and other such offerings, one should not remain standing even for a moment.
Having seen these subtle [impurities], one becomes pure through the remembrance of Śiva.
By that very [remembrance], one becomes pure even after killing a mouse, a goat, or a jackal, just like a hare.
For the killing of a dog or a jackal, the penance is double; likewise for a monkey or a cock.
For all other egg-born creatures, as well as for birds such as swans and the like, the same applies.
But for the killing of wild animals such as lions, or for the slaughter of domestic livestock such as goats,
one becomes pure by reciting the Bahurūpa mantra a hundred times, up to a thousand times.
Having killed a cow through negligence, one becomes pure by reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times with intensity;
having committed the murder of a woman or a child, one is purified by two hundred thousand such recitations.
Having cut down a boat or similar object out of desire, a wise man should recite "laṃ" [one hundred thousand times].
If one causes an abortion out of desire, one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times for the third [offense].
Even one bitten by a dog shall be purified by eight hundred recitations of the Gāyatrī;
one bitten by a cat or a mouse is purified by a hundred recitations.
One bitten by a jackal or a dog is purified by one hundred and eight [repetitions];
however, one bitten by the tusks of a crocodile or a goat is purified by a single repetition alone.
If one has been bitten by a snake through negligence, one should recite the Ghoramantra one thousand times;
if bitten by a dog or other [venomous creatures] out of desire, one should recite it ten thousand times in water.
If they should employ the science of poisons or shifting illusions of sorcery (indrajāla),
[one should use] two hundred [recitations] for the expulsion of spirits, planetary influences, piśācas, and the like.
One should not cause killing by means of the mind or even by mantra.
Having performed rites such as exorcism (*uccāṭana*) and so forth, one becomes pure through the ten thousand various forms [of practice].
Having produced suffering for others through the actions of body and mind, [one attains] the further shore.
Having recognized [the fault] through negligence, one should recite the Śiva-mantra one hundred times.
If one speaks what has not been done by deed, mind, or speech,
one shall be released from that sin by reciting the Vāmadevya hymn a hundred times.

If one has uttered a hundred [unwholesome] words, which is the highest degree of verbal transgression, one should recite [the mantra] twice that number. If there is an intention toward another's wife or property, or if there is unwholesome reflection, or an obsession with what should not be done— these constitute the fourth type, mental [transgression].
Day and night, there is idle chatter, as well as that which is untrue and unpleasant.
And vocal action is of four kinds, devoid of slandering others:
namely, eating what is not to be eaten, violence, malicious intent, and the pursuit of desire.
The expiation for mutual insults is fourfold, with the performance of ritual action as the additional element.
In the case of verbal [insults], there should be silence for three days, the fire-ritual, worship, and recitation.
When it is completed, one should announce the matter to the Guru, the deity, and so forth.
He is said to be liberated from verbal bonds and from the bonds of karma.
By fasting for three nights and immersing oneself in water at the three junctions of the day,
and by reciting the *Brahmajā* while observing silence, one is not released from the bonds of karma.
But for mental sin, when a hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) have been performed with the *Śivagāyatrī* mantra, it is held that one becomes free from hundreds of mental [sins].
Without having recited the *Śivāyuta* mantra, [one cannot achieve] the removal of all defects.
Having drunk the five products of the cow once, one is liberated from all sins.

For the fivefold [substances]— the mother’s portion, that which is equal to the father’s, and the four born together— including the sin residing in the bones and marrow, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) shall burn away in an instant.
If semen and the like are emitted while one is sleeping unintentionally,
having bathed again with one's clothes on, one should recite the Astra-mantra one hundred times. Even during the day, if such emission occurs while dreaming, one should perform double the rite.
Having united with a woman out of desire, he [becomes] the Great-Souled Praṇava.
The practitioner, having restrained the activity of the vital breaths, should rotate [the mantra] a hundred thousand times;
the ascetic, though attached to sense objects, should do so preceded by the restoration of his vows.
One should take a wife; otherwise, a fall is certain.
For as many hairs as there are in one's matted locks or on the body, for that long shall one remain in the most terrible Raurava hell, crying out in pain.
If one who is blinded by passion should approach a woman with whom he has already had intercourse, he may have her conceived again.
By a thousand Vāmadevas, one becomes purified; of this there is no doubt.
Having forcefully cast off the white [element], however, by four hundred [Vāmadevas] during the day.
If one has recited [the mantra] two hundred times at night, one should recite it one hundred times during the day if one has slept;
if one should see animal play unintentionally, one should recite it one hundred times.
When the wife has bathed after her menses, then for a period of five days—
If a wife serves her husband and yet bears sons, she becomes like a low-caste woman; otherwise, O great sage, he would become base.
One should not stay outside [the house] for even a day; having gone out, one should perform recitation, fire-oblations, and other rites.
A Brahmin who, deluded by passion, constantly engages in sexual intercourse, [is fallen].
That Brahmin should be known as being like a donkey; his mantras issue from his mouth.
There is no fault in [reciting them] before a Kṣatriya and others, but one incurs fault by doing so during the day or on a festival day.

One must not commit adultery through action, mind, or speech; ... [if one should practice it out of delusion, there is] purification by half a *lakṣa* [of recitations]. For a maiden, the penance should be doubled, as it is for other castes as well.
On the junctions of the lunar phases, on the eighth day, or at any other time, sexual intercourse is forbidden for both.
Having performed [the preliminary rites], the wise one, established in the vow of the Praṇava, should recite it ten thousand times;
having performed half of ten thousand at night, he should recite it ten thousand times during the twilight.

Having heard talk concerning sexual intercourse, one who has been initiated should recite the seed-syllable of the heart a hundred times; likewise, if he approaches a Brāhmaṇa woman or any other [woman].
A Brahmin, having recited it one hundred and eight times, is liberated from that sin;
a Kṣatriya by two hundred, and a Vaiśya by three hundred.

A Śūdra who is born of Śiva, having recited the Vāmadeva hymn four hundred times and having fasted for one night, is liberated from that sin. If he has eaten [forbidden food] for a long time, he should perform the Kṛcchra penance with a hundred repetitions of the Vāmadeva.
Or, out of delusion, having gone to a woman of ill repute who belongs to that state and acts according to her own will.
For three days, remaining undisturbed while standing in water reaching up to the navel, one should recite [the mantra] with breath control; thus one is purified from secret sins.
Having approached a woman in her courses even once, a single fast is prescribed;

however, for a secret sin committed out of desire, one should not perform [that penance], but rather a fast of two or three days. When a Caṇḍāla woman, through ignorance, has entered the house, [the following applies].
One should immediately discard earthen items, having bathed and purified that house.

Having recited the *Narāyaṇa-ṣaḍakṣara-mantra* five thousand times, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance; likewise, one who eats at sunset and other improper times should perform the *taptakṛcchra* preceded by [the aforementioned recitation].
Having recited the Vāmadeva [mantra] ten thousand times, one is purified by means of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).

If she has intentionally consumed the sacrificial porridge (*caru*), having performed the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances, she should likewise recite the Vāmadeva; this is considered the vow for the end of the *parāka*.
Having known and enjoyed it for a long time, he then becomes equal to that.
Having touched royal property or an artisan, or having stayed in a temple, purification from the abandonment of goods occurs after three days;
[the fine is] five thousand.
When one has unintentionally touched or eaten [forbidden things], one should mutter the Aghora mantra for three days;

if done intentionally, this should be performed twice as much. One should perform it once for each instance of contact. Even when multiple instances of intentional contact have occurred, the same applies to both cases.
Therefore, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance must be performed; otherwise, one is certainly not purified.
If a yoga involving many deities arises through desire,
then one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance using water alone.
Having accepted an improper gift, one is immediately purified again by twelve [recitations];
likewise, one who has been initiated and is blameless is quickly liberated.
Having taken clarified butter, oil, and sugar, one should practice on the left side.
Salt, molasses, pungent substances, and various fragrances.
Milk, curd, clarified butter, oil, honey, meats, and grains; silk cloth, cotton, woolen fabric, linen, and hempen cloth.
Having gone to each house for leather, there would be three hundred terrible [rebirths];
likewise, a collection of masses of metals such as gold, beginning with diamond (*vajra*),
and a collection of other minerals such as yellow orpiment (*haritāla*).
A bull, an elephant, a vehicle, a field, and likewise the intermediate space.
One who is disciplined regarding storehouses and the like is pure despite being associated with many forms;
one is pure even after stealing fruits, wood, and so forth from a hundred times [a hundred].
A man may take an ox, a horse, a woman, a thousand [cows], or a hundred [others];
he may take land abounding in many crops, or a thousand measures of grain;
having taken whatever object it may be, even one of many forms, the wise man should recite the mantra.
For stealing clothes, beds, seats, and the like, one hundred recitations of the Gāyatrī mantra [are required].
A wise man should mutter the Vakra-mantra one thousand times for the theft of knowledge.
He who, having abandoned his own livelihood, conducts himself otherwise;
he who, though initiated, has fallen from his own duty, must seek purification once again.
Having constantly recited the Ghora mantra for one month in the presence of Śiva.
Having offered ten thousand oblations into the fire of Śiva, one is liberated from that sin;
one should perform the terrible rite ten times for each of the three or four transgressions of the *laṅghana*.
Even when a multitude of sins has arisen through their confluence,
the formidable mantra should be recited until the mind becomes serene.
He who studies the Śivasaṃhitā day after day, remaining established in the prescribed rule, [attains the goal].
He destroys all sins, just as the sun dispels the darkness.
At the juncture of the morning and evening twilights, one should recite the Sadyojāta mantra a hundred times;
the sin committed during the day and night perishes at that very moment.
When a woman who has reached her menses has not yet become purified, she should not worship Śiva.
On the first day she is a Caṇḍālī; on the second, a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa;
on the third, she is called a washerwoman; on the fourth, she becomes pure through bathing.
Having performed a bath with clay and consumed the products of the cow (gavya), one should worship Śiva.
If [the materials] are not obtained, one should worship Śiva after reciting a hundred terrible mantras;
otherwise, internal sacrifice or meditation should be performed during the three preceding days.
If the first day of menstruation occurs during the daytime, it is considered the first day even if the third part [of that day] passes into the night;
however, if it occurs in the morning during the third part of the day, it is desired here as the first day.
If the onset of menstruation is unknown, it is treated like the *vama* [impurity] within the woman's house.
An object that has been touched is not seen, even though it is in close proximity.

Upon touching a Caṇḍāla, a woman who has recently given birth, or a menstruating woman; upon contact with a corpse or the impurity resulting from its cremation; or upon hearing of the death of a relative—until one has bathed in a river or similar body of water.
Alternatively, having performed the consecration or having eaten [with such a person], one should perform the Prājāpatya penance.
If a Brāhmaṇa woman touches a Śūdra, Vaiśya, or Kṣatriya woman who has been confined [for childbirth],
she becomes pure by performing the Kṛcchra penance reduced by one-quarter, one-half, or three-quarters respectively.
If one should eat without having bathed, one must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
A Śūdra woman and others [of lower castes] should perform gifts and fasts according to the sequence of the *pādakṛcchra* penance.
If a Kṣatriya woman touches a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, she becomes pure by performing that same *pādārtha-kṛcchra*.
Upon touching a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriya, a Śūdra, or a woman, one is purified by a quarter-kṛcchra penance.

Having touched a Śūdra woman who has not yet bathed after her menses, one is purified by giving a gift alone. [If] a menstruating woman... out of delusion, having been touched by corpses and the like—
But when three days have passed, one should perform the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances.
If one who is eating during the day should touch a woman in her menses,

she should observe a fast for three days and is purified by the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). Or, if she enters while defiled by food remnants, even if it be a *caṇḍāla*, [the same penance applies].
If one fails to bathe, there shall be a fast; if one eats [while impure], one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

If a woman of the same lineage (*sagotra*) who is menstruating is touched, one should likewise fast for three days. Having been touched by a menstruating woman, one becomes pure by bathing and fasting.
Likewise, after conversing with one who is pure, or having seen a woman in her menses while eating;
One should not eat until the time for bathing has passed; thereafter, one should drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Even if a corpse or a birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) is present, or if menstrual flow occurs, [one should still proceed].

Having bathed, she should eat her meal; ...and having [performed the rite], she should fast for the day. If there should be impurity from a corpse, or if she is menstruating, or if there be birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) in the interim, she should bathe and then eat; having touched what has been rendered impure by leftovers, she should perform the *kṛcchratama* penance.
Having eaten or drunk while menstruating, during a death-impurity, or after a birth-impurity, or likewise while fasting;

If one has consumed impure poison from women who have fallen into a state of passion without having first applied [remedies], purification may be achieved through consecration; otherwise, there will be destruction for three days.
O Earth, one should bathe with waters and clay that has been drawn up from impure places.
One should bathe in the morning on the fourth day, preferably when six *nāḍīs* have elapsed.
The purification of clothing, provided it is unstained, is achieved by means of saline earth, steam, and fragments [of cloth].
Having consumed food from a bell-metal vessel, one becomes impure and must purify oneself by sipping water and smearing ashes twenty-one times.
One should wash the bed with water containing earth and other such substances for an instant, and apply an ointment;
that spot where one has slept and used it becomes purified by the passage of a cow or a dog.

Where there is no grass on the ground and water rises only at midday, a woman who has bathed after her menses must not, out of force or delusion, approach another man, nor even her own husband, except together with her lord. In such a place, bathing is prescribed only as far as the cowherds' fly-whisks [reach].
The staff for the cowherd's fan should be of that measure, or otherwise, it should be the height of a man.
If there is the striking of grass or leaves, or if [the object] is separated by a substance,
or if it is a cowherd or even a fan— there is no ritual bath (*snāna*) in those cases.
However, if one sees her during the midst of the rite, one should mutter the householder’s *praṇava*.
Afterwards, upon performing breath control (prāṇāyāma), there is the vision of the Sun.
Others, too, having performed the visualization, should recite the root mantra one hundred times.
Mounted upon a single tree are the outcaste, the earth, and the menstruating woman.
Having stayed for one night, she is purified by the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).

For women, [the period of impurity] lasts up to twelve days, after which they are considered pure like those who have passed urine. Alternatively, there may be bathing on the eighteenth day; beyond that, one is pure after three nights.
But a woman who, while already in her menses, becomes menstruating once again;
After twenty days have passed, she shall remain impure for three nights.
She should bathe after repeatedly scrubbing away the dirt from her teeth and other parts with clay;
then, having consumed the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) or clarified butter, she should worship Śiva.
The internal sacrifice (antaryāga) should be performed by oneself during the three preceding days.
Alternatively, at the end, one should recite the terrible mantra (*ghoramantra*) one thousand times;
then, as if touched by the rising of one's own class, one should worship [the deities] beginning with Kāma and others.
At that time, one should worship the mantra of the Lord of one's own class (*svajātiśvara*) one thousand times.
And for one who does not know this, purity does not arise from the setting [of the sun].
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times when a doubt has arisen;
in the case of contact with those of low birth, one should recite it two, three, or four times respectively.

In the event of contact with one of superior birth, he who is of lower birth should perform half of the penance. During the period of ritual impurity (sūtaka), he should, according to his ability, meditate upon the Lord.
At the end of that, one should unweariedly worship the five products of the cow for Śiva.
Having touched a human bone or oily remains, one should bathe and recite the Ghorā mantra one hundred times.
If one touches someone who is unanointed with oil, one should bathe; having sipped water (ācamya), one should look at the sun.

Having sipped water, one should look at the sun [again]. One should bathe upon touching those who have touched a corpse, those who carry out a dead body, those who cremate it, or those who are under the impurity of birth or death (sūtaka-preta); likewise, upon touching carriers of corpses or those bearing other sectarian marks (liṅgin).
In the event of contact with Pāñcarātrikas, Kālarātras, Kāpālikas, or Kaulikas;

Having performed his bath with water drawn from the *Somabhṛk* [well] by others who are naked, black, and devoid of impurity, he becomes pure after the third hundred [verses], provided he remains clothed.
Upon the fourth touch, a Brahmin should perform a bath with his clothes on;
having touched all the intermediate [touches], perform two baths.
One should perform a ritual bath upon approaching a Kāmāra, Pañca, or Ṣaṭka, as well as on the Yugādi days;
or [one should bathe] when near a Vācāla, a Bhāṇa, or a Rajaka, at a distance of two *daṇḍas*.
One should bathe from a distance of one and a half *daṇḍas* when near a woman in a state of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*).
Likewise, for touching one of the lowest caste, the penalty is that of a heron-eater.

At that very time, one should perform a ritual bath upon touching jackals, crows, and cocks that have been in the cremation ground, as well as those fallen [there] with discarded garlands in their beaks.
Upon contact with a jackal, a chameleon, a bat, a kuraṇḍaka, or a dog-cooker, one should perform a *vāruṇa* bath.
Likewise, upon contact with a *divākīrti*, a funeral pyre, a sacrificial post, a *niṣāda*, or a woman who has recently given birth;
Having touched a twice-born man who persists in forbidden acts, or a Lokāyatika, or an atheist;
Likewise, having touched a tree at a shrine (caitya), one should enter the water with one's clothes on;
so too when a Caṇḍāla or similar person has climbed onto one's chest.
A Brāhmaṇa residing there attains purity through bathing;
however, upon contact with white feces or urine above the navel, he becomes pure by washing with water.
In cases of shaving, vomiting, or touching those who are untouchable, one should perform a full bath.
Whatever parts [of the body] are above the navel, all of them are pure in every respect.
From contact with impure substances such as grain,
dregs, or excrement, and when the body has come into contact with filth, it is purified by seven applications of earth.
In the event of an injury to the head, one should perform a bath with water.
In the case of contact with the excrement of dogs and other such animals, or of birds such as crows and the like,
one becomes pure by performing purification on the lower part of the body using earth after having first performed cleansing.
However, for the head, bathing with water alone is prescribed in all cases.
A wise person should perform the expiation by reciting the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times,
once purification has been performed according to the rule following contact with the leavings of food.
Having bathed, one attains purity; [the purification for] an action is tenfold for a hundred [times].
In the case of falsehood or the discharge of urine, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on.
If the face is touched by white [substances], feces, urine, or [other impurities], [one must bathe].
It is purified by being smeared with clay and cow dung, and then cleansed with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having touched human bone, fat, feces, or excrement, urine, or semen,
or having touched marrow or blood, one should perform a bath after [the area] has been thoroughly cleansed. Indeed, a woman in her courses, having touched water, becomes pure by bathing.
One who has been touched by such a person while they are impure from food remnants becomes pure only through bathing.
Bathing during the day is praised when joined with the rays of the sun;
however, it is not recommended at night, except upon the sighting of Rāhu [during an eclipse].
Or else, one should perform a bath at night according to the instructions of the guru and others.
A virtuous person should always perform the bath with ashes (*bhasmasnāna*), the initiation (*pravrajyā*), and the bath with mantras (*mantrasnāna*).
If he touches another who is impure, he becomes defiled even if that other belongs to the same caste (*ekavarṇa*).
One who is touched by that person is not defiled; however, this same rule applies to all types of leavings.
During divine processions, weddings, sacrifices, and established rites,
as well as at all festivals, touching what has been touched does not cause defilement.
At a sacred ford, at a wedding, on a pilgrimage, in battle, during a national upheaval,
and in the event of a city or village fire— having touched what has been touched, one is not defiled.
There is no fault in being impure when it concerns food remnants, nor when there is hair on the lips.
And likewise with betel-leaf, even after having eaten a distinguished meal.
There is no fault for one who has food stuck between the teeth, nor for one who is impure from eating;
likewise, [one is not defiled] by water, leaves, roots, flowers, grass, wood, or earth.
O twice-born ones, one does not become impure by using fragrant substances;
nor does one become impure after bathing, drinking, sneezing, yawning, eating, or walking upon a public road.
After sipping water once, one should sip again; likewise, after putting on the lower garment twice, and after voiding urine or excrement, one should touch water without having sipped it again.
Having touched [anything] from an unclean person... having touched the shoulder-yoke, one becomes pure after sipping water (*ācamya*).
Upon sneezing, upon sitting down, and likewise after hearing his speech when he has turned away;
Likewise, after spitting, after anointing oneself with oil, after eating, and after putting on a garment;
or if one touches those who are impure from food remnants, or if one touches a desired object such as a *liṅga*, or sees those who dwell outside the caste system (*antyavāsinaḥ*).

Having touched with the tongue that which has stuck to the teeth, one should sip water; likewise, after emerging from water, when performing the ritual sipping (*ācamana*), and at the conclusion of a rite for the gods.
[This applies also] upon encountering a woman, a Śūdra, or an Ambaṣṭha, or upon seeing the voiding of excrement.
In the worship of the deity... if [this occurs], one should sip water for purification and then sip water again toward the north.
Just as when the teeth have been rubbed with tooth-powder, whatever remains stuck inside the mouth is like what is left over after vomiting;
one should not then rinse the mouth with water.
At the half-point of twilight, or at the half-point of a vessel, and likewise for the sake of the ancestors;
one should not sip water using the hand of a Śūdra during recitation, fire-offerings, or worship.
Having touched [something] defiled by its own kind,
one should perform the fire-purification bath (āgneyasnāna) using warm water mixed with cow dung for the purpose of removing fire, oil, odor, and smearing.
Gold and silver shall be purified by rubbing and heating; iron by scrubbing and heating; copper by being boiled with alkaline ash; and a bronze vessel with ash.
Objects made from all metals become pure through acid or ash;
a vessel such as one made of bamboo or clay is purified by scrubbing with cow-urine, cow-dung, and salt;
however, an earthen alms-bowl attains purity through water alone.

A woman who has touched a wooden vessel is purified by washing it with water; [a conch shell] is purified by scrubbing it with cow’s urine or milk. A pearl is purified by washing it with churned [cow’s urine], while wheat is purified by rubbing it with husks or chaff.
The purification of water-vessels must always be performed by people through washing;
that is, by scrubbing with water, or even by circling fire around them,
using an iron [vessel] that has been churned by one who is not of the Vāruṇa lineage.

For all those who eat from lotus leaves, bamboo vessels, or from bowls, leaves, hollowed palms, and the like, [the purification is] by means of water. (p.66b, f.63a, l.1) And regarding the consumption of food [from such vessels]: |||
In this context, purification is defined as the discarding of those items that have been used;
however, bamboo products [such as vessels] should be discarded if they come into contact with feces, urine, or [other impurities].
On the other hand, anything produced from fire is purified by touching it once the fire has been kindled.
A vessel licked by a mongoose, a crow, or a cat is indeed purified.

One should avoid performing the *paryagni-karaṇa* rite with those who do not possess the seven weapons, as well as the injury caused by donkeys, camels, horses, and the like; one should abandon such [faults].

Indeed, a vessel containing a herd of cows must certainly be abandoned, as must one that has been licked by jackals, or one that contained ghee [and was subsequently licked]. Furthermore, a vessel released from a bow seven times attains purity through fire alone.
Even by means of water alone, the former [faults] attain purification, just like a vessel.
Having sipped water and sprinkled food and other items, one should touch them with the Astra-mantra and the Arka-mantra.
For oily substances, purification comes from drying; for smeared substances, by wiping away the smear;
and for foul-smelling things, purification comes from removing the odor with the Upahṛdaya-mantra.
A seat, a bed, and a vehicle are purified by means of earth and water.
One should respectfully [examine] three things: the hand of a servant, the hand of an artisan, and [the hand of] a physician;
likewise, one should examine a fruit that is free from defects, moistened with water, and pecked at by a hundred birds.
Earth purified by digging from its source, and that which is burnt and then smeared;
a chariot purified by being driven along a path; a drink purified by the rays of the moon and sun;
and whatever is mixed with flies or hair, or struck at the edge of the foot [of a cow].
One who eats food mixed with dust and inhabited by ants, while being observed by others at the end [of the meal].
Having extracted just that much, one should sprinkle it with water as a penance;
purification from the sprinkling of clarified butter or by wiping with ashes shall likewise occur. Food exceeding one *droṇa* that has been defiled by crows, dogs, or the like—
Having removed a single mouthful, would that alone not be as light as a balance-scale?
(l.4) [One should test it] with water mixed with gold... or with water from a mountain spring;
however, one should reject that which has been pecked at by crows or dogs, or that which is less than a *droṇa*.
And that food shall become purified by the Vedic chanting of the Brahmins during feasts,
weddings, and when sacrifices are being performed.
During times such as consecrations and on the days of initiation festivals,
food that has not been touched by crows or dogs shall attain purity.
The earth is purified by seven means: by digging, by filling, by burning, by scraping, by smearing, by treading upon by cows, and by the passage of time.
Likewise, [the ground is purified] from a Caṇḍāla, a dog, and one who defiles Śiva.
If he has consumed food during his planetary period, he should first wash it away with clay and water.
Having discarded the earthen vessels, one should smear [the ground] with cow dung;
[this should be done] by initiated Brahmins with gold, kuśa grass, and water.
One should sprinkle the entire house; then it will be purified, of this there is no doubt. If there has been cohabitation... [one] should prescribe penance and heat.
Water that has stayed for one night should be abandoned, even if it is considered pure.

Even when ponds, wells, and tanks have been defiled, they must be purified. If [the water] has been contaminated by bones, skin, salt, and so forth, or if it has remained stagnant for a long time, one should remove a hundred jars of water and then pour the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) into them.
One should establish [the sacred water] in reservoirs that are not situated on the ground;
however, if it comes into contact with impurities such as the touch of a Caṇḍāla, one should avoid that holy site.
That which is frequented by fools and practiced by women,
touched by mosquitoes and flies, is not defiled;
nor is it [defiled] by the tip of a flame or by a cloth made of great jewels from the depths of the earth.
The Brāhmaṇas are the true kinsmen, and likewise, the temple of the Earth-gods (the Brahmins).
That which is always pure is indeed pure, as is the cow-pen of cattle;
the entire earth is pure wherever no ritual defilement is found.
On ground consisting of impurity, there may be trees, leaves, flowers, and fruits;
yet their leaves, flowers, and fruits are not at all defiled.
[Likewise for] actors, dancers, carpenters, and goldsmiths—here the letter *m* [is used].
Those who are like a pillar, eunuchs, and courtesans are proclaimed to be unfit for enjoyment.
One greedy for his wife, a tailor, a weaver,
one who lives by his cart, a dyer, a gambler, and likewise a thief.
A flag-bearer, one who lives by his mind, a Śūdra, a teacher, and a beggar;
a potter, a painter, a dyer, a usurer, and a seller of meat.
Having recognized a pregnant woman in her household, he should enter every house [to give alms].
He is one whose labor is in vain, whose giving is in vain, and who causes the destruction of the stages of life (āśramas).
One who marries a woman of the same lineage (*sagotra*), one who sells merit, one who causes confusion of birth-classes (*yonisāṅkarika*), and one who is devoid of the initiation of Śiva.

One who lives off stage performances, one who is excessively angry, one who is averse to separation [from others], one who is secretive, a physician, a poisoner, one who lives by their appearance, and a beggar.
Śaunaka, Pauṇika, and he who is Grataka at the beginning of the initiation—
whosoever among these performs [the rite] out of delusion, and the Brāhmaṇa who persists [in such conduct],
he indeed must be avoided once the penance has been performed.
For indeed, all these very people are outcasts (caṇḍāla), though they are supposedly brāhmaṇas.
Therefore, those who perceive reality avoid both gods and ...
[lacuna] ..., as well as the sufferings associated with the path of worldly existence, prostration, and the ascetic life of one whose wealth is penance.
One who worships those initiated by Śiva who have passed away— whether they be matted-haired ascetics (*jaṭin*), shaven-headed ones (*muṇḍin*), or those bearing the sectarian marks (*liṅgadhara*)—
or these [same individuals] while still alive, or a *liṅga*, or an image (*pratimā*) and so forth,
[and] who [worships] the dwelling [of the deity], by him [is worshipped] that which originates from Svayambhū and the like.
When touched by a thousand [recitations] of the Ghoras, it is worshipped once by ten thousand.
Having recited [the mantra] and performed the rite of pacification for those desiring their own welfare,
one should [worship] Vīrabhadra, the Teacher, Durgā, Kālī, and Reṇukā.
In the proper place, one who is worthy of honor should indeed worship Śaṅkha, Bhūteśa, the Gaṇas, and the heroic devotees; he who does not do so is indeed censured.
One should not, even in one's mind, perform the viewing or salutation of a *liṅga*, an image, or a painting on a wall that has been worshipped by a *śūdra*.

If [the image] is worshipped by a Śūdra, whether out of delusion or even through ignorance, he too shall be equal to a Śūdra; though living, he shall be censured. Or, if a sacred place belonging to Īśvara is worshipped by others, such as the Kāpālikas and so forth...
Beholding and saluting him produces great fault;
one becomes one-eyed, a cripple, a child, deaf, or a wandering singer on the road.
Furthermore, one who lacks worship for his own sake, a Śūdra, one who associates with the three [lower castes],
and one who, though a knower of the four Vedas, is uninitiated— such a person should neither touch nor worship [the deity].
A Brahmin who has not been initiated into Śaivism, nor one who follows the Vaikhānasa-sūtra, nor one connected with the Pāñcarātra, nor one who knows the Parārthavidyā—
such a person should perform the worship of Śiva and Keśava for three years.
He is indeed known as a *devalaka*, despised in all ritual acts.
The fool who bears the conch, the discus, and the linga upon his body should be known as a heretic, excluded from all ritual acts.
One should touch [the image] with a thousand [blows of] terrible [weapons], and once it has been worshipped, one should perform the sprinkling.
One with deformed nails, black teeth, or even afflicted by a great disease;
A celibate student who lacks a wife, one who consumes liquor and meat,
or one who possesses either too few or too many limbs, as well as one afflicted by leprosy, vitiligo, or consumption;
If an ascetic who is either burdened with a great sin (*mahāpātaka*) or afflicted by misfortune should perform worship for the sake of another, the king and his kingdom shall perish immediately.
To remedy that fault, one should perform a propitiatory sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) accompanied by pacification rites (*śānti*).
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, on the fourteenth, or under the asterism Ārdrā in that month,
he who is devoid of fasting shall indeed be utterly defeated.
Even one endowed with the *tasta-mudrā* and other [signs] will be like one afflicted with vitiligo or leprosy.

At the time of propitiating Hara, one should not—either in sight, by speech, or even in thought—allow anyone who is naked or otherwise contrary to the rules to be present. (l. 7) If one has engaged in the Raudra-āgama, one must perform the worship and the realization of the knowledge of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-siddhānta*). If it is to be performed, one should first ensure stability and so forth; having discarded earthen vessels, one should proceed with the sprinkling of water. (p. 69b, f. 66a, [referring to] the omission of the daily rule, the omission of the daily worship, l. 1)
If one performs the worship of Śiva and other rites while seated, lying down, or while bathing,
or if one performs them together with those of mixed caste (*saṅkara*), a constant expiation must be made.
If the worship of Śiva is performed at night, it should be done as a single daily rite.
One should always perform the worship of the chosen *liṅga*, fire-offerings (*homa*), charity, and the twilight rituals (*saṃdhyā*),
except during a lunar eclipse and for rites performed for specific desires such as the attainment of supernatural powers (*siddhi*).
Purity, sipping water for purification, bathing, wearing sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads,
sprinkling, the recitation of the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn, meditation on the twilight devotions, and the libation of water.
The ritual placement on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*), the recitation of mantras (*mantrajāpya*), circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*),
and prostration to the guardians of the directions (*digdāvatānamaskāra*) are declared to be the daily duties (*nityakarman*).
Whether done knowingly or unknowingly, upon the omission of even one of these, [there is a fault].
One should recite the Ghoramantra once for the purification of each respective sin.

If one who desires worldly enjoyment should, out of negligence, worship Śiva at night, he will be afflicted by fear of kings and thieves; once that [impurity] has been digested, he becomes pure through bathing.

Having induced vomiting when suffering from indigestion and bathed, one should recite the Ghorasahasra-mantra a thousand times; then, having bathed again according to the rules, one should worship one's chosen *liṅga*. He should then mutter the Śiva-mantra one hundred and eight times each day.

One who desires liberation should perform the worship and meditation of Śambhu at all times. (p.70a, liṅgārcanam, l.1) If one fails to worship even once, one should recite the Ghoramantra a thousand times;
if this occurs unintentionally, the previously mentioned number is doubled for intentional omission.

For one who performs worship at a single time, and for another who performs it at three times— if the third [time] is omitted, the expiation prescribed for them is equal. Starting from the second day, one should perform a thousand [recitations] with the Aghora mantra.
One should increase it by three hundred [breaths] each day.
If the monthly worship is omitted here, one should recite ten million of the *ghora* mantra;
if the annual worship is omitted, one should recite thirty million of the *bahurūpin* mantra.
For a month up to a year, purification occurs through an increase of thirty thousand [repetitions] per day;
beyond that, purification from the omission of Śiva-worship comes through initiation (dīkṣā).
If one's own chosen *liṅga* is stolen by thieves, carried off by rats, or by men and the like;
or if it is burnt, broken, cut, lost, or swept away by a stream.
One should recite the Aghora mantra one hundred thousand times and install another liṅga;
this is declared to be its purification, and it should be the same for the pedestal.
For images and their pedestals that are unstable at the edges, that same [penance] applies;
however, for those from a small jar (*gaḍḍuka*) up to ten thousand, by means of recitation (*jāpa*), the great sin is destroyed. For Aghora, it is purified by double that amount.
If one's own chosen *liṅga* has fallen, one should mutter the *Ghora* mantra a thousand times;
if it has fallen twice, [one should mutter it] twice that amount; if it has rolled three or four times, [the same applies];
and if the *liṅga* has fallen into a chasm, one should mutter the *Bahurūpin* mantra one hundred thousand times.

If the *liṅga* falls upon its base (*ādhāra*), one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times for each fall; if it falls without a base (*nirādhāra*), the number is doubled. Whether intentional or unintentional, the procedure is as before.
If the *liṅga* falls due to disrespect toward men, or out of desire, or from every [possible] state of being,
and even if it should become shattered, no expiation (*prāyaścitta*) exists for that.
In the case of breaking the *liṅga* or a [wooden] pin (*śalākā*), his sin shall be great.
One should perform three hundred thousand recitations of the Aghora mantra for the sake of purification.
When the *liṅga* is damaged by lust, there is no expiation at that time;
however, if the *liṅga* is touched with the foot or even stepped over, [one must perform] twenty thousand [recitations].
When the Liṅga of the Terrible One is touched by the water from a hundred feet, [one should perform] ten thousand [ablutions];
the wise should perform the ritual bathing everywhere for the Liṅga...
