When the Liṅga is touched by phlegm, [it should be washed] with water mixed with Śleṣmātaka.
Thirty thousand or twenty thousand [beings] are proclaimed for him by means of his manifold forms.
When the linga is sprinkled with urine and water, [the lifespan] is twenty thousand [years];
when it is defiled by blood, semen, menstrual blood, or urine, it is fifty thousand [years].
If the *liṅga* is touched by water that has come into contact with those [impurities], it is purified by [the recitation of] three-quarters of that [number].
However, if the *liṅga* is touched by feces, one should mutter the Aghora mantra one hundred thousand times.
O Ambā, that [liṅga] is deficient by one foot; likewise, when a *nirmālya* [garland] falls...
(l. 7) ...when a liṅga has fallen into a pit of hot ashes, [the penance is] one hundred thousand [repetitions] plus half.
When a liṅga is touched by people who are uninitiated (*adīkṣita*), [the penance is] the *ghoraśambara*.
In that case, one hundred, two hundred, or three hundred penances have been prescribed.

If the *liṅga* is touched by a Śūdra, one should recite the Aghora mantra five hundred times. (p.71a, regarding contact with gems and so forth, free from the eight bondages, l.1) If it is touched by fishermen, actors, and the like, [one should recite it] ten thousand times.
If the *liṅga* is touched by crows and the like, one should recite [the mantra] twenty thousand times;
if it is gazed upon by outcastes (*śvapaca*), one should recite it fifty thousand times.
If the *liṅga* is touched by them, one should recite the *Ghoraśambara* mantra twice that amount.
If the linga is touched by those situated on the left or right paths, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times.
If the liṅga is moved from its pedestal, it becomes free of defect for the ascetic;
one should install that very same [liṅga] there and mutter the Aghora mantra one hundred thousand times.
He should abandon that defect along with its characteristic marks, and having served [the deity] with the *pacādi* offerings,
he establishes another linga and attains purification.
Having fasted for three nights before the Nirvāṇa fire and the fire of the Lord (*seśvara*), [he attains purity].
The ritual actions involved in both the offering and the destruction of even Yama himself.
One should recite the Śaiva [mantra] one hundred and eight times over them, and the Gāyatrī one hundred times;
this shall be the worship of the Liṅga when the eight bonds are severed.
If even a mere drop from the portion of Hari, or from the portion of Brahmā,
falls upon the portion of Rudra, a great fault arises.

If at that time the [image] is worshipped only once, twice, or thrice [a day], it is declared to be fruitless; there will be distress for the king and the kingdom, and the falling of stones and other calamities.
For either the one who performs the rite or the one who causes it to be performed, it shall result in great misfortune.
Or it should be performed at that very time, even without specifying the month, fortnight, or day.
Having performed the sprinkling with water, thereafter one should perform the fire-oblation for peace;
having recited the Aghora mantra more than a hundred thousand times, one should carry out the binding.
On the transit of the sun, on the fourteenth and eighth days, on the festival days (*parvan*),
and when the [deities] of Hara and Kṣetrapāla have been worshipped, the merit is fourfold compared to the daily [offering].
When the offering of the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*) has been performed during the months beginning with Āṣāḍha...
One should recite the Aghora mantra two hundred thousand times and then perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Having performed the rite of the purificatory cord (*pavitraka*) according to the prescribed conduct,
even if one has gone to another village during the interval between the four-month periods;
If the purificatory rite (*pavitra*) is omitted, then purification occurs through the *Cāndrāyaṇa* vow;
likewise, if the offering of *damanaka* flowers and other rites are not performed, one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times.
Furthermore, when vessels such as the *arghya* bowl have not been formally dismissed (*avisarjita*), [one must perform atonement].
When the rite has been turned back or when obstacles have arisen, one should recite two hundred [times] the *ghora* mantra.
Five hundred and ten mango trees are offered there;
through that, purification occurs for the rosary from the upper half of the foot of the Liṅga.

When the thread is broken and a new one is strung, one should recite the *Ghora* mantra a thousand times. When the old thread is worn out but not yet severed, one should recite the *Ghora* mantra a hundred times. If the well-strung rosary falls from the hand to the ground, one should wash it with water, worship it, and recite the *Gāyatrī* mantra one hundred and eight times. Furthermore, in the event of an obstruction involving the bell or the liṅga, one should perform an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) consisting of one-eighth of the prescribed [recitation], starting from the act of instigating the rite.
If touched by the foot, one should recite the Aghora mantra two hundred times;
for those with desire, ten thousand times there, while for children and others, it is from the foot [of the deity].

If the food offering (*naivedya*) is defiled by insects, meat, or the like, one should recite the Aghora mantra one hundred times; thereafter, for the fulfillment of desires, one should recite it ten thousand times (*ayuta*).
If the food offering (*naivedya*) is presented in an inferior manner during the daily rite, there shall be two hundred [repetitions of] the *ghora* mantra.
If incense made from the limbs of living beings is used, the *sadyojāta* mantra is considered to be recited one hundred times.
Having touched the *liṅga*, the Guru, and the Śiva-fire with the foot in succession, [one should proceed].
And for the Aghora [mantra], purification from intentional [offense] is ten thousand times that;
for the violation of the command of the Ācārya, Śiva, or Caṇḍa, it is one hundred thousand;
but for one deficient in their characteristics, it is declared to be seventy-five thousand.
For consuming the *nirmālya*, one hundred thousand [repetitions] are prescribed starting from the feet;
the gift is equal to the consumption, and half of that for not looking at it.
If one consumes [the remains of an offering] unintentionally, or if it is *nirmālya*,
one should become pure by reciting the *Brahmapañcaka* one thousand five hundred times.
However, if one consumes it intentionally, initiation (*dīkṣā*) is the atonement, and there is no other.
If one steps over the remains of offerings (nirmālya), one should then mutter the mantra ten thousand times with great care.
Touching, leaping over, selling, and eating—(p. 72b, f. 69a, naivedyaṣaḍvidhanirmālyaṃ, l.
1) (naivedyaṣaḍvidhanirmālyaṃ—) O God, his sixfold *nirmālya* is considered to be made of gold.
Furthermore, divine property and the offering (naivedya) that has been presented [should not be consumed].
Violent substances and ritual remains (*nirmālya*) are said to be their characteristics.
Property belonging to the deity of the city, the field, and so forth— such as gold and clothing—
as well as cooked food, perfumes, and other offerings presented as *naivedya*, are the remnants of Śiva (*śivocchiṣṭa*).
One should offer the Caṇḍa-portion to Caṇḍadatta, and the remains of the offering (nirmālya) should be cast outside after being swept away.
Even when the Lord of Gaurī is possessed by poison, the sacred remains (*nirmālya*) are not indeed a seat for him;
one who would consume the sacred remains would be a flesh-eater, the lowest of men.
For one who eats it, there is a tiger and the loss of spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*).
From giving it away, one becomes a crow; from burning it, a *caṇḍāla*.
From selling it, one becomes a woman; and from touching it, one becomes [so].

Whatever substance has been touched by the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*), even that which is held in the hands, for that one should prescribe a penance three-quarters of what was previously stated. As for flowers and such that have entered the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*) incidentally, [the same applies].

He is the fierce-rayed sun for his devotee; there is no doubt in this regarding the remains of the offerings (*nirmālya*), as well as the incense, perfumes, flowers, and so forth, at the time of worship.
Furthermore, the continuous flow of lamp-light and so forth causes defects;
therefore, once the installation is complete, the offering materials (nirmālya) must be discarded at the conclusion of the fourth-day rite.
Having offered food, medicine, flowers, water, leaves, fruits,
and so forth to Śiva, the wise person should eat the remainder of that as his meal.
One who has been initiated into Śiva (*śivadīkṣita*) should not consume what is not given as the eighth [type of food], nor that which is impure, nor leftovers (*ucchiṣṭa*).
By reciting the root mantra (*mūla*) one hundred and eight times and performing worship, he becomes purified.
Whatever has been offered to his own chosen *liṅga* is, without doubt, like the sacrificial porridge (*caru*).
Having consumed that, he shall obtain the fruit of the worship of Śiva and attain union [with Him],
as well as [the merit of] the consecration of deities, tanks, and gardens.
One should recite five hundred [mantras] here after eating food with the fifth [vessel].
In the case of the self-existent deity, the *nirmālya* is offered with the *bāṇa* [mantra].
For all [deities], there is no *nirmālya*, and likewise for the *pīṭhas*.
Having eaten food during the *puṃsavana* rite, one should recite the Vāmadevya hymn a hundred times.
He who eats on the eleventh day, or even on the twelfth and subsequent days,
should worship one hundred thousand, two hundred thousand, or three hundred thousand times with the Ghoramantra.
In the Śivārdha rite of Anumāsi, one should recite the mantra of Ghorā three hundred times.
Having eaten the food of a Gaṇa, the food of a courtesan, the food of renunciants,
or the food of a Yāpaka, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.

One who eats food at the sacrifice of cooking, at a wedding, at the gift of a cow, at the investiture with the sacred girdle, or at the tonsure ceremony of Brahmins who follow traditional conduct, does not incur sin. However,
if one of a particular caste eats the food of another caste without being formally invited, [he incurs fault].
Having combined the lords of that class and the lords of its own class, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred times.
One, two, or three days should be spent observing fasts in successive order.
The Aghora, Vāma, and Jyeṣṭha [faces] of the Puruṣa are the foremost among Brāhmaṇas and the other [castes];
Īśāna belongs to other castes—thus has it been declared by Śivadvija.
When food has not been digested, a wise person should abandon recitation (*japa*), ritual bathing (*snāna*), worship (*pūjā*), and fire-offerings (*homa*).
Once the food is digested, he should bathe and then recite the *gāyatrī* mantra one hundred and eight times.
Having touched one initiated by another who is initiated, or one who is impure from eating, or a member of his own caste (*savarṇaka*) in such a state, [he should likewise perform this].
Having repeated the mantra one hundred and eight times, the wise person should perform worship to the Lord of his own clan.
Having touched that very [person] while they are uninitiated, one who is already initiated should bathe and recite [the mantra] two hundred times;
likewise for a Brahmin, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra who has been rendered impure by food remnants.
Having been initiated and fasted for two nights or three nights,
one should unite that *tājī* with its Lord and recite [the mantra] in due order. Having touched a Śūdra who is impure from eating, one should fast for a day.
Having unified the lord of that class and the lord of its own class, one should recite [the mantra] in sequence.
Having touched those who have not been initiated, one should perform twice the penance previously mentioned. Therefore, a king is purified by half [of that], and a Vaiśya by a quarter.

A Śūdra attains purification by consuming a fourth part [of the remainder], of this there is no doubt. When one has consumed the leavings of a superior person, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times for the Lord of one's own caste (*svajātīśa*). Upon eating the leavings of an inferior person, a superior person should perform that same rite doubled.

Fasting, having bathed with purity, and intent on consuming the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should observe celibacy and sleep on the ground; this is remembered as the vow to be observed in all cases. One should worship the *liṅga* of one's chosen deity and [bathe] the great lakes in the heart.

If an object seized from thieves, monkeys, and the like is recovered later— having had its identifying marks lost and then restored to its original state— and the time for its ritual use arrives, how should the twice-born one worship it?
Having performed the sprinkling with water, one should carry out the rite of pacification (*śāntikarma*).
Having recited the Aghora mantra one hundred thousand times, and the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) an equal number of times,
one should perform worship at both lingas constantly and without sloth.
Having first honored that which was given previously, one should thereafter give what is given subsequently.
This expiation has been declared for householders in due order;
a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) shall perform it twofold, and a forest-dweller (vanastha) threefold.
One who has committed [the offense] four times should perform the penance.
If the worship of the door-keepers is omitted, there will be great affliction from obstacles.
For that reason, having completed the *saṃhitā*-oblation, one should install the door-keepers.

That worship which is devoid of the five purities is indeed performed in vain. If the sequence of seats is omitted, an unstable state arises. If the ten consecrations are omitted, one becomes a speaker of base words.
Furthermore, if there is a deficiency in the ritual services (*upacāra*), men are afflicted by hunger, thirst, and the like;
but if the sequence is broken, confusion arises on earth.
But if there is a failure of knowledge and so forth, it results in the misfortune of the attendants and the teacher;
having then performed a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma), one should perform everything according to the rules.
In the daily, occasional, or optional rites, if the materials such as water for the feet (*pādya*) are lacking,
there will be in the world a destruction of those respective symbols;
if his own materials for the feet are lacking, there will be diseases of the feet.
Likewise, if one performs the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) while laughing, a disease of the mouth will arise.
If the head, the neck, or the nose and ears are deficient, there will be [misfortune];
if the striking of the bell is deficient, Piśācas, Rākṣasas, and the like [will appear].
And afflictions and calamities are experienced by those residing there when the offering of lamps is omitted, or when the syllable *yaṃ* is dropped from the word *śogataḥ*,
or when the mantra is lost, or when the sacrificial oblation is omitted, or even when its constituent parts are missing.
If there is the offering of food that is a part of that [rite], there will be the destruction of crops;
there will be the loss of the substances used as parts of that rite, and great hunger and thirst shall arise.
In the absence of betel-leaf offering, or where there is a physical defect, or where there is disease;
and in the absence of a fine cloth (*caṇḍapaṭa*), there is a loss of the presence of the deities.
Having worshipped the deity, O Śivā, one should cause that material to be given back twofold.
Then one should perform a pacifying fire-sacrifice (śāntihoma), or one should lead the preceptor to the ritual bathing (snapana).
O Śivā, if that [rite] is deficient in limbs (*aṅga*), one should cause double [the number of oblations] to be given.
A *saṃhitā-homa* should be performed; having performed a hundred-fold *homa*, [one should use] the *aghora* mantra, or else [use] these substances in half, a quarter, or half of that again.
In the principal [mantra], the *ghora-mantra*, [the sequence is] two, four, six, and a hundred.
Having performed the recitation, one should then cause twice that amount to be given to the deity.
If these substances are offered to Śaṅkara without a mantra,
the preceptor, having worshipped them, should offer that substance belonging to the deity— which was not [formally] given— to the minor deities.
At the end, one should offer the substance with one's own mantra, either doubled or equal [in measure].

One should cause the desired bathing to be performed, even that which is of a hundredfold terrible form. In the obligatory, occasional, and optional rites, there is no omission of the triad beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*).
The practitioner, having recited the Sadyojāta mantra one hundred times, [attains] the powers of Īśāna.

One should give double the amount for the water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth, or simply that same amount in silver; however, if the *dūrvā* grass, flowers, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) are deficient, a hundred recitations with the Heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) is prescribed.

If the oil massage, body rub, bathing, or other such services are deficient when being performed, one should recite the *Hṛdaya-mantra* a hundred times and cause [the deficiency] to be redone twice over.
If the oil for the limbs or similar items have not been consecrated, there shall be an oblation from the *Saṃhitā* during the worship.
In rites that are obligatory, occasional, or performed for a specific desire, one should use arrows previously prepared and brought by hand.
If the *saṃhitā-homa* has been omitted, one should perform it twice without having done so;
by this rule, one should effect expiation with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
If the previously intended fragrance should perish, one should immediately recite [the mantra] one hundred times;
or else, one should offer as an oblation that same substance either doubled or in equal measure.

If one offers a flower in reverse order when it is either deficient or lacking [in quality], one should recite the mantra for the Lord a hundred times; thereafter, one should offer that [flower] twice as many times. Having offered incense and the *ārātrika* lamp, one should recite the *ghora* mantra at the end, doubling the number from that point.
The offering of incense and the night-rite, as well as the rite of the collyrium-water, should be performed at the proper time.
If [the fire] is interrupted, one should cause it to be performed again after revolving it a hundred times and recollecting [the deity].
Then, using either a row of lamps or the mouth of a mouse and so forth,
if the fire touches the base, the image, the limbs, or other parts [of the deity], [one must perform atonement].
Or else, some disease will befall the king.
Having purified it with fire and inspected it, one should bathe the Supreme Lord with water from a coconut mixed with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*).
Having worshipped the Lord of the Gods of gods, one should perform the image-homa (mūrtihoma).
If the fire should become as small as an atom, one should perform a rite of pacification (śānti).
If the garments placed upon the *liṅga*, the *bera*, and so forth, are burnt by fire,
one should perform the rite consisting of sprinkling with water consecrated for the ritual (*karma*).
If they are burnt only in part, then [one should perform the rite] with water from the eastern direction.
And likewise with all water-born flowers and with the water of Vaiṣṇavas.
Regarding bowls, leaf-cups, and the like used for food,
purification is prescribed;
however, those items made of bamboo that have been used at night or are contaminated by feces, urine, or phlegm must be discarded.

That which has arisen from all elements is purified by being touched in fire. A bowl licked by insects, rats, or cats is purified by sprinkling water seven times with a blade of grass and also by circling it with fire.
One should abandon what has been smelled by a donkey, a camel, a dog, or the like;
for indeed, that which has the form of a cow and a vessel exposed to the sun are to be joined with excellence.
A vessel or even clarified butter that has been touched by those of low birth does not become pure;
indeed, it attains purity only when seven times released from the fire.
By means of water, those [vessels] preceded by the ladle attain purity like a pot;
[the food] that is abundant, immersed, frequented by crows and the like, and devoid of that [purity] alone [is unfit].

If one who has given food touches someone who is impure from eating remnants, he should set aside the food, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), sprinkle water upon the food and so forth, and then touch it with a little water.
For oily substances, purification is achieved by drying; for those smeared with a paste, by removing the paste.
A pickled radish (gaḍā) purifies the eyes, and cardamom (elā) removes foul odors from the heart.
One purifies a seat, a bed, or a vehicle with earth and water;
likewise, one should respectfully accept what is brought by the hand of a servant, the hand of an artisan, or purchased through meritorious means.

A fruit that has not been damaged by insects, one pecked at by a bird, or one dug up from the earth—the end of which was previously buried—is purified by being washed with water; likewise, one that has been burnt is purified by being smeared [with ash].
A fruit found on a road or in a path is purified by the rays of the wind, the moon, and the sun.
That which is mixed with flies or hair, and that which has been stepped upon by the edge of a foot.
If one eats food that is seen to be infested with dust or ants, one should remove only that much and sprinkle it with water; such is the penance.
Purification occurs through sprinkling with clarified butter or by the removal of ashes. If a cooked quantity exceeding one *droṇa* is defiled by crows, dogs, or the like,
having removed that specific portion, the remainder shall be treated as if it were saliva or clarified butter.
And one should sprinkle it with water mixed with saffron, or else with silver water.
One should avoid food that has been pecked at by crows, dogs, and the like, or that is less than a *droṇa* in quantity.
However, that food shall become pure through the Vedic chanting (*brahmaghoṣa*) of Brahmins,
as well as in cases of abundant food at weddings and when sacrifices have been performed.
During times such as consecrations (*pratiṣṭhā*) and even on the days of initiation festivals (*dīkṣotsava*),
one should perform the purification (*śānti*) with crows and dogs;
one should effect the burning of the dwelling (*satma*) and carry out the sprinkling (*samprokṣaṇa*) of the dwelling.
One should perform the ritual bathing for the deity, which may arise from the *dhāmachoda* and other such [mantras].
One should perform the expiation prescribed for that [defilement], accompanied by the rites of reconnection (*sandhāna*) and so forth.

When the *liṅga*, the image (*bera*), or other [objects] have become a different color due to fire, if it is a human [image], it should be abandoned; otherwise, one should perform the rite of exchange (*pratikrayākarma*) as taught, taking up a domestic *svastika* [image] and accompanied by ritual sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*).
By giving perfumes made from animal parts, one should recite the fifth [mantra] one hundred times;
furthermore, in the event of a deficiency of lamps, one should recite the Ghorā mantra three hundred times.
O God of gods, one should subsequently cause twice as many lamps to be offered;
in the event of the interruption of the protection of the quarters and so forth, it should be joined with twice the recitation.
O God, having performed the ritual bathing after the offering of sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) has been presented,
one should thereafter cause the invitation (*āmantraṇa*) to be given twice as much in the sacrificial food.
Now, if the cloth for the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍapaṭa*) is deficient, one should recite the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) two hundred times.
Every year, for each month, [this is] for the purpose of [recording] the lunar days (tithi) and so forth.
Having first determined [the time], if the *mukha* and other [limbs] were previously established by days and so forth,
then [the rite] is joined with nine days and so on, preceded by the beating of drums and other such ceremonies.
If it is performed three times that day, or even twice that day,
yet done otherwise than prescribed, it will bring harm to the kingdom and the king.
Having first performed a propitiatory rite (*śānti*) there, one should conduct the festival as before.
But it may occur within another month, or it may happen during that very month.

On the second day, or on that very day, the injunctions for the installation of the image, the fire-oblation (*homādi*), and so forth are prescribed; having performed these in sequence, the festival (*utsava*) should be conducted according to its specific rules. However, when preceded by the hoisting of the banner (*dhvajārohaṇa*), it is ordained over three days.
Thus the procedure has been declared; it should be inferred in the same way even for the double [number].
If the *liṅga* is of self-manifested origin (*svāyambhuva*), this procedure is prescribed;
whether it be a human-made *bāṇaliṅga* and so forth, or one of divine origin, or even one made of clay.
The twice-born should shift the month, the lunar mansion of the pilgrimage site, or otherwise [the timing],
so that the festival may be celebrated on days when it brings about prosperity for him.
Even in times of national upheaval, famine, or fear of kings and thieves, [it should be performed].
In the absence of wealth, due to fears of others, it is impossible to perform [the rite], as previously stated.
If [the birth] should occur even there, one should perform the rites preceded by pacification;
or else, one should observe a day-fast and hold a festival according to the previous method.
Because of the loss of everything, his festivals are ruined due to the destruction of even the smallest portion of what is praiseworthy;
when a total loss has occurred, a great fault arises for him.
At that time, one should perform the rite of pacification (*śānti*), the fire-offering for pacification (*śāntihoma*), and the fire-offering for the image (*mūrtihoma*).
By this method, one [performs] everything, such as the rites for specific omens and so forth.
If a festival is commenced that is deficient in its preliminary rites due to obstacles and the like, it will bring about the destruction of the kingdom;
therefore, one should then perform a propitiatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*) and conduct the festival once again.
If a flagstaff is erected on ground devoid of trees or celestial deities, cattle will perish; therefore, one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*) as prescribed.
Therein, one should perform the bull-sacrifice (*vṛṣayāga*) at the base of the flagpole.
However, when the banner has been destroyed, one should perform the placement of mantras and other rites mentally.
If the hoisting of the banner is deficient, one should predict danger for the king;
then the minister, having performed a rite of pacification, should have the banner raised once again.
If the rotation of the banner is deficient, it brings misfortune to the village and other areas;
one should then perform a *śānti*-oblation for the removal of all defects.
A sacrificial altar (*vedi*) that is deficient or lacking in its characteristics does not bestow auspiciousness.
Then, having performed the peace-offering (śāntihoma), one should construct an altar (vedī) endowed with the proper characteristics.
A staff that is deficient in its characteristics brings misfortune to the principal [personage];
one should then perform either a formal oblation (*mūrtihoma*) or a propitiatory oblation (*śāntihoma*).
A staff that is deficient in its own specific characteristics and has a broken tip portends danger.
If there is pride regarding the aggregates (skandha), one should then perform a pacifying fire-offering (śāntihoma).

When the occurrence of staffs, counter-staffs, *skandas*, and so forth, or the breaking of the *bhūtas* and such takes place, one should then perform a propitiatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*); if [the ritual] is broken, one should lead it toward another propitiation.
If the banner is devoid of auspicious marks, it brings fear to this kingdom;
therefore, one should undertake the raising of another banner that possesses the proper marks.
One should perform rites for pacification (śāntikarma) when planting a flag with deficient characteristics;
likewise, one should perform such acts in the case of a bull, as this serves as an expiation (niṣkṛti) that removes [the fault].
If the dancing of the figures above is variegated, one should recite the mantra of Īśa a hundred times;
if it is devoid of the cane-pattern below, it is not considered a fault.
If the cord is severed, there is danger from enemies; one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma).
If bitten by a rat or similar creature, one should then perform a propitiatory fire-offering with garments and other such items.

If the banner falls to the ground, there will be distress for the kingdom; therefore, having performed a pacifying fire-sacrifice according to the ritual rules, one should raise the flagstaff once again.
When [the banner] is joined with a broken flagstaff or similar defects, one should then perform a rite of pacification (*śāntika*).
O twice-born ones, within seven days one should raise another flagstaff;
O twice-born ones, each preceding one would be more auspicious if there is only slight loss.
Then one should perform either a *mūrtihoma* or a *śāntihoma*,
when this [image] is being carried away by a *ketu* or is overcome by wind and other such elements.
If a defect occurs during the consecration of the *liṅga*, one should perform a propitiatory *homa* for the sake of Śakti;
if it is devoid of the garland of *darbha* grass, then one should likewise perform a propitiatory *homa*.
Then, one should wrap the staff with a garland of *darbha* grass possessing the proper characteristics;

or else, a rope or a *darbha* garland [should be wrapped] according to the rule of circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*). If that [garland] has been joined to the staff, then having recited the *ghora* mantra a thousand times, [one should proceed].
One should lead the garland and other items from the front to the front in a clockwise sequence.
Even if the secondary staff (*upadaṇḍa*) is crooked, one should mutter the *ghora* mantra three hundred times;
for if the banner lacks a bell, the presence of the bull will not be there.
Likewise, the preceptor should recite the Aghora mantra three hundred times;
if the bell falls to the ground, he should mutter the Dakṣiṇa mantra three hundred times.
Since Śiva is the Lord of the Staff (*daṇḍanātha*), it is not desired that He ascend the binding [rope].
If, however, the installation of the water-pot (kumbhanyāsa) has not been performed at the time of hoisting the banner;
Having caused the breaking of the bull and the jar due to a specific cause, and the mounting of the banner (ketu), as well as the falling of the drum and other instruments;
and having performed at the end a pacifying *homa* sacrifice, one should prepare [the ritual] from the jar as before.
Then, having performed the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) mentally within the heart-lotus,
one should perform the consecration with the waters from the pitcher of its enclosure, provided that it has not already been performed.
One should perform the recitation (*japa*) one hundred times for each [deity] with their respective mantras,
whether that banner has been raised or lowered from the sanctuary.
For the sake of being free from defects, one should arrange [the recitation] with one, two, three, or four measures;
then, for each subsequent [syllable], one should mutter three hundred terrible [recitations] ending at the measure of the sun.
Having performed the peace-offering (*śāntihoma*) while the banner (*ketu*) is suspended below that,
one should subsequently raise the flagstaff (*dhvaja*), but not joined with the bull-figures (*vṛṣabha*).
If the drum (*bherī*) is struck poorly or with deficient force, delusion arises;
having then performed a peace-offering (*śānti-homa*), one should thereafter strike the drum again. If the recitation of the *bṛhattāla* is not performed, one should perform the peace-offering.
Before the commencement of the festival, when the invocation of the deities has taken place;
If the invocation of the deities is omitted, the gods and others will not be present.
One should perform the peace-offering (*śāntihoma*) as before and carry out the invocation of the deities.
When Keśava, Skanda, Vighneśa, Bhānu,
and Caṇḍeśvara are not invoked, then there is no fault;
[this applies] to other [deities] except for the nine [invocations] at the occasion of raising the banner.
One should perform the act of beating the drum in exactly the same manner.
When there is a breakage of the drum, its skin, or other such parts, or when the nose-string and so forth have come apart,
one should recite the Aghora-weapon mantra a hundred times and then proceed with another drum.
In the same manner, having seized another [limb], such as the nose, one should perform [the rite] as before.
Or, if the nose falls to the ground, one should recite the Aghora mantra three hundred times.
At that time, or if the reciter (*vādaka*) falls to the ground...
Then one should perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma) for the sake of the stability of the kingdom.
If a drum should fall to the ground, it would portend great misfortune for the king.
Having then performed a pacifying fire-oblation (*śāntihoma*), one should worship the drum with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*).

If the sacrificial hall is burnt by fire, or if it is deficient in its characteristic features, or if the temple, the sacrificial pit, or the altar, or even the kingdom itself should fall into a state of distress,
one should cause [the rites] to be performed correctly during a previous festival or a new festival.
Every day, there should be a peace-offering (śāntihoma) until the day of the pilgrimage concludes.
Having recognized that festival as well as the sacrificial hall through its characteristics,
one should perform a rite of pacification for a single day in order to eliminate those defects.
This procedure is general for the consecration and expiation [rites],
as well as for the ceremonial bath, the sprinkling, the monthly worship and so forth, the cutting of the thread, (l.
4) the subsidiary parts of a festival, or any other [rite] such as the restoration of what is decayed and the eightfold offering ritual.
In obligatory, occasional, or optional rites, one should perform the recitation of mantras other than those involving purchase.

The same applies even to the ritual implements; however, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, one should recite two hundred or three hundred *aghora* mantras for the sake of the peace-offering (*śāntihoma*).
If the site is deficient or lacks its constituent parts, one should then perform a pacifying oblation (*śāntihoma*).
To remedy that defect, one should prepare the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) as previously described.
In the case of the Śiva-vessel, the Vardhanī, the covered jars,
and other vessels that constitute parts of the festival,
there may be a crack, a hole, or a break, according to the sequence of their characteristics.
The pacifying oblation for the Aghora mantras consists of four hundred and five recitations.
One should perform [the rite] exactly one hundred times for the removal of disease.
Having brought nine jars and others, one should proceed with their installation as previously described.
Whether it be a *vardhanī* vessel or a *kumbha*, [if they are] presided over by the Lords of the Vidyās (*vidyeśvarādhipāḥ*) but are devoid of a golden lotus, or possess only a small amount of gold,
they shall cause poverty for the maker after [the maker] has recited a thousand repetitions of the *āśora* mantra.
Furthermore, one should bestow what is established by the scriptures in order to eliminate that fault.
If [the disciple] is naked from the waist down, there will be a wind disease;
having recited the Aghora mantra a thousand times, the Guru should then give him a garment.
Even in the absence of the five jewels and so forth, one should perform it in this very same way;
likewise, even in the absence of the ritual implements such as the thread and the tuft of grass, one should act in this manner.
If the binding of the protective thread (*kautuka*) is performed at an inauspicious time, or if it is recited over a limb that is not appropriate,
that sacrifice is declared to be fruitless; therefore, for the pacification of that defect,
one should then perform a propitiatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*) and subsequently bind the protective thread.
One should recite the Aghora mantra three hundred times when there is a failure of its constituent parts.
Having performed the immediate protection for that [deity] who has been placed within the fire,
the binding of the *kautuka* (sacred thread) is prescribed for the deity remaining in his former station.
Having brought [the deity] to the pavilion or elsewhere, one should recite the Aghora mantra fifty times.
In the absence of offerings, cymbals, and other musical rhythms, one should recite the Dakṣiṇāmūrti mantra.
Or else, having made a handful of flowers, one should offer it to the sandals or the bearers.
Likewise, when there is a fall, or a lapse in the performance, or even the falling of the ritual sandals.
One should perform three hundred recitations of the formidable mantra and one thousand for the *pādukā*;
having caused [the disciple] to offer a circumambulation, one should lead him in the circumambulation of the *pādukā*.
In the event of the loss of three hundred lamps, one should perform twice as many lamp offerings.
If the vehicle is absent during a festival, it brings all manner of faults upon men.
One should perform the ritual bathing (*snapana*), the pacificatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*),
and the departure ceremony (*pratiyāna*) during times of rain, great winds, national unrest, or great fear.
Circumambulating the village is not desired; rather, circumambulation of the temple should be performed.
At that time, O best of the twice-born, the ceremonial bathing and the peace-offering (*śāntihoma*) should be carried out.
O lords of brahmins, while the festival of Śiva is taking place within a single sacred precinct (*ekavāstu*).
If another festival were performed there, it would cause [the village]... to perish.
To eliminate those defects, one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*);
likewise, one should perform an expiation for the mother and the preceptor.
And likewise Aṅgāṅgajavalī; these two are the Nadauṣabhas.
If Vāmabhairava is established, there shall be the destruction of the village.
If the *bali* offering is given through negligence, one should perform a propitiatory *homa*.

When the *bali* sacrifice is performed while residing in an empty village, one should know that the ruin of the kingdom has been brought about; therefore, one should perform the pacification (*śānti*).
Or when the Ālaya is powerful, or during its enclosure of the temple of the gods.
The dwelling of the gods... for him was especially [located] in another's abode;
likewise, O best of the twice-born, his dwelling was in a place that was near yet difficult to reach.
Endowed with various trees and possessed of many kinds of trees,
therefore, that which is praised brings prosperity, while the opposite brings calamity.
The site for the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas is said to be the most excellent.
If there is confusion regarding the offerings, that which is within the site is superior to that which is outside the site.
In one case, it is declared that [the primary rite] is superior when performed in a vehicle (*vāhana*);

however, for those who are incapable, there is a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*), and one should perform it in this way elsewhere. For those engaged in the secondary alternative, one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*).
If the canopy is deficient, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) of the hundredfold terrible mantra (*ghorāṇuśata*).
Even if the banner is missing, it should be the same through the recitation of the hundredfold terrible mantra.
O best of the twice-born, there is no fault at night if the banner is missing.
If the sacrificial materials (*balidravya*) are deficient, however, hunger afflicts human beings.
Therefore, having performed the *mūrtihoma*, one should carry the offering (*bali*) at the end of the procession.
When there is a deficiency in the *bali* offering at a temple, one should recite the *ghora* mantra a hundred times.
In whichever direction the village or other place lacks the *bali*,
one should offer a *saṃhitāhuti* accompanied by a hundred recitations of the mantra of the presiding deity (*dikpati*) of that respective direction.
One should offer the bali-oblation either at the time of setting out with one's companions or at the conclusion of that journey.
If, however, the liṅga is devoid of rice, famine arises on earth; (p.81a, line 1: the falling of tridents and so forth).
Having then performed a propitiatory fire-offering, one should present an offering of rice and a sacrificial oblation.
In the event of its being cut, split, or fallen, one should prescribe an offering (*bali*) for that very [deity].
Having made that *liṅga* very firm, one should worship the Weapon-mantra (*astra*) residing therein.
Having performed the *saṃhitā-homa* in that place, immediately after that—
Starting from that place where the foot bearing its [the deity's] mark stands, one should perform the circumambulation clockwise.
If the food falls, one should prepare fresh food and worship it;
having completed [the rite] as before, one should perform the *saṃhitā-homa*.
But if the vessel for the *bali* offering falls, one should recite the *aghora-mantra* one hundred times.
Having taken another [substance] for the breaking [of the vessel] and so forth, one should deposit the offering material (bali-dravya).
If the ten weapons, having appeared on the ground, fall down,
then one should perform a pacifying fire-oblation (*śāntihoma*) that brings freedom from fever and other afflictions.
If [the images] are made of wood or other materials, having fashioned them by means of cutting, splitting,
and so forth, and having likewise brought them to completion as human forms,
one should perform the specific consecration using their respective mantras.
Having led [the disciple] by reciting the ritual procedure corresponding to the metal type, one should bring him to the final placement at the end.
If the Śūla weapon appears, there will be fear for the king;
in that case, one should perform the directional oblation beginning with the Dhāma-mantra, accompanied by the worship of the weapons.
If cutting or splitting occurs, O twice-born ones, the rite of atonement should be performed as in the subsequent ritual; or else, the festival should be conducted as before using another weapon.
When their own task is completed, it should be concluded like the concluding rites (*sāyānukarma*);
at that time, one should perform a sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*) with the consecration of the King of Weapons (*astrarāja*).
Whether at the time of transport or at another time, when the image (*bera*) or other [objects] have fallen...
The king meets with death; one should immediately perform the remedial rites.
Even when the image has fallen to the ground, O Aṅga, you should maintain the [proper] cooking;
or else, one should proceed with two or three [offerings], and lead them upward in sequence.
The collective [rite], the *śānti-homa*, peace, liberation, and the oblation for that; the ritual bathing (*snapana*) and the thousandfold... at every rhythmic beat (*tāla*), joined in due order.
Or else, the ritual bathing or the recitation (*japa*) with the *ghorā-mantra* ten thousand times.
One should perform the offering of food (naivedya), the general [concluding rites], and the remainder of the festival.
However, if a ritual limb is deficient, one should perform the expiation beginning with the reconnection (sandhāna) as prescribed by the ritual texts;
the rites such as the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) should be performed immediately.
Indeed, where would a teacher look for considerations of the month, lunar mansion, lunar day, weekday, and so forth?
Furthermore, having performed the ritual bathing [of the image] either five hundred or one hundred times—
Furthermore, having tied the sacred thread (*kautuka*), one should arrange the festival and other rites;
even if the head or other parts [of the image] are missing, one should perform the ritual according to the instructions for remedial action (*anukarma*).
In that case as well, the joining together [of the parts] and the festival should indeed be performed with another image (*bera*).

The wise preceptor should perform the daily rite for pacification (*śānti*)... (l.2). O best of the twice-born, it should be performed by one who has entered the interior of the sanctuary, provided he possesses the measurement of the eighth part of the dimensions of the sanctum, the door, and so forth; not otherwise.
Then,
having fashioned the image according to the prescribed description, and having performed its consecration preceded by the rite of sowing seeds (*aṅkurārpaṇa*),
one should conduct a festival for the deity during the festivals of the new [image] and so forth.
The same would apply to the *liṅga*; [the procedure is] like that for consecrated [images of] Maheśī.

But when the image (*bera*) has been brought outside the village during a festival, the twice-born should tie protective cords (*pratisara*). At that time, for the sake of pacifying any faults that may arise for the king, [the following should be done].
Then one should perform a *śāntihoma* or indeed a *saṃhitāhoma*. If, while performing [the rite], the preceptor should fall into water, [he must perform the following].
For that purpose, the mantra-practitioner, assuming many forms, should recite five hundred [times] even while standing in a village; indeed, it is exactly the same even when falling.
When many such rites for the gods have been commenced, (p. 82b, f. 79a, ācāryāmatādi, l.
1) — [regarding] the teacher’s opinion and so forth — through the negligence of the teacher or by means of diseases, death may occur.
If the death of his parents occurs, how indeed should he act in that situation?
Or else, one should have it performed according to the rules by a son, or by one free from delusions;
and here, the Guru, being without a brother, having bound the Sarasvata [vow] upon the disciple—
Having bathed with his clothes on, he should perform that rite according to the prescribed procedure.
If the rite for the two parents has been performed by another, the most excellent preceptor,
having bathed, should remain right there in the hall and partake of food in their presence.
Having performed the sacrifice according to the rules until its conclusion— whether during a festival or even when it is not—
the disciple, having bound the protective thread (*pratisara*), should bathe preceded by the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*).
Having commenced the bull-sacrifice (*vṛṣayāga*) on the right side of the staff,
facing northward and mentally worshipping the bull,
one should recite the *Bṛhattāla* and worship the deities upon the staff.
Having performed the *devayāna* offering there twice, at the end of the day, one should lead [the ritual] either around the village or the temple,
or else perform the circumambulation of the staff (*daṇḍa*) according to the sequence of two times.
At that time, one should perform all the appropriate rites up to the final ablution at a sacred site (tīrtha),
including the bathing and propitiatory ceremonies (śāntika-karma), for the removal of those defects.
Having caused the ritual for the deity to be performed there, one should carry out the procedure;
likewise at birth and at death, with the protective cord firmly bound.
Having consumed the remnants of the oblation (*hutaśeṣa*), the Guru should reside right there.
[If] the king, the chief queen, her father, his brother, or his son,
as well as the chief wife, should die, there is danger for the king.
At that time, while the sacrificer has fallen, one should mutter the *patiteśa* mantra one hundred times.
When the bearer of the image of the Lord of Weapons has fallen,
the Guru should recite the Ghoramantra one hundred times, and for the two Śaṅkara-weapons, double that amount.
The supreme Guru should prescribe that penance which has been previously mentioned for the destruction of the fire, the lamp, the food offering (*naivedya*), and so forth; likewise,
for the omission of even a single twilight worship (*sandhyā*) or other part of the ritual.

In the case of the water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings, of cow-products (*gavya*), of flowers, of the offering of incense and lamps, and when the fire-body has been extinguished or the materials for the *homa* have been lost; or when the fire has gone out, whether it was associated with Śiva or devoid of Śiva—as before. (p. 83b, f.
80a, line 1) (rathahanam)
If a person on earth is unable to mount the chariot,
they should perform a peace-offering (śānti-homa) and then proceed to mount the chariot.
Whether at the time of mounting a chariot or descending from it,
or at the time of bringing a chariot, or if a cow or a Brahmin dies;
The best of the twice-born should perform the *diśāhoma* and the great ablution (*mahāsnāna*) right there for the sake of averting the death or destruction of the king;
likewise [in the case] of the death of a Naga, a Kshatriya, a Vaishya, a Shudra, a woman, or others.
Even in cases such as the amputation of limbs, it would bring blame upon the king.
The best of practitioners should perform the *mūrtihoma*, the *śāntihoma*, and the *śāntika* rite for each respective direction in order to destroy those specific defects.
But if the parasol falls to the ground due to wind or other causes,
it brings about the destruction of the king and is a cause for the destruction of the subjects.
Then, having performed the oblation to the quarters (*diśāhoma*) and the ceremonial bath (*snapana*) of the Supreme Lord (*parameṣṭhin*),
the Guru, having prepared another parasol, should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited.
Having consecrated the parasol according to the rules as before, the Guru should lead it forth.
If the banner falls to the ground, or is cut, burnt, or [damaged] above;
or if it is climbed upon by vultures and the like, or seized by enemy men,
there will be fear for the king from other kings.
To avoid those defects, one should have the Śiva-liṅga bathed;
and when all its limbs have fallen, one should bring about a ritual bathing.
Even when the support of the elements is severed, or when a part of the chariot is cut and falls away,
one should again join another part together with the five products of the cow and water purified with *kuśa* grass.
If at the time of traveling, a breakage or a fall of the chariot or other vehicles should occur,
one should perform the pacification of the fault either at that location or at one's own residence upon returning from the journey.

And having brought [the deity], who is fit for the act of rejoining, along the path of the Rathantara [chant]... (l.4) ...or having placed Maheśvara upon a palanquin or similar vehicle, one should bring him there.

As before, one should install the Lord of the Gods of gods in his own abode. Those chariots, however, [should be handled] by Caṇḍālas and others... likewise. At the end, one should cause the ceremonial bathing to be performed and carry out the rite of pacification (*śāntikarma*).
If [the omen] occurs at the time of seeing an amusement,
one should perform a *śānti*-homa or recite the *aghora* mantra.
If the sight of amusement is absent, one should perform the *saṃhitā*-homa.
In the rite of *nīrājana*, however, there is no expiation (*prāyaścitta*) as before. (p. 84b, f. 81a, nṛttamūrtihīnam, l.
1) (nṛttamūrtihīnam—) ........... there is no expiation (*prāyaścitta*) as before.
At the end of the vehicle, when the ablution is deficient, the peace-offering (śānti-homa) must not be omitted.
In the absence of the presence of the deity, one should perform a substitute fire-offering (*mūrtihoma*),
a ritual of atonement (*pratikriyā*), a ceremonial bath, and a peace-offering (*śāntihoma*) for the sake of achieving continuous success.
Or, [this should be done] in a place presided over by an inferior [deity], or when the vehicle of the deity has been set in motion.
One should perform abundant ablutions during a great propitiatory fire-offering.
If the anointing with oil is omitted, men here will suffer from diseases of the head;
therefore, having performed a propitiatory fire-offering, one should perform the anointing with oil.
If the festival of the dancing form is deficient on the day previously ordained, all the water-offerings shall take place; one should perform the rite of pacification for half of that [period].
Thereafter, one should perform the circumambulation of Naṭeśa at the prescribed time;
if there is an interruption in the giving of the pilgrimage offerings, that pilgrimage will become fruitless.
Having then performed a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma), one should carry out the distribution of gifts as before.
If there is a deficiency in the king’s hunting expedition, victory shall indeed come;
having then performed a propitiatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*), one should lead [the king] on the hunt for eight days.
If the auspicious site (*kautukatīrtha*) is deficient, there will be no presence of the *gambhā* and so forth.
When the rites of the previous *tīrtha* have been performed prior to sunrise at the [new] *tīrtha*,
there shall be expiation through the performance of a pacifying *homa* (*śāntihoma*) and the *saṃhitā-huti* in due order.
This [is the rule] regarding the raising of the banner at Kautukatīrtha when you are present here;
otherwise, one should either perform the auspicious bath elsewhere or avoid it.
During the Cūrṇotsava, if that [bath] or its constituent part is omitted, there will be affliction by disease.
The pacification oblation (śāntihoma) should be performed for the limbs of the Aṅginī, following the oblation of the Saṃhitā.
If the vessel is lost, one should perform a ritual bath at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), or otherwise;
if the sequence of the powder festival (*cūrṇotsava*) is omitted, one should perform the *saṃhitā-homa*.
O twice-born ones, if that great *tīrtha* should disappear, that sacrifice would become fruitless;
therefore, having performed a propitiatory rite (*śānti*) for that purpose, one should then lead the ritual to another *tīrtha*.
Previously, when that [original site] was a river or similar location, it was otherwise.
When that occurs, one should then perform a peace-offering (*śāntihoma*) for the sake of pacifying those defects.
A *saṃhitāhoma* which grants desired results should be performed at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) when there is a loss [of a limb].
When a human is born within a temple, there will be great fear for the king.
Then, having cast away the mud and so forth from that place outside,
one should sprinkle with cow-dung water the area by which they have departed.
One should indeed perform the sprinkling with water on that spot during an auspicious day;
however, if a death or birth has occurred there, one should then have it dug up and smeared with unguents.
Having wiped it clean, one should fill it with pure clay;

having washed the seat, one should not use a *darvī* ladle, but rather apply a coating of cow-dung to the ground. One should then perform the *puṇyāha* rite and the sprinkling with the products of the cow (*tantragavya*) in the proper sequence.
And at the conclusion of the communal feast for the Śaivas, one should perform the sprinkling with water.
If the ceremonial bathing (*snapana*) and the propitiatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*) are to take place in the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*),
one should perform that which is appropriate for the *śāntihoma* in the case of a half-canopy (*ardhamaṇḍapaka*).
If [the rite] is performed in the image-shrine (*pratimāmaṇḍapa*), there shall be a peace-offering (*śāntihoma*) and an ablution (*snapana*).
However, if it is within the inner hall (*antaḥsālāntara*), one should employ a sprinkling with water (*jalasaṃprokṣaṇa*).
For the deities situated in the inner hall, the ablution accompanied by the peace-offering [is prescribed].
One should sprinkle it with cow products for the purification of the pedestal and so forth.
One should discard intoxicants and *bhiṇḍa* fruits, and wash wooden items with water.
Both inside and outside the hall, there is the offering to the quarters (*diśāhuti*) by means of the ritual bathing (*snapana*).
When death or other such events occur at places such as the site of a sacrifice,
one should first bring about purification as previously described and then perform the rite of circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*).
At that time, one should likewise perform the oblation to the directions (*diśāhoma*) or the oblation to the forms (*mūrtihoma*).
One should perform the rite of pacification (*śāntikarma*) outside the enclosure wall;
if those who died within twelve *daṇḍas* of the temple have become immortals, [then it is so].
Having thus abandoned [the site], one should then perform the obligatory, occasional, and optional rites.
If [the rite] is performed [on such a site], there will be the destruction of the village; therefore, one should lead half [of the materials] for the ritual bath (*snapana*).
Even when [a person] has died while on the move, at the dwelling place, animals, birds, and wild beasts [are affected].
Or a serpent is born in the kingdom, and here the condition of men becomes wretched.

One should apply a coating of cow dung there and sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). If the consecration by bathing takes place in the inner sanctum (*garbhageha*), one need not perform the *śānti* fire-oblation.
One should arrange the ritual bathing alone in the half-pavilion (*ardhamaṇṭapa*).
Having sprinkled the deities stationed in the deity-pavilion (*devatāmaṇṭapa*) with the five products of the cow (*gavya*), [one should proceed].
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should perform the *śānti* oblation.
All of this, moreover, is common to both festivals and non-festivals.
If even a drop of blood falls from a cow, a Brāhmaṇa, or a human body within a temple or an assembly hall, one shall lose one's kingdom and death will ensue. At that time,
one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering and feed an incalculable number of Brāhmaṇas.
The turban, the upper garment, the lower robe, or the sacrificial thread.

If the head [of the diagram] is burnt by fire, there will be harm from the preceptor; if it is burnt by deceit, there will be affliction by fever in the village. And for the pacification of that defect:
Having bathed and become pure, the guru should perform the propitiatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*).
O best of sages, it should be exactly thus for the performer and the officiating priests.
This applies whenever there is the occurrence of tearing or other damage to garments, beds, seats, and so forth.
The results here are stated in order for one bitten by a mouse or other such creatures:
in a corner there is an increase in enjoyments; at the edge, it is proclaimed as undesirable;
and in the middle of the noose, there is a son, a wife, and fame.
An undesirable outcome is declared at the end: either disease or death from another cause.
Or, having fashioned a garment with three qualities, [one should offer it] to Brahmā, Indra, Yama, and Agni.
This great fault has been declared; the fault is not described elsewhere.
In this very same way, for men and for one who has been bathed at that time, having recited the Aghora mantra a thousand times, one should cause foul garments to be given.
And for the sake of men who are devotees of Śiva and have been initiated for Śiva.
If [the image] is divine, one should indeed purify it with cow-products after sprinkling it with water for the sake of purification;
then one should cause the Saṃhitā-homa to be performed, or otherwise recite the Aghora mantra.
If uninitiated persons, such as Śūdras and others, have entered the sacrificial pavilion,
one should sprinkle it with the Astra-mantra and mutter the Ghoramantra ten times.
However, if the water-jar or other vessels have been touched by them, one should set down another [vessel] instead.
But when dogs and other such animals enter [the sacrificial ground], one should first perform the *saṃhitā-homa* and then apply cow-dung [as a coating],
followed by the sprinkling with water on an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-prokṣaṇa*) and so forth;
this, accompanied by the sprinkling of products from the cow (*gavya*), should be performed even for those who have fallen into the inverse order (*pratiloma*).
Or, due to birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), death-impurity (*pretaka*), and so forth, one should discard the water-jars and other items contained therein;
having smeared them with cow-dung, one should perform the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*).
At the conclusion of the ritual for the burnt offering of the image (*mūrtihoma*), one should install the water-pot (*kumbha*) and other items as previously described.
In this same manner, the expiation for [the presence of] dogs and so forth is proclaimed.
If a *caṇḍāla* or similar person has entered, having performed this [expiation] at its end, [the rite is completed].
O Śambhu, one should cause the ceremonial bathing (*snapana*) to be performed and the *dīśāhoma* sacrifice to be carried out... (l.
3). If the image and other objects are touched by them, one should perform an expiation as previously described.
If the sacrificial hall is consumed by fire, there will be danger in the royal palace.
Having removed the earthen mound (*parvaka*) and so forth, and having consecrated the bull-bannered Lord [Śiva],
one should perform the *mūrtihoma* at the conclusion, as before, in the sacrificial pavilion.
Having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) immediately,
one should first carry out the rite of elevation (*utthāpana*) within a well-constructed sacrificial pavilion equipped with the installation of the water-jar (*kumbha*).
[One should also perform it] in a pavilion for the great boundary-marking (*mahāmaryādā*), in the assembly hall (*āsthāna-maṇḍapa*), or in the gateway (*gopura*) and so forth.

If [the structure] is burnt, one should perform a propitiatory oblation (*śāntihoma*) and proceed as before. When a water-shed (*prapā*) is burnt by fire, a *saṃhitā-homa* is prescribed; likewise when the inner sanctum (*garbhageha*), the half-pavilion (*ardhamaṇṭapa*), or the image itself is burnt.
In the inner hall, in the intermediate space, and outside the hall, it should proceed in due order;
likewise, there is the rite of bathing, the oblation to the directions, and the oblation to the forms.
One should perform the *śānti*, the *śāntihoma*, and the *saṃhitāhoma*.
However, if the *liṅga*, the *bera*, or other [images] are defiled, one should carry out the prescribed expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
In the temple of the retinue deities, one should construct an image as described for the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*).
In a festival, by means of a non-festival, that commonality is considered equivalent to the ritual act.
Upon entering a village, however, one should perform the *saṃhitā-homa* in the event of a fire;
if a great conflagration occurs in the village, one should perform the *śānti-homa*.
If one does not give back the garment and the upper cloth,
along with the turban of the Lord of Teachers,
even if it be only a finger-ring’s worth of gold— that act is considered to grant the desired result.
Having recited the *Aghoraśata* one hundred times, one should offer the *tanāndarā...* [oblations].
In the confusion of teachers, [the king] destroys the kingdom... [of those who follow] unrighteousness. (l. 5) By a single teacher, [the community] situated in a single temple must be maintained.
The fruit of an action performed by another would then accrue to him; therefore, there would be a confusion of teachers.

[The duties include] fetching water and so forth, the preparation of perfumes, flowers, and incense, the offering of lamps and food, the mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*), and whatever constitutes the daily worship of the deity.

Whatever constitutes complete worship—including the ritual adoration of the retinue and so forth; the characteristic installation of the life-force (*jīvanyāsa*) in the *liṅga*, the image, and other objects;
the daily festival with singing and the like; the arrangement of the constituent parts of the bathing ceremony and other rites;
the preparation of the components of the festival and so on; or the invocation of the deities and the rest.
At that time, the root-ritual worship and the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*)—which require the efforts of many men—how can one person alone perform them? Oh! How amazing!
Those virtuous ones are possessed of great wisdom; I shall explain it to you in brief:
that which is the single abode of both obligatory and optional ritual action.
It has been rightly stated by me that this must be performed by the teacher alone.
The sons, grandsons, and kinsmen of this teacher;
those men initiated by him, those who follow his instructions, and those who seek refuge out of fear;
and the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas born into the lineage of the primordial Śaivas.
...at the time of slaughter... those Gandharvas, dancers, and others, as well as the daughters of Rudra and my maidservants, were then [present] at Jñāpila; what was the state of the body? || 5 ||
The performance of that rite by them would be equivalent to its performance by the preceptor himself;
for just as a sacrificial vow or a royal duty [is valid] even when performed by vassal chiefs and others joined with those possessing knowledge, so too is it accepted here.
If it were otherwise, when that which ought to be done [is neglected], one should perform it right there.
In that case, the fault of confusion (*saṅkara*) is equal, and likewise the expiation (*niṣkṛti*).
Everything regarding ritual action proceeds in this way; thus it is established by the scriptures again and again.
One who performs the Śaiva rites should abandon [the weapons] established by the *astrasiddhas*.
Otherwise, if [the rites] must be performed, it is declared that the destruction of the king will occur.
The meaning of the scripture must be established through the removal of its defects;
first, by means of those very [principles] established in the scripture, it then bestows happiness.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform everything according to the prescribed rule.
And regarding the object of knowledge known as *nāda*, in which year of the current Kali Yuga does it reside?
And it has been written by me once again in two thousand [verses].
Thus ends the procedure for the mind (*cittavidhi*) in the *Kriyākramadyotikā*, composed by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya, whose other name is Parameśvara.
The two breasts of the Liṅga reside at its head; those of the Bindu reside within the heart of the thirty-two-fold image;
those of the Trident reside in its center; those of the Bull reside in its [the Trident’s] glory...; those of the Mountain reside in the middle of its peak;
those of Stone, Water, and Metal reside in the womb of the Peak; and those of Śakti reside in her heart. These breasts always dwell there, endowed with life. Salutations to the venerable Gurus.
(The Bathing Ritual)—
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the bathing ritual for the Supreme Lord:
on the eighth or fourteenth lunar day, or at the equinoxes and solstices.
During an eclipse, on an auspicious month or lunar mansion, at a festival (*parvan*), or even when both [conditions] coincide;
or during a favorable conjunction, on a Sunday, or at the conclusion of a festival, on any given day.
On the day of the creator’s birth, on the day of his [the king’s] own natal asterism, or even daily;
on the asterism of the king’s consecration, during a famine, or when there are ill omens.
O Lord, one should perform [the rite] during an earthquake, a conflagration of the quarters, affliction by fever, māryā, and the like;
at the conclusion of a consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), or when all diseases arise, or during a drought—
whether it be a daily (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), or optional (*kāmya*) rite.
As for the ritual bathing (*snapana*), it follows the established procedure (*nyāya*)... and that may be of many kinds.
At the beginning of the great bathing rite, there should be the offering of sprouts;
this may take place either in the previously mentioned pavilion or even on a sacrificial altar (*vedikā*) devoid of such a structure.
Alternatively, in the previously established [measurement], regardless of those specific dimensions,
it may be from one cubit up to six or seven cubits.
Whether it possesses from four limbs up to eight times eight limbs,
is endowed with all ornaments, or even provided with arches;
In a place endowed with dance, instrumental music, and the like, and accompanied by the sound of singing,
one should purify the ground with the Astra-mantra and smear it with Vāmadeva. One should perform the laying of the lines with Aghora, using [the measurement] of a palm’s length.
The Śivakumbha is two tālas high, and the Vardhanī is one tāla in height.
The measurement of the pericarp is three tālas; all of this is declared to be common.
Alternatively, there may be a northern walkway, situated like a water-pot.
Likewise, the measurement of the pericarp is said to be two *tālas*;
when there are four petals, there is the installation of five jars in the cardinal directions.
In the intermediate directions as well, there shall be that which is called the "nine-fold" (*navākhya*), equal and surrounded by a single *nāda*.
The number twenty-five completely surrounds each of those.
...O twice-born ones, one should arrange a hundred and eight [offerings] consisting of five types,
joined with milk, in an enclosure outside of that...
Having set aside twenty-five jars situated in the center,
one should [arrange] the path on all sides by means of two [jars],
and from the outside, two for each of the eight gates.
One should arrange [the mantras] in nine triangles according to the number of lunar days (tithis) in the middle [circle].
However, in the case of the middle [circle], one should omit the central triad;
for this [total] is one hundred and eight, or one thousand and nine.
There may be forty arrangements, or there may be twenty-five individually;
the interval between the steps is traditionally taught to be one, two, three, or four cubits.

The central array (*madhyavyūha*) and the four surrounding groups of eight should be arranged according to their respective numbers in a symmetrical formation for the purpose of the fire-oblation (*homa*). Having invoked [the deities] into the internal path, this is proclaimed in the scripture as the ritual procedure (*vidhi*).
One should leave a space of exactly sixteen [units] all around the array of Śiva.
The arrangement of the threads may be designated differently;
however, in the one called the "One Hundred and Eight," there are twenty-five in the center.
Outside the path, however, there should be a corner numbering twenty-one;
with the remaining [squares], four doors are formed in the cardinal directions—this is further stated when [the mandala] consists of one thousand [squares].
One should lay down two threads for the front and back parts, extending toward the south and north;

their distance from the edge should be one and a half cubits, or otherwise according to the measurement of the interior. There should be fourteen [threads] in total, including those drawn outside the prescribed area by means of rotation.
Outside of that, the desired fire-oblation (homa) should be performed in the four directions or in the eight directions.
The sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) should be one *puruṣa* in size; this is the supreme measure, consisting of four *prasthas*.
The middling is three *prasthas*, and the inferior is proclaimed to be two *prasthas*.
A measurement of one *karaprasṭha* is called the lowest of the low.
Therefore, this [work] is for the sake of the wise; it is indeed like a mountain for those who seek its purpose.
If it is performed for the sake of supernatural power (*abhicāra*), there will be no doubt that it will be so.
Starting from a double measure by way of progression up to ten times,
the measurement for the *śivakumbha* (Śiva-pitcher) shall be such, while for its half-pitcher (*ardhakara*) it is [one] tenth.
One should know that half of that is a measure of rice, half of that is a measure of sesame;
a measure of parched grain would be half a sesame-measure, and there are eight droṇas in a thousand [of these].
In the assembly of Śiva consisting of thirty-eight [deities], the measurement is proclaimed as one with a surplus of rice (*śālimāna*).
One should place the pitchers with the Heart-mantra and install [them] with gold and other materials.
The twenty-seventh measurement is that which has the station of Śiva and others in its center.
The measurement for the Śivakumbha should be as stated, while for the Kuraka, it is considered to be half of that.

The vessel, measuring one *prastha*, is filled with [substances] numbering four, three, two, and one; it is then wrapped around the jar with two or three threads of sky[-colored] thread in successive order.

Alternatively, one should encircle the triad with the *vyomasūtra* mantra; that which is performed with the *varman* mantra is considered the placement of the *kumbha*, while that with the *hṛdaya* mantra is the placement of the heart.
One should arrange the kuśa grass, intestines, and so forth, up to the limit of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*).
One should indeed place the ritual tufts (*kūrca*) with the *vaiśeṣika* mantra and the substances with the root mantra.
[The gems are] ruby, sapphire, lapis lazuli, and coral.
And pearls should be given along with the five jewels; in their absence, they should be combined with gold.
A quarter less than one [pala], or half a quarter, when there are ten māṣas or eight māṣas;
for those two, half of that, or half of that again, or even a single māṣa, in the case of a poor person.
Therefore, half [of the materials] should be for the agent, and the substances should be placed in jars.
A quarter [is for] the rinsing water, and half [is for] the *pañcagavya* in the four directions.
Fragrant water and a quarter-measure of pure water are prescribed for the first [layer].
Then there should be water with *kuśa* grass, milk, curd, and warm clarified butter;
or alternatively, scented water in the corners, making eight [substances] in sequence.
This is declared as the second installation (*sthāpana*), and the third is now described.
Honey, parched grain, powdered dung, parched grain powder, turmeric, *bhūtīsāra*,
plantain, sesame, mustard, and jackfruit.
Bhasita, tilasāra, kadalī, tila, and sarṣapa;
nālikera, the two types of nāraṅga, and mātuluṅgaka;
likewise, ḍāḍima and makamūdaka, and so forth, are on the outside.
From the jackfruit, the mango, the plantain, the coconut, and the mustard seed.
Then sesame, bilva, and at its end the mātulaṅga fruit; thereafter ...
[the sequence] from that [consists of] barley, nīvāra, and māṣa. (1.2) But *satva* is said to be honey at the beginning.
Afterwards, one should add sugar, milk, mustard seeds, and cloves.
Takkola, curd, and cloud-seed (*megha*), sesame oil, ghee, dung,
roasted barley flour (*saktuka*), coconut, and likewise turmeric powder— thus,
these three types are eternally the triad [of the elements], consisting of twenty-five [principles].
One should abandon the end within the middle, and abandon that which is enclosed within.
When this has been done, there shall be sixteen jars;
in the four directions and the corners, the eightfold set beginning with water for the feet (pādya) is prescribed.
The intermediate space is said to consist of eight units, like honey and the other [seven] treasures;
above that, forty-nine [units] are recited in regular succession:
*gulacandana*, *lohādi*, *kuṣṭhaka*, *kalvallo(llo)la*, and *pucchaka*.
Betel leaf, camphor-water, self-restraint, meat, and the murattṛṇa grass.
Śamī and dūrvā, white arka, bilva, campaka, and śaṅkhinī; then apāmārga, viṣṇukrānti, and that which is known as dhūrta.
The forty-ninth [chapter] is on the white Nandyāvarta design.
Alternatively, that same [subject] is stated again in another manner:

the water for the feet (*pādya*), the water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the respectful offering (*arghya*), as well as the products of the cow (*gavya*), are indeed [to be placed] in the directions starting from the east.
Milk, curd, clarified butter, and honey should indeed be placed in the intermediate directions starting from the southeast.
Takola, ash, *...ryāsa*, hiri-bera, and mañjarī; (l. 2) coconut, bilva, jambu, kaccola, and pāṭalī.
Punnāga, śaṅkhapuṣpa, lakṣmī, and vyāghratara are considered [the first four];
together with dhūrta and dhūstūra, one should prescribe sixteen [plants] according to the treatise.
Dūrvā, sarṣapa, āmra, nāraṅga, and panasa are also recognized.
Kadalī, śatapatra, dhātakī, and śvetalodhraka; the essence of sugarcane, parched grain, camvaka, and fragrant oil;
nīvāraka, kumārilā, mājuka, and murasaktu.
Mātulaṅga, malayaja, gara, and girarātrija—
O best of the twice-born, these are the five Brahmāṇis to be offered in the northeast.
In the outermost [circle] fashioned by Vidyeśāna, [the deities] beginning with Amṛteśvara [are located];
likewise, the eight Gaṇeśvaras beginning with Aṅguṣṭha are situated in the exterior, along with the twenty-five [deities] beginning with Aghora and Vāmadeva.
The [deities] beginning with Krodha are eight in number; may there be a hundred mudrās for them.
By this [method], however, fifty deities are considered to be present in the ablution (*snapana*).
Having made thirty-six steps, one should leave aside four mouthfuls of food.
There should be a count of thirty-two steps; he should place them there, beginning from the south side and ending at the northern limit.
Now, that which was not mentioned here is considered to be similar to the forty-nine [mantras].
I shall now describe the one hundred and eight; that is said to be of three kinds.
[It consists of] sandalwood, agallochum, kuṣṭha, and so forth, as a wave upon the petals of flowers.
Camphor, long pepper, ivory, black gram, and ura-tṛṇa grass.
