In the third enclosure, there are indeed twelve substances located [there]:
the Campaka flower, along with the goddess, the Śatapatrī flower, and Rocanā.
Bilva, barley, śamī, dūrvā grass, and the plant known as megha;
dhātrī, vocaphala, lakṣmī, and the blue water-lily (bhūmyaravindaka); rāsnā, vyapalāśa, white arka, and karavīra.
Dhātakī, Droṇadhu, Dhūrā, Locumā, Mārga, and Arjuna;
and in the Plakṣa and Bilva known as Liṅga, Viṣṇukrānti, Nṛpa, and Ambikā;
and Aśvattha and Nāgapuṣpa—these are declared to be the substances for the fourth [rite].
Tulasī, nagara-jvara, turuṣka, and again ijani; (l.2) vibhīta, jīraka, kṛṣṇajīraka, and reṇuka.
Śrīveṣṭaka, Gandharasapalinī, red sandalwood, Sairīpaka, Vyāghranakha, Sallakī, and Svarṇapuṣpaka.
Dārvī, śakti, *khaṃ*, dārusitāṅga, kuṭa, and naṭa; likewise gulgulu, madvikā, vasiṃ, rogi, and karṇikā.
The banyan-fruit (*vaṭaśṛṅga*), the plant called *kriyāhva*, *phaṇijambū*, realgar (*manaḥśilā*),
*śaṅkhinī*, *bhūtarāja*, wild rice (*nīvāra*), and likewise red ochre (*gairika*); the mango (*āmra*), the one known as *jarasa*, as well as *pāṭalī* and *arjuna*.
For this is explained differently in the fifth enclosure.
The *punnāga*, the *jātipuṣpa*, the *pāṭalī* together with the *devikā*, the *śatapatra*, and *lakṣmī*—these are [the flowers]; then the *bhūpadma* and the *dhātakī*.
Tulasī, Karavīra, Kṛṣṇavallī, and Mallikā—
having gone to the two enemies [of those flowers], he then joined his palms in reverence.
Furthermore, Mahādroṇa, Droṇa, Mahābhadrī, and Bhadrikā.
Indravallī, rudraparṇī, dhātrī, agni, and harītakī;
vyākhranakhyā, māñjiṣṭha, sarala, and bhadrakāṣṭhaka;
navanīta, drāviḍāhva, and sarjantaka, which is designated as kāla.
Varcaḷā and palāśa, bālā and siṃha, priyaṅgu; lodhra, chakra, [sa... pūrvaja, jambu, and kapittha;
aśvattha, gulgulu, lājira, and kṛṣṇajīraka.
Subtle saffron, incense, aloeswood, and black rocanā.
Śrīveṣṭaka, the juice of the *vera* plant, long pepper (*pippalī*), hand-pepper (*hastapippalī*)... (l.3) ...hot aloe-wood (*uṣṇāguru*) and *tarakaṃ*; thereafter, realgar (*manaḥśilā*) is mentioned.
One should place at the end red sandalwood, known as *raktacandana*, cloves (*lavaṅga*), and *rātricūrṇika*, along with a cleansing decoction, while reciting the heart-mantra (*hṛdayāṇu*).
The four milks and kuśa grass should constitute the decoction;
that which is produced from mango, ghee, and the bark of the aśvattha tree is proclaimed as the essence.

The sprinkling (*mārjana*) is prescribed with the tips of *dūrvā* grass, *kuśa* grass, and sesame seeds; it is held to be desirable up to the youngest child. [One should perform] the eighty-one jars... (l.
5) ...as well as water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the respectful offering (*arghya*), using products of the cow (*gavya*) in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
One should place curd, clarified butter, honey, and milk beginning with the northeast (Īśāna) direction.
Sesame, the fivefold auspicious powder (*śrīvakṣapañcāṅga*), sandalwood known as *saṃjñaka*,
*campaka*, *hiribera*, mustard seed, and *nāgakesara*.
Takkola, fruit, kuṣṭha, kaccola, and that which is called iron;
cloves, leaf, and camphor—these sixteen [substances] are on the outside. In the third enclosure, even upon the sacrificial fires, ashes are scattered.
Then, one should place the powder of *rātri* and the powder of *śakra* in sequence;
likewise, *dhātrī*, coconut, *likuca*, and *mātuluṅga*.
These should be arranged on the four outer corners of the fire [mandala], specifically in the seven [positions].
One should duly place Lakṣmī, Sahadevī, and Viṣṇukrānti,
together with Rudraparṇī, as the four [deities] in their proper order.
The measurement of the limbs [of the sacrificial pits] extends up to the Lord of the Kuṇḍas;
one, two, three, or four *prasthas* is the measure for the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth.
For those of middling capacity, it is likewise prescribed that [the offering] be one quarter or even half;
one should likewise determine the measure of clarified butter or oil.
One should offer camphor, saffron, and so forth, as desired.
The Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) are to be worshipped in the center, while the Hundred Rudras are considered to be on the outside.
In this manner, by the method of threefold multiplication, one hundred and eight [units] are obtained.
By means of ninefold arrays (*vyūha*) numbering nine, there are two *kāṣṭhās* situated in the middle.
Eighty-one [deities] are worshipped, joined with eight gates;
now, that which is called the "thousand and eight" is not recited here.
From the excellent tuṭi-karpūra, the nyagrodha and biraja are produced.
Combined with these, it should be placed in inauspicious water that has been consecrated with auspicious mantras.
With that very [water] he should fill the *kumbha*, the *vardhanī*, and the nine jars... (l.
6) ...the water for the feet (*pādya*), the water for sipping (*ācamana*), the water of honor (*arghya*), the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and water with *kuśa* grass.
One should place milk, curd, and ghee in the first enclosure;
then, having placed honey, barley, and jaggery, one should thereafter place sugar-cane and plantain fruit.
...Vipaṃ, known as nālikera, rajanī, and mātuluṅka; lāja, āḍima, satva, āpanasa, bhasma, and that which is born from cūta.
These sixteen substances situated in the center of the twenty-five—
consisting of gems, metals, minerals, seeds, and scented water in sequence—
are to be known as being located in the eastern [quarter], excluding the two corners.
Sprinkling with water around the principal [deity], and sprinkling accompanied by leaves and flowers.
In the south and the west, the other [weapons] should be known as joined with arrows and fruit;
this is to be known as the "five jewels," and in the absence of the first, the second [is used].

That which is called "jewel-water" (*ratnodaka*) has been described; after that is the "army-water" (*vāhodaka*). Gold, silver, copper, [iron], tin, lead, brass, and then bell-metal—these, when combined, are known as "iron-water" (*lohodaka*).
Saurāṣṭra-mañjana, śyāmā, haritāla, and manaḥśilā.
Gairika and yellow orpiment at the end; this is known as the *kṛtakam*.
Śyāmāka, wild rice, priyaṅgu, sesame, and mustard seeds.
The seeds of *śyāmā*, *aṣṭika*, and *dhava* are here declared to be "seed-water" (*bījodaka*).
Fresh butter (*navanīta*) and [the substances beginning with] *kalpa*... combined with *gelā* and *astra*. Sandalwood, *laghukuṣṭha*, *varā*, *uśīra*, and *mustaka*.
Saffron, gold, a water-pot, and jasmine flowers.
When these are ground together... it is known as "scented water" (*gandhodaka*).
[It should be prepared] on a mountain, at the bank of a river, on an anthill, or in a hole made by crabs.
At the horn of a bull, in a sacred field, at the ocean, and at the tusk of an elephant—
clay and water from these eight locations are highly praised.
With cow’s milk... together with the goddess Viṣṇukrāntā and with hands joined in reverence;
Śirīṣa and Abhivara—by these, the cleansing at night is prescribed.
A blade of dūrvā grass, a lotus, the tip of a kuśa blade, and a white mustard seed—
when these are held with joined palms by one who is auspicious, that is called the *pāvamāna*.
Tulasī, a bilva leaf, and tamāla are likewise [to be offered] by the ascetic.
The water from the leaves of Apāmārga and Śamī combined is prescribed here.
The lotus, the red water-lily, thereafter *pā...ṭalī*, *padmaka*, *kaḥ* (the tree),
*punnāga*, *kurava*, *nandyāvarta*, and *mallikā*.
The mixture of white arka and bakula flowers is known as "flower-water" (*puṣpatoya*).
Then, kuṭa, naṭa, loha, sandalwood,
and saffron, combined with camphor and uśīra, are here declared to be "grain-water" (*ānyodaka*).
Then there is Śūla, Kapālabharaṇī, Pinākī, and Paraśu.
A rosary of rudrākṣa beads and golden [beads]—with these, the water for the weapons-offering (*astrārghya*) should be prepared here.
Then there is the breadfruit tree, the coconut, and two citron trees.
In this [rite], there is fruit-water provided with two oranges, plantains, and so forth;
as well as *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *madhūka*, *plakṣa*, and *pāṭalī*.
The decoction water, said to be prepared with *jambhukṛt* [plants], is then combined;
after that, three parts of *abhraka* (mica) and three parts of *mākṣika* (pyrite) are added.
The combination of the three fragrances is known as "middle water.
Uśīra,
sūryakānta, ayaskānta, bhrāmaka, and carukāntaka.

Nikṛnta, joined with five [ingredients], is known as *kāntodaka*. Uśīra, hika, bera, vipari, puṣkara, and that which is spread [therein], along with *śrīgandha*— joined with these five— it is known as *mūlodaka*.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, ghee, and kuśa-water:
when combined with these substances, it is known as the *brahmakūrca*.
Peacock feather, elephant [glandular secretion], birch bark, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), and *bhṛṅgarāja*— these five, joined with *añjali*, constitute the "white-bark water" (*valkodaka*).
It is also combined with the two types of *loddhra*, cloves, and birch bark.
From the southeast corner, one should sequentially place oil, milk, curd, and ghee.
These forty substances for the central jar have been declared.
Furthermore, [the herbs are] Lakṣmī, Bhadrā, Kuśā, Dantī, Nīvāra, and Campaka.
Gokṣura is prescribed; Tvaṣṭṛ is considered to be located within the enclosure of the cave.
Then there are raktotpala, śamī, that which is known as padmasurasa, nandyāvarta, apāmārga, dūrvā, and karavīraka.
Barley, blue lotus, droṇapuṣpa, viṣṇukrāntā, and mallikā; (l.2) jāti, bilva, white arka, and the single-petaled lotus.
These sixteen substances constitute the first [arrangement]; the second is called Praparṇa.
I shall now describe the sequence of the circular arrangement below, with the Śivakumbha in the center.
To its left, the Vardhanī is to be known; one should place the eight [substances] beginning with gems [therein].
A ruby, together with the five precious gems, should be placed in the Śiva-pitcher.
Outside the pericarp, either in the middle of the petals or in the eight directions,
one should place the thousandfold offering of water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth, in sequence, on the outside of that.

One should place water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), water with *kuśa* grass, milk, curd, and clarified butter in the second enclosure (*dvitīyāvaraṇa*).
In the third enclosure (*tṛtīyāvaraṇa*), one should place gold on the sixteen steps.
Those twenty-four [items] are outside the coconut fruit.
It is stated that [the first] thirty-two [vases] contain the essence of sugarcane;
in the fifth, honey; and in the fifty-sixth vase, liquor is stated to be contained thereafter.
In the sixty-fourth [chapter], various flowers are proclaimed;
in the seventy-second, and in the eighth, all seeds are taught.
In the ninth [square], ending at eighty-four, one should place a plantain fruit;
thereafter, in the ninth [square], ending at ninety-six, one places ashes.
In the tenth [chapter] of the *Śatasaṃyukta*, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) are proclaimed;
in the hundred increased by four, the *pañcagavya* is used in the eleventh part.
In the one hundred and eight [vessels] on the outside, water with decoctions is prescribed;
thereafter, in the world of the elements, there are sixteen [vessels],
and in the one hundred and twenty [vessels] on the outside, water with clay is proclaimed.
And one should place all kinds of fragrant substances into all the jars.
In the middle [section], for each of the twenty-five [deities],
there should be either a jar or a pitcher, numbering forty.
One should properly place a vardhanī vessel containing half a suvarṇa, along with a cloth and a brush; or one may likewise deposit the ritual substances individually.
O best of the twice-born, one should know that both [methods] are excellent when the substances are deposited.
If [the number] obtained among the aforementioned groups is divisible by eight, it is proclaimed as "excellent" (*śreṣṭha*).
Half of that is declared "middling" (*madhyama*), and a quarter is called "inferior" (*kanyasa*).
In the middling [case], the deities are the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśāḥ*); elsewhere, however, there is Śiva alone.
And she is praised together with her name as the Goddess;
among fruits, the plantain is [best], and among jasmine leaves, the bilva leaf.

Among flowers, the blue lotus (*nīlotpala*) or the *utpala* is prescribed; sandalwood is [the best] of all fragrances... the clay should be that produced from the roots of *darbha* grass. Bark is said to be that from the *aśvattha* tree, and likewise, the root is the *makuṭa*.
In the absence of sugar, jaggery is prescribed; and that [jaggery] is for both the *makuṭa* and the *kṣāra*.
In the absence of [the aforementioned] substances, one may use the vessel and so forth themselves.
All these materials should be consecrated with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
Having first offered the primary seed [syllable] with earthen bowls and *palas*,
and having given various garments with the heart-mantra (*hṛdayamantra*).
Having avoided the black [flowers], [one should offer] in the autumn...
fragrance with the name-mantra, and likewise flowers and incense...
...one should not worship the *saṃhitā-mantra*, the *liṅga*, or the *mudrā*. Having then enveloped [the deity] with the *kavaca*, one should commence the rite of *homa*.
In the *sahasrakalaśa* [ritual],
I shall perform the [consecration] of this [deity] in a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), both endowed with all the required characteristics.
Having performed the consecration of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and other requirements according to the procedure taught for the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*),
one should offer oblations (*homa*) in sequence with fuel-sticks (*samit*), clarified butter (*ājya*), parched grain (*lāja*), and sesame seeds (*tila*).
The *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *vaṭa* trees are used in order, starting from the east.
Śamī, khadira, māyūra, śrīvṛkṣa, and pāvaka, and so forth.
In the eight-fold rite, however, one should offer fuel-sticks with [the mantras] beginning with *sadyojāta*.
In the procedure for the four oblations, either the principal [officiant] or the worshipper [should perform them].
One hundred, fifty, or half of that is proclaimed as the number for the root-homa;
for the ancillary mantras (aṅga), it is one-tenth of the root-mantra, and likewise for the Brahma-mantras, minus one part.
...having performed the worship of the door, let them enter for the *homa*;
having entered the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*), they should purify the *liṅga* as before.

Having conceived the image upon the seat, one should invoke the form and worship it. With the Brahma-mantras... [one should worship] according to the *prakṛti*. Then one should project the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*).
One should offer the rites beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*), as well as fragrance, flowers, and incense.
And having offered a lamp accompanied by musical instruments with the root mantra.
Accompanied by dance and song, joined with the sound of conchs,
the gods then offered that hymn of praise, endowed with the resonance of bells.
Having lifted the auspicious *kumbha* and the *vardhanī*, accompanied by the sound of "Victory!",
one should place the fire-vessel upon the three [pots] at the front.
Having gone there, one should perform the three rites beginning with the *pādya* for the Goddess in that very vessel.
Having removed the perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps,

and the water-offering (*arghya*) according to the ritual procedure, the preceptor, while recollecting the *Śiva-mantra*, [should take up] a bundle of *kuśa* grass (*kūrca*) provided with flowers and water in his hand.
Having gathered [the offerings] and worshipped the reality, one should place it upon the top of the *liṅga*;
one should also place the Lord of Gods to the left of that deity.
Recalling the Śiva-mantra, one should bathe Śiva with the water from the pitcher;
recollecting the Goddess in the form of the pedestal, one should bathe her as well.
...Having generated [the deity], one should offer water for the feet at the feet and at the faces;
one should present these with the five [mantras] beginning with Īśāna and ending with Sadyojāta.
One should cause the arghya offering to Śiva to be presented with the Śiva-mantras ending with the *cūḍā* [mantra],
accompanied by the great sound of a bell at the beginning of the consecration with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and other rites.

One should also offer incense associated with the ritual attendances (*upasthāna*). At the conclusion, one should remain veiled from view; there should be a ritual bath accompanied by incense, as well as various fruits, products of the cow (*gavya*), and offerings brought from afar.
Knowing [the mantras], one should bathe the Supreme Lord with those [mantras] ending in *nṛceta*.

Having carefully cleansed the small liṅga with fragrant water and having worshipped it thoroughly according to the prescribed rite of worship, one should complete the remaining portion, the fire-oblation (homa).
If, however, the complete ablution is to be performed, it should be done as prescribed for the installation of the *sakala* [deity].

Having prepared a seat, one should deposit the jar-form (*kumbhamūrti*) upon it. Having deposited the body of knowledge (*vidyātanu*) there, and having meditated upon the form [of the deity], one should deposit Śiva.

Having performed the rites of *sthāpanā* and so forth, and having offered water for the feet (*pādya*) and the rest, the Guru, having presented perfume, flowers, incense, a lamp, and the *arghya* offering with the heart-mantra,
should display the *liṅga-mudrā* and protect [the deity] with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*).
Having performed the fire-oblation with the *vardhanī* vessel and having displayed the *yonimudrā*,

one should then invoke and worship, in due order according to the previously mentioned rule, the Rudras beginning with Kuṇṭhī who abide as the surrounding retinue (*āvaraṇa*) by means of the *dharma-mantra*.
Having gone to the vicinity of the All-pervading One, [he offered] a seat and even his own formless self.
Having performed the mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*) and the ritual integration of the limbs (*sakalīkaraṇa*), one should deposit the mantra of the Vidyā-body;
having performed the rites beginning with the ablution (*snāna*) and ending with it, and having offered the triad beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*).
One should offer fragrant flowers, incense, and a lamp.
Having brought the jar and the water-pot as before, one should place the subtle body within the heart.
One should then install the mantra of each respective deity into the heart of the Goddess.
Having bathed [the deity], one should offer the water for the feet and so forth in sequence, divided into two or three portions.
Having offered the avaśuṣṭa to the God, one should present it to the Goddess;
or, having set it aside separately, one should consecrate the Mistress of the Gods.
And one should consecrate the base of the deity with cow-products and other substances;
or, in the case of a reflection in a mirror and so forth, one should perform the bath as prescribed for the ritual bathing (*snapana*).
For the goddess, one should place the central jar or the water-vessel in the middle.
In this [system], no distinction of deities is accepted among the substances (*dravya*) by way of differentiation.
However, in the arrangement of the five [deities] beginning with Śāntā, there are those beginning with Vāmā in the ninefold conceptualization.
Those beginning with Dhārikā are situated on the three sides in the directions starting from the Great One (Mahādi).
In the twenty-five-jointed [system], the elements beginning with food (annādya) are manifest;
therein, the deities from Earth up to Pradhāna are indeed pervasive.
The deities of the upper [levels] have been declared; they are said to end in feminine gender-terminations.
In that very context, O best of the twice-born, I shall describe the ritual bathing with milk and other substances:
[with] curd, ghee, honey, and also with the nectar of the five products of the cow.
With the essence of sugarcane fruits, all kinds of seeds, parched grain, and roasted flour;
With powders of turmeric, with flowers— especially those of the coconut—
and with the waters contained within those fruits, but not with water kept in jars or similar vessels.
With waters from the Gaṅgā and other sources, purified and endowed with fragrant substances such as medicinal herbs, and with scented oil, according to the very path previously described.
One should bathe the Supreme Lord for the removal of all defects,
for the attainment of all desired goals, and for the sake of victory for kings;
specifically, for the attainment of health and for the sake of long life.
For the sake of accomplishing all prosperity, for the benefit of children, and for the cause of splendor.
For the destruction of famine and ruin in the kingdom, and for the turning back of those evils—
especially when there is an ill omen such as the occurrence of an oblation during a national upheaval.
For the purpose of subjugating all the worlds, for the successful acquisition of elephants, horses, and so forth, for the destruction of their diseases, for the cause of the non-arising of cattle,
and for the sake of strength when one's own army is engaged in battle— or even if death should occur— [one should practice].
For the purpose of terrifying the enemy army, for its destruction, and for causing confusion therein.
And for the sake of destroying the diseases of men and others,
on the day of one's birth-star, or during the king’s consecration, or even at any other [auspicious] time.
Furthermore, that [rite] should indeed be performed on the eighth lunar mansion or asterism, or when there is a favorable conjunction;
specifically on the eighth, the fourteenth, or the fifteenth day. It should be carried out during rites of expiation or in the performance of the offering of nine-fold food (navanaivedya).
And at the time of a person's death, which is a wound for men, there occurs the auspicious birth of a new life.
And at the time of special worship, as well as during festivals for the devotees,
(l.5) at the time of the circumambulation of the deity, and especially during the hunt.

O best of gurus, one should perform this daily, or at the three junctions of the day, or at two junctions, or even at a single one; one should cause the ritual bathing (*snapana*) to be performed for Śiva. A certain specific detail regarding that [procedure] is now stated according to the previously mentioned path.
Whether with a single *kumbha* or a *kalaśa* joined with the *vyoma*,
he shall before long become the sovereign of all;
for him, there shall be longevity, health, and whatever is intended by his mind.
All authority shall belong to him, and devotion to Śiva arises within him.
He who, upon seeing perverse actions, maintains neutrality—such a wise king attains prosperity; there is no doubt to be made here regarding this.
Therefore, by that preeminent teacher who dwells within the five spheres of sensory experience...

One who has mastered the full knowledge of the Śaiva Āgamas and is engaged in ritual action should carry out these rites for the prosperity of his own kingdom. One who is highly proficient in the scriptures of Śiva should be accepted as a Guru even greater than a Guru.
O best of sages, he should have that very same [image] used for the purpose of the ritual bathing.

For the sake of increasing that very [merit] and for the attainment of desired success, one should perform special bathing and worship of the divine Lord with milk, curd, ghee, honey, and other such offerings.
Having bathed the Lord with a paste of *āmalaka* and other substances, and having dried the altar,
one should bathe him with scented water and wipe him with a cloth.
Having anointed Śiva with sandalwood paste and other unguents, one should adorn him with silk cloths and other ornaments;
immediately thereafter, one should fumigate him with incense, flowers, meat, and so forth.
One should present the *ārātrika* lamp, joined with a camphor wick;
or [offer] oblation of five colors, or milk-rice, or pure [food].
Having offered [the food] accompanied by various side-dishes and provided with various fruits,
he should then give betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*) together with mouth-perfumes—
namely, cardamom, cloves, camphor, nutmeg, and *takola* powder.
This mouth-freshener (mukhavāsa) should be mixed with a moderate amount of sugar-candy.
Having prostrated and made a formal request, and having received permission, he should resort to the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) for the purpose of the fire-oblation (*homa*),
provided with fuel-sticks (*samit*), clarified butter (*ājya*), sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and sesame seeds (*tila*).
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations, he should perform the final full oblation at the end;
then, taking the ashes from that, he should cause them to be given to the patron.
Having prayed for the desired goal, one should prostrate again and again;
beginning on a single day, one should practice until the end of seven days.
Whether it be twofold, threefold, or four or fivefold,
or reckoned as sixfold or sevenfold, or even until the success of the rite is achieved—
this worship, known as the Śeṣikā, bestows the fruits previously described.
And the occasional rite (naimittika) should be performed at the end of the regular rite (nitya), provided there is no contradiction.

But when an occasional rite (*naimittika*) occurs while the obligatory rite (*nitya*) is already in progress, one should complete the obligatory and occasional rites within a short time and then perform the [subsequent] obligatory rite. If the time for the latter part of the twilight (*sandhyā*) falls during the former part [of the day], [one should act accordingly].
If this is indeed for a specific occasion (*naimittika*), having commenced it at its own proper time,
one should complete the first enclosure (*āvaraṇa*) and the remainder of the twilight rite (*sandhyā*).

And one should offer oblations and bathe [the deity] with all the ritual jars according to the prescribed method, when the two occasional occasions have arrived—namely, on the king’s birth star, during preparations for war, upon victory, at initiation, and at consecration. (Siddhāntaśekhara, Snapanavidhi, p. 101b, f. 101a, l. 1)
It is seen during drought, in fever, and in the possession by spirits.
In the case of a rite for expiation (*prāyaścitta*), likewise in the event of a portent, regarding [offerings such as] ghee and woolen blankets,
in all rites for pacification (*śāntikarman*), in auspicious ceremonies, and in the accomplishment of mantras (*mantrasādhana*).
At such times as these, a wise man should perform the ceremonial bathing;
likewise, he should construct a pavilion in front of the temple in nine sections.
That [stūpa] is considered to be five, six, or seven cubits in width for the three smallest sizes;
and for the three middle sizes, it is eight, nine, or ten cubits wide.
And for the three superior [mandalas], the number of cubits is twenty-one,
sixteen, thirty-six, and sixty-four, respectively, corresponding to the pillars.
The *tāla* measures should be increased by one; [the pillars] should be ten or eleven *bhāgas* in height.
The pillars situated within the ritual space (*vidhi*) are to be excluded from the central pillar.
Thus has the pavilion been described; one should construct it adorned with gates and arches.
Endowed with the eight auspicious symbols and adorned with auspicious sprouts.
Equipped with a canopy and a banner, adorned with a garland of *darbha* grass,
it should be one *tāla* in height and width, and decorated with fruits and sprouts.
Once that place has been smeared with cow dung, the Guru should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made.
Auspicious jars fashioned from gold, copper, or other materials—
jars endowed with the proper characteristics as described in the *Kāraṇa* [Tantra]— should be taken.
Those that are decayed, broken, or ancient and so forth should be avoided with great effort.
The vessels beginning with the *uttama* are filled with measures (*prastha*) increased by four, three, and two [vedas and agnis] respectively;
the *vardhanī* is filled with double that amount, and the *śivakumbha* with four times that.
The wise one should wrap all the *kalaśas* with a single thread;
the *vardhanī*, however, with [more], and the *śivakumbha* with three threads.
It should be five, six, or seven cubits in height and one-fifth of that in width.
A new, white cloth was placed over the covering of the jar.
One should perform the stabilization (*sthiti*) with darbha grass as prescribed by the sages; it may be of the highest, middling, or other grades.
The highest [grade] is that which resides in the *śivakumbha*, while the middling is that which is contained in the *vardhanī*.
In the lowest [vessel], a bundle of grass (*kūrca*) in the jar called Śiva; five jewels and half-measure of grain and rice in the middle [vessel].
Having prepared nine compartments as before, one should arrange the jars.
One should worship Śiva and the eight Vidyeśvaras, and one should bathe them with those [substances].
The inferior and the middling have been explained; next, I shall describe the low and the excellent.
One should lay down eight threads with their tips pointing eastward and northward.
In the center of the nine squares, the wise one should place the pitcher known as Śiva.
Around that, he should perform the rite enclosed by a single square.
He should make eight doors and, at the end of the procedure, place the Vardhanī vessel.
And one should place eight pitchers in order in the first enclosure.
Water for the feet, water for sipping, the *arghya* offering, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and *kuśa* grass water;
[these are placed] from the east to the north, while fragrant water is in the corner square.
In the second enclosure, there is honey, the five spices (*koṣṭha-pañca*),
sugar-candy (*gulī*), milk, mustard, cloves, black pepper (*takkola*), and *dadhimeghaka*.
One should place sesame seeds, *anuśīra*, clarified butter, *śakracūrṇa*, roasted flour (*saktuka*),
coconut, and turmeric in sequence, starting from the east.
One should worship Sadāśiva in the center, but not Nonmanī in the *vardhanī* vessel.
The eight powers beginning with Vāmā are considered to be in the first enclosure.
Śakra and the other eight [lords] are in the cardinal directions, while the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśas*) are situated in the intermediate directions.
Having thus worshipped the jars, one should then perform the fire-oblation (*homa*).
Then, having gone to the inner sanctum and performed the purification of the *liṅga*,
the wise practitioner should invoke the deity into the *liṅga* and perform the tenfold consecration (*saṃskāra*).
Then, taking [the materials] with divine clarified butter (*devājya*), he should perform the ritual bathing (*snāpana*).
Having lifted up the Śiva-pitcher and having entered the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), |||
The Guru should place those two jars upon the sacrificial mound in the presence of the deity;
with auspicious sounds, he should bathe the Liṅga with the root mantra.
One should slowly sprinkle the vardhanī with water from the Śiva-pitcher, using a measure equal to the tip of a cow's horn and reciting the Piṇḍikā-Śakti mantra.
[Then one should sprinkle] the liṅga from the pitcher of the first enclosure, starting from Indra and proceeding in order.
In the second enclosure, likewise, one should perform the consecration with the limbs of Brahmā.
One should sprinkle the liṅga with a stream of nectar and with fragrant water;
one should worship the liṅga and the deity ending with Caṇḍa as prescribed in the Nitya [Tantra].
The performer should worship the Guru and present him with a pavilion and other offerings.
That which is to be contemplated as the twenty-five-fold [deity] has been described by me as the *snapana* (ablution).
By the wise Viśvanātha, who has performed the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice,
I shall now describe the ritual bathing with forty-nine jars:
one should place the jars and the *vardhanī* vessel on the path in the nine directions beginning with the east, filled with fragrant water.
In the center of the ninefold grid, one should place water for the feet (*pādya*) and water for sipping (*ācamana*) in the cardinal directions;
and in the corners, one should place the *arghya*, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), milk, curd, ghee, and honey,
just as in the second enclosure.
Kusha-grass water, parched grain, and the powder of chariot-wheel rims mixed with roasted barley flour.
Turmeric, ash, chickpea flour, ... banana fruit, sesame seeds, white mustard, jackfruit, and likewise coconut fruit.
Nārābhā, *takra*, mātulaṅga, and ḍāḍima—one should place these sixteen [items]; this is called the third substance. Sandalwood, iron, and that which is designated as carmadoṣa;
Kaccola, kuṅkuma, patra, kapraka, and hariberaka.
Dānta, mauja, mura, kṛṣṇa, campaka, along with devikā,
rocanā, śatapatrī, bilva leaves, and śamī leaves.
Barley, white *tūrvā*, *takkoḷa* together with *ṣaḍgrasa*,
*tṛṇalā*, and the clove-creeper (*lavaṅgavallī*)— these are the twenty-four [substances] mentioned for the third enclosure; now the substances for the fourth are being stated.
The *jāti*, the *rāsnā*, the lotus from the marshy ground, and the flower born of the *palāśa* tree;
the *tārka*, the *karavīra*, the *dhātakī*, and the *droṇapuṣpaka*; as well as the *dhurdhūra*, that which is called white *lodhra*, the *apāmārga*, and likewise the *arjuna*.
Plakṣa, iha-pippalī, viṣṇukrāntā, and vanapippalī; keśara, [nāgakeśara], and the flower of tulasī, as well as tagara;
kuṣṭha, tejinī, vilaṅga, and likewise jīraka.
Kṛṣṇajīra, areṇa, śrīveṣṭa, and gandhasāraka are synonyms.
Likewise, *phalanī*, red sandalwood (*raktacandana*), and *sairyaka*—
these thirty-two substances should be placed in the fourth enclosure.
I shall describe the presiding deities of the jars; in the one called Śiva, the Praṇava is traditionally taught.
Manonmanī resides in the Vardhanī, while the path of the feet is in the jars.
These are to be worshipped in sequence starting from the east, as declared in the first enclosure.
All of them should be meditated upon as facing Śiva, with water-pots in their hands.
One should perform the remainder as previously described and bathe Śiva with the water-pots (kalaśas).
Thus is proclaimed the consecration known as the eighty-one-pitcher bath (ekāśītikumbha-snāpana).
I shall describe the supreme bathing ritual of one hundred and eight jars.
One should perform everything as previously stated; only the specific details therein are now being told.
There are fourteen threads [drawn] with their tips pointing eastward and northward.

One should place [the substances] there in the center within twenty-five squares... (p.104b, f.114a, l.1) ...water joined with three *bhalas* is for the *bhodhakāraga* (or *bhodhakāraka*); decoction-water is not for the *kāraga* (or *kāraka*). These are declared to be the substances for the five jars of the array in the direction of the Moon (*somadigvyūha*).
One should place milk in the central jar, or in the one belonging to Agni;
likewise, one should place a product of curd in the corner of the Rākṣasas.
One should place [the substance] for the letter Ā in the jar located in the northwest corner;
[the substance] for the letter Bha should be placed in the jar situated in the middle of the array of directions.
Situated in the midst of the array of consonants (*vyañjanavyūha*), [the deities] are gathered by means of the substances of the jars (*kumbhadravya*).
Furthermore, the substances for the arrays (*vyūha*) are in the first enclosure.
One should place eight [deities] in the eight jars; they are enumerated in sequence as follows:
Phelana, devadāru, māṃsī, tālīsapatra...
[and] rīṣabhidhāna, rosnā, and also nāgakeśara—
one should place these eight substances in the first enclosure, starting from the east.
Furthermore, the *padmaja*, the *punnāga*, the *mallikā*, the *raktā*,
the white *arka*, the *vakula*, and that which is known as *caturaṅgula*.
One should place the substances— namely *madhavīka*, *rava*, as well as *ketakī*,
*pāṭalī*, *nandyāvarta*, and the flower called *bandhūka*—
in the sixteen [directions] starting from the eastern direction.
In all the ritual jars of the array, the substances are thus described.
The gods [worship] Śiva and the others... [they are] fully established.
Having worshipped Śiva in the Śiva-vessel and Manonmanī in the Vardhanī-vessel.
With the consecrations beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the ritual services (*upacāra*) as before,
one should display the *liṅgamudrā*, the *namomudrā*, and the [other] mudrās. Then,
one should install the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśas*) in the eight jars starting from the east.
Then, among the sixteen jars situated in the midst of the arrangement of vowels, [one should place them].
[He worshipped] the gods— Śambhu, Rudra, Mahādeva, Hara, Śiva,
Īśāna, Girīśa, Sarva, Sarvajña, and the Lord of the Immortals.
"Kapardin, Karālākṣa, Kālanāśana...
(l.5) and Triṇetra—these are the sixteen [names] ending with the visarga among the consonants beginning with 'ca'."
The Guru should worship all [the deities] at the water-mouth with perfumes, flowers, and so forth,
just as in the first enclosure (*prathamāvaraṇa*) among the arrays (*vyūha*).
[He should worship] the God of gods, the greatly radiant, the most excellent Supreme Lord (*parameṣṭhin*).
It is of the nature of truth, infinite, and the abode of supreme bliss.
In the first enclosure, one should place [the deities] upon eight jars:
in the second [enclosure], Kāmada, Kālaka, Phala, the supreme [deity], Kandarpāri, Mārādhyā, Khaḍga, and the all-pervading Lord Ghaṇṭādhara.
The wisdom of the Lord of the Gods... the knowledge that is the abode of knowledge; Śrīkaṇṭha, who is to be known through the mind, the source of the Vedas—this is the sixteenth [chapter].
One should worship these deities in the sixteen jars situated within the flood of the array of vowels (*svaravyūha*), beginning with the letter *a* and following the sequence.
The deities of the array (*vyūhadeva*) are proclaimed to be situated in the midst of the enclosure of vowels (*svarāvaraṇa*).
We do not praise the gods born of union who dwell in the midst of the array of syllables.
...and indeed by means of the sequence beginning with *avagama*, [one performs] twenty *kumbhaka*s.
[The deities are] Varada, Vṛṣavāha, Vajrāṅga, and Mahādhanu.
Śūlin, Bhīma, Varga, Havyagra, and likewise Īśvara;
Puranāśa, Pura..., Lokasākṣin, and Matsyaga;
Gaṅgādharan and Indracūḍa, as well as Sarvaga and Sarvada.
He is association, the benefactor Śaṅkara, the peaceful one, the giver of peace, the eternal, and the pure.
Regarding the knowledge of the *bhasma*: "The twenty-four deities [are located] within the jars in the midst of the *vyūha*s, from the letter *ka* to the letter *ha*. (l. 6)
Having worshipped them in the prescribed order with perfumes and other offerings, situated within the enclosure of the consonants, [one should worship] the first... of those arrays in the eight jars:
Ananta, Matirakta, Virakta, and Vedalocana.
The pure essence of the Vedānta, the vessel of the universe.
One should worship Viśvāsa first, and then [the other] eight; furthermore, among those arrays, one should worship them in the second enclosure starting from the southeast.
I shall now describe, in sequence, the presiding deities of the sixteen jars:
Sthāṇu, [saha]..., Huṃ, and Dhūrjaṭi, who has the radiance of fire;
the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara), whose matted locks shine with the yellowish-red luster of lightning, is raised up.
He is Bharga, the Terrifying One, with a fearsome face, the Lord of All, adorned with the moon.
"Kṛtatī... *rādhyaṃ sarvagaṃ ca"—thus is the sixteenth [deity].
One should worship [these] in the sixteen external jars within the enclosure of the consonants (*vyañjanāvaraṇa*).
Thus, the deities have been proclaimed for all the arrays;
then, having covered the jars with cloths, one should worship the gods.
One should thus offer the five types of worship— perfume, flowers, incense, lamp, and excellent food offering— to the deity and others in their proper sequence.
The preceptor should perform the *homa* on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with the image-bearers,
using sacrificial fuel sticks (*samidh*) and sacrificial porridge (*caru*).
Having taken hold [of the vessel], he should cause it to be carried around the path by a single step.
In the fifteen-fold [mandala], there are eight doors at the three directions.
One should eliminate three by three cells outside the prescribed boundary;
in the cardinal directions there are twelve [cells], and in the intermediate directions nine cells.
Therein, O Śivā, there would be one hundred and eight additional squares.
One should place the Śiva-kumbha in the center and the Vardhanī on the north (in the path).
One should place the jars upon them according to the sequence beginning with the east; this is called the installation of the jars. Now, the substances for the jars are described.

One should place the water for the feet (*pādya*), the water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), water with *kuśa* grass, milk, curd, and ghee— these eight— in the first enclosure (*prathamāvaraṇa*).
[Then] honey, parched grain, cow dung powder, turmeric, ashes, and sugarcane.
The fruit of the rambhā plant, sesame seeds, mustard seeds, and likewise the panasa fruit.
A coconut and an orange [are placed] in the second; a citron... (l.
5); and a lime and a pomegranate—one should place these as the sixteenth in the second.
Sandalwood, *laghukoṣṭha*, a water-pot (*kaccola*), a flower-leaf, camphor, *hiribera*, ivory, a girdle of muñja grass, and *ura* grass—
these twelve [items] one should place in the third enclosure.
Cavya, sahadevī, śatapatrī, and rocanā.
Bilva, śamī, barley, dūrvā grass, and that which is known as takkola; ...
cocaphala, jāti, lakṣmī, and the land-lotus.
Rāsnā, cavya, palāśa, śvetārka, karavīraka, dhātakī, as well as droṇa, dhūrdhūra, and that which is known as lodhra.
Apāmārga, cloth, ... for the purpose, and indeed Plākṣa, Hastipippalī, Viṣṇukrānti, as well as Aśvattha, Patraka, and Nāgakesara.
One should place the thirty-two substances enumerated in the fourth enclosure;
likewise, *tulasī*, *tagara*, and *turuṣka*. Also, *vilaṅga*, *jīraka*, *kāpi*, and *reṇuka*.
Śrīveṣṭa, fragrant resin, heartwood, and red sandalwood from the fruit.
Saireyaka, vyāghranakha, sallakī, catuṅgula, dārvī, śuktinakha, dāru, sitā,
and fresh kuṭa; guggulu, mṛdvikā, uśīra, and girikarṇikā.
Banyan bark, indravallī, parṇa, jambū, and manaśśilā;
Śaṅkhinī, Bhṛṅgarāja, nīvāra, and likewise gairika;
also āmra, the juice of mauñjī, as well as pāṭalī and arjuna.
With *vācā* and *jātivacā*, there are forty-four in the fifth [chapter].
Thus, what is designated as "substance" is proclaimed as the deities of the jar (*kumbhadevatā*).
Kapālīśa, Abhyaja, Buddha, Vajradevapramardana,
Vibhūti, Avyaya, Śānta— these are the first eight.
One should offer the required substances along with gifts such as clothing and other fees.
One hundred and eight ablutions have been proclaimed, which grant all desires.
For the wise, when the Viśvanātha sacrifice has been performed with the Agniṣṭoma, [one should perform] the rite called Kumbha on the second day of the fortnight, consisting of sixteen [units].
One should perform everything as before; however, the specific details are stated as follows.
One facing east and north should lay down twenty threads.
One should then fashion the central array consisting of twenty-five squares. Outside of that, on all sides, there should be a path consisting of two squares.
And there are eight gates at the front of the pathways... indeed, [there are] eight [deities] in the eight directions;
in the central array consisting of twenty-five squares, divided into nine parts.
One should place the Śiva-pitcher in the center and the Vardhanī pitcher to its north;
there, in the first enclosure, one should arrange sixteen pitchers.
One should place the jars in a counter-array numbering twenty-five.
Thus the materials for the jars are specified as one hundred and sixteen;
the *vardhanī* and the *śivakumbha* are considered to extend from the second onwards.
The installation of the jar has been described; now the materials for the jar are stated:
water for the feet, honey, water with *kuśa* grass, oil, and then water for sipping;
furthermore, sugarcane juice, milk, that which is called sugar-candy, the *arghya* offering, breadfruit, and curd.
One should place the sixteen substances— plantain, the five products of the cow, mango, horse-gram, citron, barley,
mustard, parched grain, palm-leaves, and turmeric— in the first enclosure.
Cow dung powder, ashes, sandalwood, and a light digestive tract.
Then tuṭikarpūraka, likewise the triad of fruits,
dāṣakarvā, as well as drākṣā and that which is known as nāgakeśara.
Babara, guggulu, annajuṣṭha, lodhra, añjana, gorocanā, turuṣka, kuṅkuma,
visarga, gairika, rāsnā, takkola, and manaḥśilā.
Viṣṇukrāntā, Sahā, and Lakṣmī constitute the collection of thirty-two substances.
Having placed [the items] in the second enclosure, the substances for the third are now described:
balvaja grass, darbha grass, śamī leaves, and likewise two types of apāmārga.

The white lotus (*śvetapadma*), the night-lily (*kumuda*), the *dhūrdhūra*, the *vellikā*, the oleander (*karavīra*), the *punnāga*, [and] *pa...* (the rest of the line is missing due to a broken folio). The outer layer (*bāhyatala*), which serves as the secondary layer (*upatala*) situated beneath the lotus, extends from Vidyā upwards to Śiva. ... [It is] pervaded by Vidyā; the principle of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyātattva*)... having reached the root-corner, it remains fixed in the water above, extending up to Śiva, reaching as far as the Śiva-principle (*śivatattva*). The lotus...

Above that... (l. 3) ...as prescribed, the throne of the Lord of Rūppattāyi—the Brahmā-Viṣṇu-Rudra-pīṭha—is the seat of Śiva. [It is] endowed with the portion that transcends all paths (sarvādhvādhikabhāgasaṃyuta), the knowledge of Śiva... (l. 4) ...having the nature of the Liṅga, it exists as that which surpasses all paths, even the six paths (ṣaḍadhvā). It is joined with the portions of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra... (l. 5) ...together.

The *yirukkuṟ* (the two existing ones), known as Śivajñāna, are said to be of the nature of the will (*icchā*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) of Paraśiva. Having assumed the form of the *liṅga*—that is, the essence of the *liṅga*—it exists with a stalk (*nāla*) consisting of more than half a part (*ardhādhikabhāga*), together with the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*). Being superior to these, it consists of three parts (*tribhāga*) along with the stalk; it is joined with the *gomukha* [and other features]. The pedestal (*pīṭha*) exists as the *yirukkuṟ*, not as the nature of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), for it has transcended the nature of the power of action.

[the] powers. Consisting of power (*śaktyātmaka*). By the offering of the *mātrā* according to the sequence of the radiant Lord of the Kalās.

Uttering the mantra, the Guru, having formed a firm *añjali* [mudrā], having reached the Supreme Śiva (*paraśiva*)... having contemplated [this], then, while causing the *puṣpāñjali* to descend, [ringing] the bell up to the forehead; then, with his mind fixed upon the Great Target (*mahālakṣya*) within the flower... thus, with his mind gone to his own *mūlādhāra*, he remains with his consciousness dissolved.

By whomsoever, Śiva, the Supreme Self, those who are devoted to Śiva were created through the rite of initiation involving installation, sprinkling, and other causes.
He shall gradually proceed from the mouth of Śaiva-Brahmā to the world of mortals;
he is celebrated under the name Kāśyapa and in the forms of sages. Because he possesses the nature of Śiva from the beginning, he is called Ādiśaiva (the Primordial Śaiva).
Those who have been initiated by Śiva are remembered as Śiva-brāhmaṇas.
The supreme teachers of all, the best of Brahmins, the highest of Śivas, and indeed the most excellent among the best of the twice-born— these divisions of Śiva are identical with Śiva himself.
These synonyms have been told to you in brief:
from worms, insects, and moths come animals;
among animals, humans are superior; and among them, the twice-born are the most excellent.

Among the twice-born, the Brahmins are superior; among the Brahmins, those whose intellects are fixed on ritual action; among those whose intellects are fixed on ritual action, the performers of such rites; and superior even to them are those who have renounced all action.
Among those [stages], renunciation (*sannyāsa*) is more eminent and superior; therein is the one worshipped by Śaṅkara.
(Caryāpāda: Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sequence of the ritual procedure for the Caryāpāda. (p. 110a, l. 1)
But first, hear the origin of the Śaivas from this previous quarter.
The Śaiva, Pāśupata, Soma, and Lākula traditions are fourfold;
they are traditionally remembered as being of this nature due to the distinctions between their scriptures.
One who has been initiated according to the sequence with devotion into these four types of scriptures—
However, the entire limit is proclaimed by the name of the three scriptures.
But for those established in the fourth [state], it is partless (*niṣkala*) and devoid of parts (*kalavarjita*).
It exists within men in the Śaiva [tradition], and thus they are proclaimed as "Śaivas."
In the Pāśupata and other scriptures, they are likewise proclaimed by name;
in these three scriptures, the divisions are distinguished according to their respective paths.
Now, the divisions of Śaivism shall be explained in brief.
The scripture is to be known as fourfold: Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, and Miśraka.
Thus, that which is conjoined with the Siddhānta is proclaimed as the Fourth [Tantra].
Those who would administer initiation in due order according to the various divisions of the Vāmā and other scriptures—
The Vāmā, Dakṣiṇā, and Miśrī are proclaimed as the Siddhāntas.
The Vāmā consists of the Śāmbhava and Śākta [traditions], while the Dakṣiṇa is of the nature of Bhairava.
This Miśrī is said to be "yamabhu" (the abode of Yama), having the Seven Mothers as its primary element.
The Siddhānta is indeed pure Śaiva, as well as the exclusive Śāmbhava.
The Siddhānta is indeed remembered as the essence of all, pure in its reality and auspicious;
[as are] Vāma and Dakṣiṇa... ॥
They are declared to be outside of Śaivism, and they are not honored even within Śaivism.
By means of the divisions beginning with the *Kāmika*, there are twenty-eight compendia (*saṃhitās*).

...their final conclusion (*siddhānta*), along with its divisions and subdivisions, is called "Mixed" (*miśra*) and is ninefold, designated by the name "Earth" (*bhū*). There are indeed five Vāmācāryas, and likewise five in the Dakṣiṇa [tradition].
Thus, five teachers for each of the two [classes] combined have been prescribed.
Listen to the definition of the five mixed Śaiva systems according to our established tenet:
the Ācārya, the Sādhaka, the Samayin, and likewise the Putraka.
Known as Citrakeṭaka, he was honored in the sacrifices to the Mothers;
he was gradually initiated by means of the initiation known as Śuddhasiddhāntaśaiva.
He is remembered as the preceptor (*ācārya*) of the four classes beginning with the *sādhaka*, and [he is] your protector (*pā*).
The installation and worship of the Mothers, and the libation for them and for the Fire.
The master himself should perform the bathing festival, the propitiatory rites, and so forth;
the practitioner and others should carry out the rituals taught in those [tantras] in conjunction with him.
The elder brother of Śiva, having become twofold as Ācāha and the rest of the four,
is called Pāraśava, known by the name Citraketaka. Listen now to the origin of the mixed Śaivas in brief, exactly as it is.
The first is Anādiśeva, and the second is Mahāpa.
The first is the Ādiśaiva, the third is the Anuśaiva, and the fourth is the Anuśaivaka;
the fifth is the Antaraśaiva—thus the Śaivas are remembered as being of five kinds.

The capable one (*śakta*) and the one presiding over power (*adhiṣṭhita-śakti*), as well as *nāda* and *bindu*, are traditionally known [as the stages]. Sadāśiva and Īśvara—those who abide in these six locations—I am declared to be the beginningless Śaiva; therefore, listen to me, O Great Śaiva!
Likewise, the Great Lords of Mantra (Mantramaheśvaras), beginning with Ananta and ending with Śikhaṇḍin.
They are called the Mahāśaivas; now hear about the Ādiśaivas.
Among them reside those born from the principles beginning with Māyā and ending with the Earth.
These have been declared as the Ādiśaivas; now hear of the Anuśaivas:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the other gods, as well as the Daityas, Kiṃpuruṣas, sages, Siddhas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rakṣasas, Uragas, and so forth.
All the disciples of Śrīkaṇṭha, as well as the powers (śaktis) such as Umādevī and the others, [were present].
These are indeed remembered as followers of Śiva; now hear concerning the Yantaras. The four castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, originated from Kāśyapa and the others.

By the grace of the Supreme Lord, the qualified [officiants] have been appointed for the purpose of illuminating the Śiva-dharma and for the awakening of all. Through the performance of rites according to the prescribed rule, they carry out the installation, the sprinkling, and the initiation.
By Śiva, the Supreme Self, having assumed the forms of the sages.

And all those who have been favored there, being averse to worldly enjoyment, I offer along with their very bodies; whereas he who is dependent on enjoyments and takes up the means for them [offers] the kindling of his life-breaths to the limit of ten-fold [the five senses].
In this manner, the village headman, having gathered together, should give him half a field or a collection of useless things, or they should provide him with food in abundance.
Furthermore, what is the duty?
It is this: having surrendered one's entire self to the Lord, the Great Soul himself is beheld by the vision of knowledge (*jñānadṛṣṭi*).
One should not, however, remain attached to anything whatsoever, but abide according to the rule in the proper manner.
For those who have set out for what is wholesome, [this applies] even to themselves.
For one who thus bestows grace or causes it to be bestowed, impelled by Śiva—
it is impossible to describe the mass of merit he has acquired.
This much can be said: by [attaining] twenty-one generations of one's lineage, one may dwell in heaven with one's parents and go oneself to the state of Śiva.
In the *Somaśambhupaddhati*, the fivefold [mantras] beginning with Sadyojāta are [placed] upon the five excellent lotuses of five colors.
One should worship in due order for the sake of the vow-form (*vrata-mūrti*) of Śiva.

According to the number of limbs of the vow, one should sacrifice a hundred times a hundred oblations into the fire for a hundred days, using the Brahma-mantras or the limbs beginning with the Heart; at the end, [the rite is performed] when the fire has been nourished by the Vāsini.
Therefore, even his ascetic observances— his staff, ashes, and matted hair—
he should offer with devotion to Sadyojāta and the other [faces] in their proper sequence.
Then, having worshipped Caṇḍanātha and released the limbs of the vow,
the preceptor, having given a pair of new garments, should speak thus according to this rite while [the disciple] is being carried away in the flow of water.
And you shall marry a maiden who is both suitable and of noble birth.
"The abandonment of the vow by Śaivas occurs through such [means]," says the Teacher (*deśika*). In the *Suprabheda*:
"At the end, having performed the sacrifice to Vrateśvara, there is the release from that vow."
Listen now to the summary of the vow, the Lord of Vows, and the sacrifice, according to their true nature.
Having fashioned a square mandala and smeared it with cow dung, one should draw five lotuses there; in the center, a white lotus is prescribed.
The eastern lotus is yellow in color, while the southern one is black;
it is white in the western part and red in color in the north.
In the central lotus of Īśāna, as well as in the eastern lotus, there is Puruṣa.
One should worship Aghora in the southern lotus and Sadyojāta in the western lotus;
having thoroughly worshipped Vāmadeva in the northern lotus and Īśāna and the others,
one should, being well-composed, worship them with their respective mantras using perfumes and other offerings.
Having performed the recitation (*japa*) of that respective mantra one hundred or even fifty times,
and having paid homage to Vrateśvara, [one should perform] it again once the vow is fulfilled.
Having informed the Lord of the vow, one should dismiss him in the forenoon; then, having performed the ritual bathing especially for the God of gods,
one should bow to the Lord of Vows and, while observing the vow, cause the truth to be proclaimed.
Thus, one should indeed perform the worship of the Lord of Vows for the sake of the successful accomplishment of the vow.
In its absence, [worship] in water, a linga, or a tree... (incomplete, p. 112b, l. 1).
The determination of Śivarātri:
on the thirteenth day [the ground] has the form of a yoni (bhaga), and the fourteenth day has the form of a linga.
At the time of the conjunction of those two,
one should observe the Śivarātri vow when the sun is situated in Aquarius and the moon is in Scorpio;
the thirteenth lunar day is the form of Śivā, and the fourteenth is the form of Śiva.
"When the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight falls during the months of Kumbha or Phālguna, that night is Śivarātri; this was declared by Śiva in the Śiva-āgama.
It should be observed when the sun is in Aquarius (Kumbha), but it should not be observed when the sun is in Capricorn (Mṛga)."
If worship is performed through negligence, the king and his kingdom perish.
When the Lord of Day is situated in the pitcher [Aquarius] and the Moon is situated in the deer [Capricorn],
and it is the night of the fourteenth day— this was declared by Śiva in the Śiva-āgama.

Thus [ends] Śivarātri. ... O you whose radiance is like that of seven suns, protect me, protect me! O friend of the one with seven rays, protect me, protect me... [she] whose hair is bound in a topknot. [She who possesses] passion, the mountain beloved by her crown, the rhythm with its liquid measure. The instrumental music is played by the eloquent; the dance is the graceful movement of serpents. Thus, O Lord of Śaṅkarasena, what shall I do? Homage to Vāyu. Or one should cause it to be proclaimed with eighteen kinds of musical instruments. 7. Homage to the King of Kāśī, homage to the Lord of Wealth.

Salutations again and again to Kubera, the friend of the Supreme Lord; he whose mind requested the great celestial vehicle *puṣpaka* through compassion, who is the lord of the Śabara women, who maintains the protection of the Yakṣas and others by means of his treasures, and who is the crest-jewel upon the moon. I praise him, the source of beloved happiness, worthy of praise, the son of Pulastya, whose station is situated on the edge of the quarters of the sky—a wondrous being with a manifold refuge.

[He whose] power was renowned through his friendship with Śaṅkara, who is difficult even for the foremost gods such as Hari and Viriñca to behold; [he whose] footstool was worshipped by the entire multitude of deities led by the Lord of Treasures (Kubera); [he who took] delight in wandering through the regions of the famous and wondrous Caitraratha garden; [he who was] the very embodiment of praiseworthy majesty; [he who was] the abode of the best of men in Alakāvatī; [and he who was] the beloved of the heart of the Goddess Lakṣmī, who is intent on granting the prosperity of the entire world.

The beloved [Lord], whose neighing of his horse Mekhala is deep as a thundercloud, who obstructs [the world] with his mount, O Lord of the World; who is beautiful with hands joined in salutation to Śiva; whose hollowed palms produce the rhythmic *tāla* and the five-fold musical modes (*pañca-mukha-vādya*); whose voice is like the melody of the *mālava-giri-tarkarāga* during the twilight dance; Kubera, who protects the northern quarter by the command of the Supreme Lord; [he who is the destroyer of] Mahā... Prahallādana, Mucina, Narakavahnijihva, Kālaprahṛd, Śaṅkukarṇa, Śā...ri, Śiśupāla, and Dundubhi; [he who is the one] whose descent as Tāraka was severed... (Pañcākṣaravidhiḥ—
) Hereafter I shall explain the sequence of the five-syllable rite:
the syllable *na*, the syllable *ma*, the syllable *śi*, and the syllable *va*.
The syllable *ya* is declared to be the fifth [syllable] among the six syllables beginning with *praṇava*.
From the syllable, the *praṇava* is primary; it is devoid of blood and lacks vital breath.
Among all mantras, the *praṇava* is said to be the life-breath of mantras;
it is the name and form, the syllable *oṃ*, the imperishable and eternal.
The fifth [consonant] joined with the third vowel,
the final [consonant] of the labials joined with the pair [of vowels] and Smara, and the final [consonant] of the nasals— this is the excellent five-syllable [mantra].
The letter *na* is declared to be the threefold masculine gender,
while the letter *ya* is the neuter gender among the five syllables.
The letter *va* is the stationary, and likewise the letter *ya* is the moving;
the letter *na* is the *Ṛgveda*, and the letter *a* is the *Yajurveda*.
The syllable Śa is the Sāmaveda, and the syllable Va is the Atharva-śruti;
the syllable Ya is the Praṇava, which consists of all the Vedas.
The syllable Na is white in color, and the syllable Ma is red in color.
The letter ŚA is black in color, while the letter VA has the luster of saffron.
The letter YA is the color of crystal; it is the syllable of the eyelashes.
The letter NA is the eastern face, while the letter MA is the northern face.
The letter *a* is Aghora, the letter *śi* is Śikhaṇḍin, and likewise the letter *va* is Puruṣa;
the letter *ya* is Īśāna—thus the five-syllabled Liṅga comes to be.
The letter *na* is the form of earth; the letter *ma* is the form of water (*vāma*).
The letter *śi* is the form of fire, while the letter *va* is the form of wind.
The letter *ya* is the form of space, and the syllable *pakṣa* is Śiva.
The foundation is indeed the void itself, conjoined with the supreme power.
One should know that this place, associated with the Jagatī meter and the seer Bhāradvāja,
is situated at the summit and is celebrated as Īśāna.
This very syllable *yā*, which has the luster of crystal, is proclaimed;
the syllable *na* is the form of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), while the syllable *ma* is the form of persistence (*sthiti*).
The letter Śa is emanation, Sa is withdrawal, Va is invisibility, Ya is grace; this world consists of these five syllables.
In the syllable *na*, Brahmā is the presiding deity; in the syllable *ma*, Viṣṇu is the presiding deity;
in the syllable *śi*, Rudra is the presiding deity; and likewise, in the syllable *va*, Īśvara.
One should meditate upon Sadāśiva in the syllable *ya*, and in the remaining syllables as well.
In the syllable *na*, Vasiṣṭha is present along with the Śakti Sāvitrī;
in the syllable *ma*, the Vaiṣṇavī-Śakti and the sage Viśvāmitra likewise reside;
and in the syllable *śi*, the Icchā-Śakti and the sage Marīci are said to be located.
The power of enjoyment (*bhogaśakti*) is in the syllable *va*, and the seer (*ṛṣi*) is Kāśyapa; in the syllable *ya*, however, the power is Ambikā, and the seer is Bhāradvāja.
The Praṇava is the form of the self, with the Supreme Self as its presiding deity;
it is the abode consisting of Śiva, and indeed that which is to be grasped by the ear.
The syllable of the Praṇava is said to be conjoined with the awakening of that [Self].
That which is called the "liṅga" is composed of the syllable *ya*, endowed with *ra*, *ta*, and *ma*. This is declared to be the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
The syllable *va* is the stalk, while the syllable *śi* is the upper lotus; the syllable *ma* is said to be the throat.
The letter *na*, which is the lower lotus, is the syllable in the form of the *liṅga*.
O Six-faced One, listen to the fruit of the prescribed five-syllable rite,
which consists of five variations mixed with the *tāra* and *prasāda*.
The gross, the subtle, and the pure—listen now to the method of their utterance.
Then, "Oṃ namaśśivāya" becomes the five-syllabled mantra with the Tāra;
for example: Oṃ namaśśivāya.
Having first uttered the Praṇava, [one should utter] that which ends with *sa*, endowed with a long vowel;
[then] that which ends with *bindu*, joined with a mobile [consonant], and accompanied by *bindu* and *nāda*.

For example: *oṃ hāṃ hauṃ śivāya namaḥ*. This is the five-syllabled *prāsāda* mantra. One should recite *namaśśivāya śivāya namaḥ* according to the sequence. Thus, this consists of the gross and the subtle. "To Śiva, salutation; to the Auspicious One, salutation"—this is always said. For example: *śivāya namaśśivāya namaḥ*; this is the mixed five-syllabled mantra. The word *namaḥ* is the subtle [element]. The pure five-syllabled mantra should come first.

Having uttered the word *namaḥ*, [one says] "salutation to Śiva" (*śivāya namaḥ*). "Salutation to Śiva" (*namaśśivāya*) is the subtle five-syllabled mantra. "Salutation to Śiva" (*śivāya namaḥ*)—this is always the pure five-syllabled mantra. Regarding how "salutation to Śiva" (*śivāya namaḥ*) is the pure five-syllabled mantra: this pure five-syllabled mantra is the means for one’s own realization. Having meditated upon the Lord within that [mantra], according to the expression of the Lord (*pati*), the bonds (*pāśa*), and the bound souls (*paśu*): [one meditates on] Śiva as the Lord (*pati*), and within His bond (*pāśa*), the five-fold impurities (*mala*) and the individual souls (*aṇu*).
In the midst of that, one should perform the visualization of the self separately for the sake of seeing the Self;
first, however, the worship of the Brahmin in the Tāraprāsāda is prescribed.
For initiated Brahmins, this worship is especially distinguished at the beginning.
And the five-syllable mantra of the palace is said to be neither gross nor subtle.
For initiated Kṣatriyas, however, [the worship] and so forth is prescribed;
for initiated Vaiśyas, the "mixed five-syllabled" mantra is traditionally taught.
For yogis who possess knowledge, the subtle five-syllabled mantra is prescribed there;
for initiated Śūdras, the pure five-syllabled mantra is prescribed.
For those who have been initiated and for lifelong celibates, one should always practice the pure five-syllabled mantra;
likewise, one should practice it in the same manner for women and for Śūdras as well.
For the Brahmins who are foremost Śaivas, [the rite] is joined with nine or more water-pots;
others should mutter the five-syllabled mantra as previously stated for the Brahmins.
The procedure for the time of recitation and so forth shall be stated here;
it is the provider of the rules for the aforementioned letters and ritual actions.
It is taught here for Śaiva Brahmins who have been initiated.
At the time of recitation, [the mantra] is preceded by "namaḥ"; during worship, it ends with "namaḥ";
at the time of the fire-oblation (homa), it ends with "svāhā"; but in other cases, it follows the manner already described.

Now the procedure for initiated Śūdras is being stated: regarding recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), worship (*pūjā*), ritual performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), expiation (*niṣkṛti*), initiation (*dīkṣā*),
the final rites (*carameṣā*), ancestral offerings (*śrāddha*), and giving (*dāna*) at other times.
One should perform everything in this manner using that very mantra beginning with *namaḥ*.
Likewise, one should act in exactly the same way for women and Śūdras.
He who, abandoning the scriptural injunctions, acts according to his own whims—
"Having lived out one's life, one shall dwell in a terrible hell for three hundred kalpas.
Having thus reflected thoroughly, [one should recite] the great five-syllabled mantra.
The supreme guru should apply the great five-syllabled mantra, which destroys the five heinous sins, among the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas.
One should contemplate it with the mind and through speech, and one shall attain union with Śiva.
This syllable, though extremely small like the seed of a banyan tree, is indicated by the Vedas.
The greatness of the five-syllabled mantra cannot be fully described by me.
The word "namas" is indeed a prayer for life; "Śiva" is the word [for liberation].

The word *āya* expresses that ultimate reality; thus, the fourth case ending is used in the sense of being devoted to that goal. It has been said: "I am that Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, the indivisible syllable *Śi*, which is bliss. The syllable *Yī* is called *Śakti*. The syllable *Va* is *Amṛta*. They say the two syllables [Śi-va] are *Śiva*. (p. 118b, line 1) O Supreme Lord Paraśiva, O Parāpara, O Supreme Light, O Supreme Self, endowed with the lineage of the five sages!

To the grandson of the stainless Lord Nirañjana—who has a form transcending the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) consisting of phonemes, words, principles, mantras, worlds, and kalās, which arise from the lineage of Paraśiva; who is endowed with the fivefold cosmic acts known as creation, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, and grace; whose nature is both manifest (*sakala*) and unmanifest (*niṣkala*); who is born of the lineage of Paraśiva; who is the Lord renowned in the Siddhānta and presides over the Tantras; and who is the lover of the supreme Śakti, his primary consort, who possesses the eight sovereign powers beginning with *aṇiman*.

To the son of the stainless one—who is born of the lineage of Paraśiva, who is the agent of the creation, maintenance, destruction, concealment, and grace of all the worlds, who dwells in the lotus-heart of yogins, who is the beloved of the Goddess Ādiśakti, and who is the essence of the qualities of the three forms—to that excellent [son] born of the lineage of Paraśiva, the refuge of all the world, the bringer of happiness to all the world, the venerable Lord Śrī Hariprasādeśvara.

[The grandson] of Parañjyotiśarman—who is to be known through the Vedāntas within the solar orb; who is the progenitor of the names of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others; who dwells on Mount Kailāsa situated above the city of Vaikuṇṭha and all the worlds beginning with Bhūr; who belongs to the lineage of the Supreme Power (Paraśakti) endowed with the activity of the Supreme Power (Parā), the Higher Power (Parāparā), and the Lower Power (Aparā); and who is born of the lineage of the Supreme Power—[he was praised] by Sanaka and the others who dwell in Satyaloka, who are born of the lineage of the Supreme Power.

"O you who are served by celestial sages (*deva-ṛṣi*) and brahmin sages (*brahma-ṛṣi*), accept from me this maiden Girijā—the granddaughter of the four-faced Brahmaśarman, the lover of his beloved Sarasvatī, born of the Paraśakti lineage; and the daughter of the venerable Hivataśarman, the lover of his beloved Menakā, the sovereign lord of the eight mountain clans of Gandhamādana, also born of the Paraśakti lineage—she who embodies all auspiciousness and bestows complete sovereignty. I shall give her to Dharmavardhana.
